acarbose.notes: hepatotoxic is the non-obvious tag and I verified it before applying: acarbose causes dose-related serum transaminase elevation, with hepatic effects reported as more likely above 50mg three times daily — and this entry's medical dose row is 50-100mg 3x daily, so it sits at and above that threshold. Rare clinically apparent hepatitis (mostly Japanese and Spanish case series, with a documented case at 300mg/day for two months) and rare jaundice are reported; the historical recommendation was transaminase monitoring every 3 months in the first year. The longevity row at 25-50mg per meal is likely below the risk threshold, but the entry documents both. The entry's own monitoring line already lists liver enzymes, so the tag is consistent with it. hypoglycemic is applied even though the entry correctly says acarbose causes no hypoglycaemia as monotherapy — the tag covers potentiation, and acarbose meaningfully potentiates insulin and sulfonylureas. Critically, and this deserves to survive into whatever rule consumes the tag: hypoglycaemia occurring on acarbose MUST be treated with glucose/dextrose, NOT sucrose, table sugar, juice or most candy, because acarbose blocks the sucrase step that would liberate the glucose. That is a genuine emergency-management rule and it is exactly the kind of thing this tagging exists to surface, especially against insulin, which is in this same batch. absorption-sensitive is applied in an inverted sense that should be recorded: acarbose itself is barely absorbed (~1-2% systemic), so its own pharmacokinetics are not the issue — but its EFFECT is abolished by co-administered intestinal adsorbents (charcoal) and digestive enzyme preparations (pancreatin/amylase), it must be taken with the first bite of the meal or it does nothing, and it reduces absorption of some co-administered drugs including digoxin. If the tag is used strictly for 'this drug's own blood levels change', drop it and record the above instead. gastric-emptying-delaying applied with explicit uncertainty: the primary mechanism is brush-border alpha-glucosidase inhibition delaying carbohydrate DIGESTION, not gastric emptying per se, though acarbose does raise endogenous GLP-1, which slows emptying. I applied it under the asymmetry rule mainly because it produces the correct practical caution — additive GI burden and additive emptying delay when stacked with a GLP-1 agonist, which is a very likely combination in this app's user base. store=ok: FDA-approved drug, doses at or below label, entry is clinical in tone with no cycle or stack language, and the longevity claim is honestly sourced to the NIA ITP mouse data and honestly caveated.

ai1.notes: lipid-suppressing is the record's own con ('Negatively affects lipid profile') and is mechanistic — oestradiol suppression raises LDL and lowers HDL in men; at 1mg E3D this is clinically meaningful. neuropsychiatric covers the depression and mood effects of iatrogenic low E2, which the record explicitly warns about. teratogenic: anastrozole is contraindicated in pregnancy with embryotoxicity/pregnancy loss in animals. cyp3a4-substrate applied on a label-level interaction, not a theoretical one: rifampicin (strong 3A4 inducer) reduces anastrozole AUC by roughly 27%, so a 3A4-induction rule should fire. Anastrozole is also a weak in-vitro inhibitor of CYP1A2/2C8/9/3A4, but that is not considered clinically relevant at 1mg, so I did NOT apply cyp3a4-inhibitor. Deliberately NOT applied: hpta-suppressive — AIs do the opposite in men, raising LH/FSH and total T; tagging it would fire exactly the wrong rule. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: accelerated bone mineral density loss / osteoporosis risk from sustained low E2 is the main long-term harm of this compound in men and has no tag; arthralgia likewise. store=reframe: anastrozole is an approved drug, so this is a soft reframe, but the entry documents male off-label dosing (0.25-1mg E3D, not the approved 1mg daily for breast cancer) and sits in a class literally named 'Ancillaries — AIs and SERMs' next to PCT protocol content, which reads as steroid-cycle support. Ship it framed as clinician-supervised management of laboratory-confirmed elevated E2, with the ancillary/cycle positioning removed; the entry's existing 'lab-guided dosing ONLY — not prophylactic' warning is good and should stay.

akg2.notes: Note first: the id 'akg2' is wrong for this record — the compound is GlyNAC (glycine + N-acetylcysteine) and has nothing to do with alpha-ketoglutarate, which is the separate 'akglutarate' record in this same batch. This looks like a copy-paste id collision and should be corrected before ship, otherwise two unrelated compounds will collide in any id-keyed rule. Both components are OTC supplements, neither is scheduled. neuropsychiatric is inherited from the glycine component at the documented 5-10 g (and far more at the Baylor 1.33 g/kg protocol, which is ~100 g/day for an 80 kg adult) — same inhibitory-neurotransmitter and sedation reasoning as the standalone glycine-supp entry, and the two must be tagged consistently since a user could take both; NAC additionally has glutamatergic activity used in psychiatry. nitrate-contraindicated is applied deliberately but with a caveat the rule text must carry: NAC is not formally contraindicated with nitrates, but the NAC-plus-nitroglycerin interaction is well documented and clinically real — NAC potentiates nitrate-induced vasodilation, producing severe headache and hypotension. I chose to apply rather than merely note it because it is the only v1 slot that generates the nitrate warning, and a user on nitrates taking 1200-1800 mg NAC is the exact scenario the rule should catch; the tag name overstates the strength of the relationship, so v2 should offer a 'nitrate-potentiating' gradation. NOT tagged and recorded here: NAC can precipitate bronchospasm in asthmatics (no vocabulary slot); NAC at these doses is a mucolytic with GI intolerance; the entry's insulin-sensitivity improvement was judged below the hypoglycemic threshold since neither component causes hypoglycaemia. Store ok — both are supplement-shelf products described at supplement doses with no performance framing. One regulatory wrinkle worth recording: FDA has taken the position that NAC is excluded from the dietary supplement definition (prior drug approval) while exercising enforcement discretion, so NAC's US supplement status is contested rather than settled — this does not reach the bar for reframe, but if the store posture ever tightens, this is the record it would affect.

akglutarate.notes: Krebs-cycle intermediate sold as a supplement (calcium AKG for the longevity use, arginine AKG for the older bodybuilding use); not scheduled. No v1 tag applies. The only reported adverse effect at the documented 1-2 g calcium AKG or 3-6 g AAKG is dose-related GI discomfort, which has no vocabulary slot and does not meet the 'clinically meaningful' bar. The mTOR-inhibiting and AMPK-activating mechanisms the entry claims have no v1 tag; if the app later ships rapamycin, metformin or berberine, an 'mtor-modulating'/'ampk-activating' tag pair would be worth adding in v2 so additive-mechanism rules can fire — record this as the gap. One substantive caution the tags cannot carry: the entry itself flags that calcium AKG and arginine AKG are different products with different evidence, and the calcium salt contributes meaningful elemental calcium at 2 g/day, which matters for anyone already supplementing calcium. Store ok.

ala.notes: OTC supplement in the US (prescription/approved for diabetic neuropathy in Germany), not scheduled. hypoglycemic is explicit in the entry's own cons ('can cause hypoglycemia in diabetics') and is real at the documented 600-1200 mg/day insulin-sensitivity dose — this is the tag that must fire against insulin, sulfonylureas and GLP-1s. absorption-sensitive applied on two grounds: ALA's own bioavailability drops roughly a third when taken with food (hence the standard empty-stomach dosing), and as a dithiol chelator it binds di/trivalent cations, so iron, calcium, magnesium and zinc co-administration matters. Note the direction of the levothyroxine interaction in the cons is the reverse — ALA/chelators impair thyroid hormone absorption, so the 4-hour separation protects the thyroid med, not the ALA; v1 has no tag for 'impairs absorption of other drugs' and that is a v2 candidate. Not tagged: thiamine depletion at 1000mg+ (no vocabulary slot), heavy-metal chelation (no slot). Store ok — dietary supplement used within supplement-dose range, no performance framing.

amino1mq.notes: Small-molecule NNMT inhibitor — not a peptide, so no peptide tag; no v1 structural tag applies (an 'nad-pathway' or 'metabolic' tag would be the v2 candidate). hypoglycemic applied precautionarily, not from documented events: the compound's claimed mechanism is improved insulin sensitivity, and the app's own monitoring block asks for fasting glucose/insulin/HbA1c, so a user stacking this with insulin, a sulfonylurea, a GLP-1 or metformin is the scenario a rule should catch. No documented hypoglycaemia exists in the (entirely preclinical) literature — recorded as inference. No hepatic, cardiac or endocrine signal is characterised either way at 50-100mg/day oral; absence of evidence here is genuinely absence of data, not reassurance, and I have not manufactured tags to cover that. Store = reframe: 5-Amino-1MQ is not federally scheduled and is not an AAS/SARM, so exclude is too strong, but it is an unapproved investigational drug with zero human trials that this entry frames for 'body recomposition' with a concrete self-dosing row. Google Play's prohibition on promoting unapproved substances applies irrespective of legality. Ships once the dose row and the recomposition/longevity-protocol framing come out and it reads as a neutral preclinical-evidence reference.

anadrol.notes: DELIBERATELY NOT TAGGED aromatizing. Oxymetholone is a 2-hydroxymethylene DHT derivative and does not convert to estradiol; its oestrogenic effects come from direct agonism at the estrogen receptor by the parent molecule. This distinction is safety-relevant in the other direction from usual: if this were tagged aromatizing, any downstream rule would suggest an aromatase inhibitor, and AIs do not control oxymetholone gyno or bloat. Recorded here because the entry's own con line ('Estrogenic effects without aromatization') will otherwise look like a tagging miss. dht-derived applied on structure (2-hydroxymethylene-17alpha-methyl-DHT) even though it behaves oestrogenically. hepatotoxic is the strongest in this batch — Anadrol-50 carries a boxed warning for peliosis hepatis, hepatic adenoma/carcinoma; 50-100mg/day with 2-weekly LFTs as the entry itself specifies. hematocrit-raising is the compound's original therapeutic mechanism (anaemia), so this is a primary not incidental effect. nephrotoxic applied — high-dose oxymetholone is associated with FSGS/proteinuria and the entry already monitors kidney function. store=exclude: Schedule III. Oxymetholone IS an FDA-approved drug (Anadrol-50) for acquired aplastic anaemia and a reframe to that indication is theoretically constructible, but the approved indication is a haematology-supervised one that has no place in a consumer app and the entry as written is pure mass-phase performance content — exclude is the correct call.

andarine.notes: Non-steroidal arylpropionamide SARM, so no aas/17aa-oral/dht-derived — sarm is the only correct structural tag. hpta-suppressive and lipid-suppressing are documented in the entry itself (moderate suppression, PCT required, lipid panel monitored); HDL suppression is a consistent SARM class finding. hepatotoxic: applied. S-4 is not 17-alkylated, but SARM-associated drug-induced liver injury (cholestatic and hepatocellular) is well documented across the class in case series, and the entry's own monitoring block asks for liver function — a user reading this will be taking 50mg/day of an unregulated black-market product. hematocrit-raising and virilizing/teratogenic are AR-agonist class inferences (erythropoietic stimulation; virilization of women and of a female fetus); hematocrit is NOT in this entry's monitoring list, which I consider a gap in the source record rather than evidence of absence. NOT applied, deliberately: photosensitizing. Andarine's signature adverse effect — a yellow/green visual tint with impaired dark adaptation, from the nitro-aromatic moiety acting at the retina — is ocular, not cutaneous. Firing a photosensitizing rule would tell the user to avoid sunburn, which is the wrong warning entirely. v1 has no way to express a retinal/ocular toxicity and this is the clearest case in the batch for a v2 'ocular' tag; recorded here so it is not lost. dea = null: SARMs are unapproved drugs, not federally scheduled — different legal category, and worth stating in copy so users do not read 'unscheduled' as 'safe' or 'approved'. aa = null: no conventionally cited testosterone=100 assay figure exists for S-4. The commonly quoted figure is a tissue-selectivity ratio (roughly 3:1 muscle:prostate, AR Ki ~7.5nM, full agonist in muscle / partial agonist in prostate), which is not the same axis as the rodent A:A ratio and would be misleading if entered in that field. Store = exclude: unapproved drug, explicit cycle/PCT framing.

aod9604.notes: NOTE FOR THE PARENT: this record and 'hghfrag' are near-duplicates of the same molecule and should be deduplicated upstream. AOD-9604 is the hGH 176-191 C-terminal fragment with an added N-terminal tyrosine, and this entry's own aka field already lists 'HGH Frag 177-191' and 'HGH Fragment 176-191'. Two records for one compound will double-count in any interaction or total-load calculation. gh-axis applied, but with an explicit caveat: the defining claim for AOD-9604 is that it does NOT bind the GH receptor and does NOT raise IGF-1, which is the literal opposite of what gh-axis normally implies. I applied it anyway under the stated asymmetry — it is a GH-derived fragment, any rule keyed to the GH family should catch it, and the resulting false positive (an unnecessary IGF-1 check) is benign. But downstream rule authors must not infer IGF-1 elevation from this tag on this compound. Withheld hypoglycemic and any glucose tag: the evidence is that it is glucose-neutral, which is its selling point. No risk tag clears the bar; the honest caveat is not toxicity but efficacy — the Phase IIb obesity programme did not separate from placebo on weight loss, so the entry's 11-item pros list is substantially overclaimed and 'stimulates fat oxidation' should not survive a rewrite as a settled fact. The pros/cons arrays also contain internal duplicates ('Not FDA approved' twice, 'Results modest without diet' twice) and the doses array merges two different dosing schemes — data hygiene issue for the parent. dea=null, not federally scheduled. aa=null. store=reframe. Regulatory status checked this session and it is more favourable than the other peptides here: FDA placed AOD-9604 on Category 2 of the interim 503A bulks list in September 2023 but REMOVED it on 27 September 2024 after the nomination was withdrawn, and it is now pending PCAC review rather than barred from compounding. It also carries self-affirmed GRAS status as a food ingredient. Still unapproved as a drug, so it needs neutral framing and the efficacy claims trimmed, but exclude would be too strong.

ara290.notes: IMPORTANT NEGATIVE — record this so no rule or reviewer infers otherwise from the EPO lineage: ARA-290 (cibinetide) is an 11-amino-acid peptide derived from the helix B surface of erythropoietin and engineered specifically to activate the innate repair receptor WITHOUT the erythropoietic effect. It is NOT hematocrit-raising, and it is not a blood-doping agent. Anything that pattern-matches 'EPO' to haematocrit risk would be wrong here, which is the single most likely tagging error on this compound. No hepatic, renal, cardiac or endocrine tags apply. I considered immunosuppressive because the mechanism is anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory, and rejected it: the sarcoidosis and small-fibre-neuropathy trials showed anti-inflammatory benefit without an opportunistic-infection or immune-suppression signal, so this is not genuine uncertainty and the tag would be noise rather than caution. Store: reframe. No approval despite Phase II data, but the documented uses are neuropathic pain and small fibre neuropathy — clinical, not performance — and the entry's own cons concede body-composition data is limited. Ships as neutral reference stating investigational status.

argireline.notes: Structurally these are synthetic peptide analogues of the SNAP-25 N-terminus (acetyl hexapeptide-3 and acetyl octapeptide-3), so peptide is the only structural tag. NO risk tags applied, and that is a considered conclusion rather than an omission: applied topically these are cosmetic-grade ingredients with negligible transdermal penetration to the systemic compartment and a long consumer-safety record; the mechanism (competitive SNARE-complex destabilisation reducing acetylcholine vesicle fusion) is peripheral and these peptides do not cross the blood-brain barrier, so neuropsychiatric would be wrong. Not tagged neuropsychiatric, not tagged teratogenic (no data either way, but topical systemic exposure is negligible). If the SubQ route were the primary documented use I would want a local-neuromuscular-weakness caution, but v1 has no tag for that and the exposure is tiny. dea=null; not a controlled substance and not a drug at all in its normal form. store=reframe rather than ok, and this is the non-obvious call: as a topical cosmeceutical this ships without complaint — it is a cosmetic ingredient, which the policy treats like an OTC product. The problem is the single line 'SubQ (experimental): 50-100mcg'. That instructs injection of an unapproved, non-sterile-by-default cosmetic raw material at a dose the entry itself admits has 'very limited' data, which is promoting an unapproved drug use of a substance and is precisely what the Play policy targets. Delete that row and the entry is ok as written — this is a one-line edit, not a rewrite.

berberine.notes: This supplement is far more interaction-heavy than its OTC status suggests, and the entry under-warns badly. 'qt-prolonging' and 'cardiotoxic' verified rather than assumed: berberine inhibits hERG (IKr) both by direct block and by disrupting channel trafficking, and also inhibits KCNQ1/KCNE1 (IKs), markedly prolonging action potential duration in vitro; there is a published case of polymorphic VT with QTc 616ms and R-on-T preceding torsades in a berberine user, and reviews describe QT prolongation, bradycardia and hypotension. This is the single most important addition to this record — the entry's cons list mentions only GI upset and CYP3A4, and says nothing about the heart, so anyone stacking berberine with another QT-prolonging agent gets no warning at present. 'cyp3a4-inhibitor' — stated in the entry itself and well documented; berberine also inhibits CYP2D6, CYP2C9 and P-glycoprotein, which broadens the interaction surface well beyond 3A4 (statins, ciclosporin, and anything narrow-therapeutic-index). 'hypoglycemic' — glucose lowering is the intended effect, with additive risk on metformin, insulin, sulfonylureas or a GLP-1 agonist; the entry documents exactly that co-use in its 'Metabolic / GLP-1 support' row. 'warfarin-potentiating' — via CYP2C9 inhibition and plasma protein binding displacement; INR monitoring is warranted on starting or stopping. 'absorption-sensitive' — oral bioavailability is under 1% because of P-gp efflux and first-pass metabolism, so co-administered P-gp inhibitors, formulation and food materially change exposure; this cuts both ways, since a 'bioavailability-enhanced' product can deliver a much larger effective dose than the 500mg 3x/day row implies. 'gastric-emptying-delaying' applied with acknowledged uncertainty — constipation is a common dose-limiting effect and animal data show slowed emptying; relevant chiefly because of the documented GLP-1 co-administration. 'teratogenic' — berberine crosses the placenta, displaces bilirubin from albumin and is associated with kernicterus risk in neonates; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation, which the entry does not state anywhere and should. NOT tagged 'hepatotoxic' despite the entry's quarterly LFT monitoring row: berberine is not an established hepatotoxin, LiverTox does not implicate it meaningfully, and the isolated reports involve multi-ingredient products. Recording this as a considered exclusion rather than an oversight — the LFT monitoring is precautionary. STORE 'ok': legal OTC dietary supplement, not scheduled, described at supplement doses with no performance framing. The 'nature's Metformin' and 'comparable efficacy to Metformin' claims are drug-comparison marketing language that a reviewer may want softened on general accuracy grounds, but they are not a platform-policy problem.

boldenone.notes: Boldenone is 1-dehydrotestosterone — a testosterone derivative, so aas only: NOT 19-nor and NOT dht-derived, and no prolactin rule should fire. Not 17-alkylated, so no 17aa-oral and no hepatotoxic. hematocrit-raising is the defining risk of this compound and should be weighted above every other tag: the entry itself concedes it 'can raise hematocrit significantly' and asks for monthly hematocrit, haemoglobin and RBC count, and at the documented 300-600mg/week polycythaemia requiring therapeutic phlebotomy is a routine outcome. cardiotoxic is tagged largely as the consequence of that — hyperviscosity and thrombotic/embolic risk — layered on the usual AAS remodelling; bp-raising follows from the same mechanism. aromatizing: applied. The entry's framing of 'moderate/lower aromatization' is only half true — boldenone aromatizes at roughly half testosterone's rate but the 16-20 week cycles and 600mg doses documented here mean absolute estradiol exposure is not low, which the entry half-admits in 'estrogen can become issue at high doses'. hpta-suppressive: profound and slow to recover given the ~14-day half-life documented here. lipid-suppressing per class. neuropsychiatric: applied under the asymmetry rule — anxiety is boldenone's most consistently reported subjective effect, though the evidence is anecdotal rather than trial-derived. virilizing/teratogenic per androgen class. assay-interfering: boldenone is a single double bond away from testosterone, so cross-reactivity in testosterone immunoassays is highly likely (inferred by structural similarity, same mechanism verified for nandrolone) and this entry monitors testosterone — specify LC-MS/MS. warfarin-potentiating: androgen class effect. aa = [100, 50], conventionally cited rodent figure only. dea = 3 (Schedule III; note it is a veterinary-only product, never approved for humans anywhere, which strengthens the exclude call). Store = exclude.

bonomarlot.notes: Khavinson bone marrow bioregulator. `hematocrit-raising` applied deliberately and with the evidence caveat stated: the human data are weak single-group Russian literature, and the entry itself claims the effect is bidirectional ('relevant for anyone experiencing hematocrit issues on TRT (both too high and too low)') — direction is not established. But the claimed mechanism is stimulation of erythropoiesis, the app positions it explicitly for TRT users, and additive erythrocytosis on top of testosterone-driven polycythaemia is precisely the interaction a rule should catch. A false positive here costs a redundant CBC reminder; a false negative lets someone stack an erythropoietic claim onto an already-raised haematocrit. Tag applied. The record's own monitoring line (CBC, haematocrit, haemoglobin, platelets) already implies this. Note the bidirectional claim is not pharmacologically coherent and should be removed from the entry text. Sequence attribution (KEDP) is uncertain across sources, as with the rest of this series. dea null; aa null. STORE reframe: remove the TRT-adjunct framing and the Thymalin stack pairing, drop the dose row, state the evidence as unvalidated.

bpc.notes: Structurally just peptide — a synthetic pentadecapeptide, not a GH-axis agent despite the entry's claim of GH receptor upregulation (that is a downstream tissue effect in rodent models, not action on the GH/IGF-1 axis, and tagging gh-axis would wrongly pull it into GH interaction rules). No risk tag reaches the clinical-meaningfulness bar at 200-500mcg/day: the human adverse-event literature is essentially empty, and the entry's own cons are about evidence quality and sourcing rather than toxicity. Two things the vocabulary cannot express, recorded here for v2: (1) BPC-157 is strongly angiogenic via VEGFR2/eNOS, which is the basis of a theoretical concern about promoting growth of occult malignancy — there is no oncogenic-risk tag; (2) it is WADA-prohibited under S0 (non-approved substances) since January 2022, which matters for any athlete-facing feature — there is no wada-prohibited tag, and I'd argue for one. dea=null: not federally scheduled anywhere; note that 'not scheduled' is not 'legal to sell for human use' — FDA placed it on Category 2 of the interim 503A bulks list in 2023, barring it from compounding. store=reframe rather than exclude: the documented framing is therapeutic (tendon/ligament repair, IBD, gut barrier), not performance enhancement, and it is not a controlled substance, so Apple 1.4.3 does not bite. But it is an unapproved substance, so a store build needs neutral investigational framing — drop 'Gut Protocol' as a prescriptive protocol row, state plainly that human RCT evidence does not exist and that it cannot be legally compounded in the US.

bpc157sys.notes: Synthetic pentadecapeptide from gastric juice protein BPC. neuropsychiatric is applied on the entry's own claim rather than on a harm: the record asserts dopaminergic system modulation, mood/motivation effects and neuroprotection, and the rodent literature (counteraction of haloperidol-induced catalepsy, modulation of amphetamine and dopamine-antagonist responses, 5-HT system effects) supports CNS activity. Recorded uncertainty: this is animal-model pharmacology with essentially no human data, and the tag here is a CNS-activity flag driving a co-medication caution with dopaminergic and antipsychotic drugs, not a claim that BPC-157 causes psychiatric adverse effects. If the tag's downstream rule reads as 'this compound causes mood/CNS adverse effects', it is a false positive and should be dropped — flagging that ambiguity for v2, since the tag currently conflates 'is CNS-active' with 'has CNS side effects'. VOCABULARY GAP: the substantive theoretical concern with chronic systemic BPC-157 is VEGF-mediated angiogenesis and possible tumour promotion; no tag expresses proliferative/oncogenic risk, and the entry's 250mcg/day open-ended systemic protocol is exactly the use case where that would matter. No hepatic, renal, lipid, pressor, haematological or endocrine signal at documented doses. STORE reframe: BPC-157 has no marketing approval in any jurisdiction and FDA placed it on the Category 2 bulks list (Oct 2023) as presenting significant safety risks, so it cannot lawfully be compounded in the US — an app shipping a daily dosing protocol for it is promoting an unapproved substance under Play's rule 'irrespective of any claims of legality'. It is not exclude-level because the framing is therapeutic (gut healing, injury repair, anti-inflammatory) rather than performance-enhancing and there is a large, if preclinical, research literature; a neutral reference entry describing mechanism and the absence of human evidence is a different posture from a protocol table. Rewrite must delete the dose rows, state the Category 2 compounding restriction and the unapproved status, and state that no human efficacy trials support the systemic protocol. Note the record also conflates oral and SubQ routes, which have very different systemic exposure. Not scheduled.

caberbromo.notes: Ergoline (ergot-derived) D2 agonist; approved as Parlodel for hyperprolactinaemia, prolactinoma and acromegaly, and as Cycloset for type 2 diabetes. cardiotoxic APPLIED and this is the most under-appreciated risk in the entry: ergot-derived dopamine agonists cause fibrotic reactions — cardiac valvulopathy, plus pleural, pericardial and retroperitoneal fibrosis. Bromocriptine's valvulopathy risk is lower than pergolide's or cabergoline's and the evidence is weaker, but it is an ergot derivative and the class effect is established, so under the stated asymmetry rule it is tagged. The entry currently frames bromocriptine as simply the cheaper, slightly-more-nauseating cabergoline; it says nothing about fibrotic risk or the echocardiographic monitoring that long-term ergot agonist use warrants. serotonergic APPLIED because it is the mechanism of the above — agonism at 5-HT2B receptors on valve interstitial cells drives the fibrosis — and because it makes co-administration with other serotonergic agents an interaction worth flagging. neuropsychiatric applied for the dopamine agonist class signal: impulse control disorders (pathological gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive spending), somnolence and sleep attacks, hallucinations and psychosis, plus the common dizziness/fatigue the entry already lists. cyp3a4-substrate applied — labelled interaction; strong 3A4 inhibitors (azoles, clarithromycin, ritonavir, and relevantly grapefruit) raise exposure and toxicity. NOT TAGGED, recorded: (a) bromocriptine LOWERS prolactin — there is no prolactin-lowering tag and prolactin-raising would be inverted and dangerous, so this entry carries no prolactin tag at all despite prolactin being its entire purpose; recommend a `prolactin-lowering` tag for v2, since the pairing rule with the 19-nor compounds depends on it. (b) BP: the common effect is orthostatic HYPOtension (first-dose syncope, hence titration) — bp-raising would be wrong-signed and is not tagged; separately there is a rare but serious hypertension/seizure/stroke signal, historically in postpartum lactation suppression, which is why that indication was withdrawn, and the risk is amplified by concurrent sympathomimetics — relevant in this app, where clenbuterol/ephedrine/stimulant entries are likely neighbours. A `hypotensive` tag would cover the common case. (c) Take-with-food is a nausea-tolerability measure rather than a true absorption interaction, so absorption-sensitive is not tagged. store=reframe: approved prescription drug, not scheduled, but the entry is written as on-cycle prolactin management for trenbolone and nandrolone users. Reframe to the approved hyperprolactinaemia/prolactinoma indication under endocrinology supervision, drop the 19-nor cycle framing, and add the fibrosis and impulse-control warnings.

caberg.notes: Ergoline D2 agonist. 'cardiotoxic' is the headline tag: 5-HT2B-mediated fibrotic valvulopathy (and pleuropulmonary/retroperitoneal fibrosis) is a direct structural cardiac risk beyond BP. The entry correctly notes the risk is dose-dependent and concentrated at Parkinson's doses (3-5mg/day) rather than the 0.25-0.5mg twice-weekly documented here, but the tag is still warranted — the echocardiogram row in monitoring exists for exactly this reason. 'serotonergic' applied because the valvulopathy mechanism IS 5-HT2B receptor agonism; note this is receptor agonism at a specific subtype, not reuptake inhibition, so any rule consuming this tag should not treat cabergoline as a serotonin-syndrome contributor — it is not. Flagging that as a place the v1 tag is coarser than the pharmacology. 'neuropsychiatric' for dopamine-agonist impulse-control disorders (pathological gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping — a class effect that is under-warned in this entry and appears nowhere in its cons), plus psychosis/hallucinations, somnolence and sleep attacks. 'cyp3a4-substrate' applied after checking: cabergoline is cleared predominantly by non-enzymatic hydrolysis of the acylurea bond and CYP-mediated metabolism is minor, BUT grapefruit juice raises exposure ~1.7x and clarithromycin ~2.7x (combined 3A4 and P-gp inhibition), which is a clinically meaningful interaction at a compound with a 65h half-life. NOT tagged 'bp-raising' — cabergoline causes orthostatic hypotension, the opposite direction; v1 has no 'bp-lowering' tag, so this belongs in notes and matters for anyone stacking it with a PDE5 inhibitor or an antihypertensive. NOT 'qt-prolonging' (not on CredibleMeds). NOT 'teratogenic' (pregnancy category B; it is in fact used to restore fertility in hyperprolactinaemic women). STORE: FDA-approved for hyperprolactinaemic disorders and prolactinoma, so it ships — but the current entry's whole framing is 'essential when using progestogenic compounds such as Nandrolone, Trenbolone, or high-dose HCG', i.e. it exists to support an AAS cycle. That AAS/HCG-stack framing must be stripped and the indication restated as physician-diagnosed hyperprolactinaemia confirmed on labs; hence 'reframe' rather than 'ok'.

cagrilintide.notes: IMPORTANT NEGATIVE: `glp1` deliberately NOT applied. Cagrilintide is a long-acting amylin (and calcitonin receptor) analogue — a distinct receptor family from GLP-1/GIP. Tagging it glp1 would be factually wrong and would actively misfire any duplicate-incretin rule, e.g. suppressing a legitimate warning or falsely flagging redundancy. The clinically important point is the opposite one: because the mechanism is complementary, it IS co-administered with a GLP-1 (CagriSema = cagrilintide + semaglutide), so GI, renal and satiety effects stack rather than duplicate. If the rule engine needs to know 'behaves like a GLP-1 for interaction purposes', that needs its own tag (`amylin-analogue` or `incretin-adjacent`) in v2 rather than misuse of glp1. `gastric-emptying-delaying` is a core amylin action and is well established. `hypoglycemic` applied on the class precedent — pramlintide carries a boxed warning for severe insulin-associated hypoglycaemia requiring pre-emptive insulin dose reduction; cagrilintide has not shown this as monotherapy, but the mechanism and the co-administration pattern justify the tag. `insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue` NOT applied: amylin is co-secreted with insulin but does not drive insulin secretion — it suppresses post-meal glucagon and slows nutrient delivery. `nephrotoxic` for the same volume-depletion AKI pathway as the GLP-1s, given nausea/vomiting rates at 2.4mg/week; applied for consistency with retatrutide since the mechanism is identical. `neuropsychiatric` precautionary for weight-management mood monitoring, same caveat as retatrutide — no causal signal established. dea null; aa null. STORE reframe: verified unapproved — Novo Nordisk submitted the CagriSema NDA in December 2025 and no FDA decision had been announced as of this tagging; cagrilintide as a standalone agent is not approved anywhere. Remove the 0.5-2.4mg/week dose rows and the 'Muscle preservation still requires testosterone support' con, which is anabolic stack language identical to retatrutide's. Note for whoever does the rewrite: if CagriSema is approved before the store build, the combination becomes describable as an approved product for its approved indication, but standalone cagrilintide dosing still would not be.

card.notes: STRUCTURAL CORRECTION: do NOT apply the sarm tag. Cardarine is a PPARdelta agonist with no androgen receptor activity - the record's cls field says 'SARMs' and the summary itself concedes it is not one. Tagging it sarm would wrongly pull it into every AR-based suppression, PCT and virilization rule, so the class field is wrong and the tag set must not follow it. Correspondingly: no hpta-suppressive, no virilizing, no aas. VOCABULARY GAP - THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE: the defining risk of GW-501516 is that GSK terminated development after 2-year rodent studies produced rapid multi-tissue carcinogenesis (liver, bladder, stomach, thyroid, skin and others) at multiple dose levels. v1 has no tag that can express carcinogenicity, so the single most safety-relevant property of this compound is currently unrepresentable in the tag system. Requesting `carcinogenic` for v2 - it would also apply to IGF-1 LR3 (mitogen) and arguably dihexa. hepatotoxic applied under the uncertainty rule and is a partial proxy only: it is driven by hepatic tumour findings in the rodent carcinogenicity work plus the entry's own liver-enzyme monitoring line, not by documented transaminase elevation in humans. Do not let the presence of hepatotoxic imply the carcinogenicity concern is captured - it is not. No lipid tag: Cardarine improves HDL, and the vocabulary has no lipid-improving tag (also worth noting for v2, since a lipid rule that only knows about suppression will mis-handle this compound). store=exclude, and this is the least debatable exclusion in the batch: no approval anywhere, development abandoned for carcinogenicity, WADA-prohibited, and the entry still ships a dose row ('If used, with full awareness of risks: 10-20mg/day'). A dosing protocol for a compound withdrawn for causing cancer is promotion of an unapproved substance under Google Play's rule and cannot be reframed - there is no supervised medical use to reframe toward.

cardiogen.notes: Khavinson short-peptide bioregulator. No risk tag clears the clinical-meaningfulness bar: there is no human PK, no toxicology, and no reported organ toxicity at 10mg/day; short peptides of this class are hydrolysed to constituent amino acids. Deliberately not tagged cardiotoxic — the claim is cardioprotection, and there is no evidence of arrhythmia or hypertrophy risk in either direction. DATA ERROR: the record gives the sequence as Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp (KEDW); published Cardiogen is the tetrapeptide Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg (AEDR). Worth fixing — several entries in this Khavinson group have swapped sequences (see chonluten, sigumir). dea null; aa null (not an androgen). STORE reframe: the framing is longevity rather than performance so it is not exclude-grade, but the injectable form has no approval in any jurisdiction and the record presents a dose row ('Cardiac / Longevity: 10mg/day'), which reads as a protocol for an unapproved substance. Reframe to a neutral evidence summary — Russian-only literature, single research group, no Western validation — without the dose row, and soften 'Validated Khavinson research series', which overstates the evidence.

cerebrolysin.notes: A porcine-brain-derived low-molecular-weight peptide and amino acid mixture, so peptide is structural — with the caveat that unlike everything else tagged peptide in this batch it is a biological extract of variable composition, not a defined synthetic sequence, so batch-to-batch consistency and the source country are themselves safety variables. neuropsychiatric is the substantive tag and I verified the basis: the manufacturer's contraindications include epilepsy and status epilepticus, on the grounds that Cerebrolysin can lower seizure threshold and rapid infusion may increase seizure frequency — anyone with a seizure history, or on any other threshold-lowering agent, must not use it. Reported adverse effects also include agitation, dizziness, vertigo and insomnia, particularly with fast administration. NOT tagged nephrotoxic despite severe renal impairment being a listed contraindication: that is a clearance concern for the peptide fragments, not evidence that the drug injures the kidney, and tagging it would misdirect the rule. Also unexpressible in v1 and important: rare anaphylactoid/hypersensitivity reactions to a xenogeneic porcine protein — the entry's test-dose recommendation is correct and should be kept — and the theoretical transmissible-spongiform-encephalopathy consideration inherent to any porcine CNS-derived product. dea=null; not scheduled anywhere, it simply is not approved in the US. store=reframe, not exclude: this is a genuinely approved drug in 50+ countries with a large trial literature in stroke, TBI and vascular dementia, so excluding it would remove real clinical reference information. But two specific things must go before it ships. First, the 'Cognitive Enhancement: 5-10ml' and 'Micro-dosing: 1-2ml' rows prescribe IV/IM injection to healthy people for an indication no regulator has approved. Second, the con line advising users to 'source from countries where it's approved' is, read plainly, instruction on importing an unapproved injectable drug into the US — that is the clearest policy violation in this batch and it is a single sentence. Restate the entry around the approved neurological indications under physician administration, drop the nootropic dose rows and the sourcing advice, and it is fine.

chonluten.notes: Khavinson bronchial/lung bioregulator. No risk tags meet the bar — no human toxicology and no plausible systemic burden at 10mg/day. DATA ERROR: the record lists Lys-Glu-Asp, which is Ventfort's sequence; published Chonluten is the tripeptide Glu-Asp-Gly (EDG). dea null; aa null. STORE reframe: the framing is clinical rather than performance, but two things must change before it ships. First, the post-COVID lung recovery claim is an unsupported therapeutic claim for a respiratory condition attached to an unapproved injectable — that is the highest-risk sentence in this entire batch from a store-review standpoint, higher than the dose rows, and it should be deleted rather than softened. Second, remove the 10mg/day dose row. Also worth flagging in the rewrite: targeting smokers and people with chronic respiratory disease positions an unvalidated product at a population with a real treatable disease.

cjc.notes: CJC-1295 without DAC (mod GRF 1-29) is a GHRH analogue — peptide plus gh-axis, the latter being the tag that should drive IGF-1 monitoring and any rule about combining it with other GH secretagogues or exogenous GH. The entry's own monitoring line (IGF-1 q3mo, fasting glucose) confirms the axis is genuinely engaged. Considered and withheld: bp-raising — GH-mediated sodium and water retention is real and the entry lists bloating and carpal tunnel, but at 100-200mcg producing near-physiologic pulses I do not think a clinically meaningful BP rise is established, so it fails the 'clinically meaningful at documented doses' gate; recording the uncertainty here rather than tagging. Also withheld: electrolyte-disturbing (sodium retention without a real derangement) and hypoglycemic — note the direction is the OPPOSITE, GH axis stimulation causes insulin resistance and can RAISE fasting glucose, and the vocabulary has no hyperglycemic/insulin-resistance tag. That is a genuine gap, because it is the reason the app monitors fasting glucose; flagging for v2. dea=null, not federally scheduled. aa=null. store=reframe: the compound class has legitimate clinical standing (tesamorelin, a GHRH analogue, is FDA-approved), but CJC-1295 itself is unapproved and the entry is written as a stack — 'Starting: 100mcg CJC + 100mcg Ipa' is literally a combination protocol row, which is the specific pattern the Play rule distinguishes from neutral reference. Those rows must become a neutral pharmacology description before it ships.

clom.notes: cyp3a4-substrate verified: clomiphene citrate is an isomer mixture — the E (en-) isomer is cleared primarily by CYP2D6 with CYP3A4 secondary, while the Z (zu-) isomer is metabolised by CYP3A4/3A5. Since the marketed drug contains both, 3A4 is a genuine clearance route. (v2 needs `cyp2d6-substrate`; 2D6 poor-metaboliser status is a documented driver of variable clomiphene response.) neuropsychiatric is well supported and is the record's own lead con — the mood disturbance is attributed to the long-half-life zuclomiphene isomer, which accumulates over weeks. teratogenic: contraindicated in pregnancy (historically category X); note the nuance that it is deliberately given to conceive, so the rule should be 'stop before conception occurs', not 'never in someone who may become pregnant'. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: the visual disturbances (scintillating scotomata, blurring — occasionally persistent) are clomiphene's most distinctive AE and have no tag; also untagged are ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and multiple gestation in female use, and VTE risk shared with the SERM class. Did not apply hepatotoxic or qt-prolonging — neither is established for clomiphene at these doses. store=reframe: approved drug, but approved only for ovulation induction in anovulatory women, whereas this entry is entirely male PCT/HPTA-restart framing. Ship it stating the approved female indication plus the recognised off-label clinician-supervised use in male secondary hypogonadism, with the 'PCT: 50mg/day wks 1-2...' cycle scheduling removed.

collagen-pep.notes: Hydrolysed collagen is a mixture of short peptides (glycine/proline/hydroxyproline-rich), so peptide is correct structurally, though it is functionally a food protein rather than a bioactive peptide drug and any rule that treats 'peptide' as implying injection or prescription status should not fire here — the route is oral and the material is food. NO risk tags, and none are warranted: this is dietary protein at 10-40g/day, the tolerability profile is that of any protein powder, and there is no established hepatic, renal, cardiovascular, endocrine or CNS signal. The only things worth recording, none of which v1 can express: it is not a complete protein (no tryptophan) so it should not displace total protein intake in someone lean-bulking; the glycine load at 20-40g/day is pharmacologically non-trivial and can be mildly sedating; there is a theoretical caution in advanced kidney disease from the total nitrogen and hydroxyproline load (hydroxyproline is an oxalate precursor, so very high chronic intake is a minor consideration for calcium-oxalate stone formers); and marine-sourced product is a fish/shellfish allergen. dea=null, aa=null. store=ok: dietary supplement, no drug claim, no performance dose framing, RCT-supported cosmetic and joint claims stated with appropriate modesty.

cortagen.notes: Khavinson tetrapeptide Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro. No risk tags. Specifically NOT cardiotoxic despite being a cardiac-targeted compound — the documented direction is cardioprotective (reduced ischaemia-reperfusion damage, improved HRV), and cardiotoxic denotes harm; tagging it would invert the meaning. No electrolyte, QT or BP signal reported at 10mg. Store: reframe, same reasoning as the rest of the Khavinson series — unapproved investigational peptide, no performance framing, research base essentially confined to Russian literature. One thing worth flagging to the entry author independent of tagging: the monitoring row asks for BNP and a lipid panel, which implies a cardiac-patient population, and cardiac patients are exactly the group for whom an unapproved injectable substituting for guideline therapy is most dangerous. The reframed text should say explicitly that this is not a substitute for evidence-based cardiovascular care.

creatine.notes: Dietary supplement, not scheduled, the best-characterised safety profile in the batch. assay-interfering is applied with an explicit caveat about its meaning: creatine does NOT interfere with an immunoassay in the biotin sense. It raises measured serum creatinine because supplemental creatine is non-enzymatically converted to creatinine — the elevation is genuine analyte, not analytical artefact — which then propagates into a falsely low calculated eGFR and can trigger a spurious CKD workup. I used the tag because it is the only v1 slot that will make a downstream rule say 'this compound will distort your labs, tell the lab you take it', which is exactly the caution the entry's own monitoring text asks for; a v2 vocabulary should split 'assay interference' from 'shifts a real analyte'. neuropsychiatric is the marginal call in this record: creatine's documented CNS effects at the standard 3-5 g/day are mostly benefit-side (working memory, cognitive fatigue, neuroprotection), but there is a genuine, repeatedly reported signal of treatment-emergent hypomania/mania when creatine is added in bipolar depression, so the tag is applied under the stated asymmetry and should be scoped in the rule to psychiatric-history users rather than surfaced to everyone. Explicitly NOT tagged nephrotoxic: no evidence of renal harm in healthy individuals, and tagging it would compound the very creatinine misreading described above. Store ok.

crystagen.notes: Khavinson lymphocyte bioregulator. `immunosuppressive` deliberately NOT applied — the claimed direction is immunostimulation (lymphocyte activation, T-helper enhancement), and applying the tag would fire an infection-risk warning that is the opposite of the compound's claimed action. This is the one place in the batch where the apply-when-uncertain rule should not be read as 'apply anyway': the tag is directional, and a wrong-direction tag is a misinformation, not a caution. VOCABULARY GAP: the entry's own con — theoretical autoimmune caution in people with existing autoimmune disease — is a genuine clinically relevant property with no tag to carry it. Recommend an `immunostimulant` tag (or an `autoimmune-caution` tag) in v2; it would also serve Thymalin and Thymosin alpha-1. Until then the caution survives only in prose, which no rule engine can consume — worth flagging to whoever owns the interaction rules. No other risk tags at 10mg/day. dea null; aa null. STORE reframe: longevity/immune framing, no performance language, but unapproved injectable with a dose row; remove the row and the Thymalin complementarity pairing, and keep the autoimmune caution prominent in the rewritten text since no tag will carry it.

dac.notes: Long-acting GHRH(1-29) analogue with albumin-binding maleimidoproprionic acid (DAC), half-life 6-8 days — the record's 168h value is right. gh-axis is definitional. bp-raising is the judgement call: applied for GH/IGF-1-mediated sodium and fluid retention, which the entry itself flags ('may cause more water retention than pulsatile version') and which the non-pulsatile 'GH bleed' pharmacology makes worse than with short-acting secretagogues; sustained supraphysiological GH exposure raises BP, and the app documents 1-2mg doses, so this is meaningful rather than theoretical. Recorded uncertainty: the effect is mild-to-moderate and fluid-driven, not a direct pressor action. VOCABULARY GAP worth raising for v2: the real metabolic risk of sustained GH elevation is insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia — the app's own monitoring line asks for fasting glucose — but the closest tags run the wrong way (hypoglycemic is the opposite effect; insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue does not describe GH). I deliberately did NOT apply either, because a false 'hypoglycaemia' flag would be actively misleading rather than merely over-cautious, which is the one case where the asymmetry rule should not apply. A 'hyperglycemic'/'insulin-resistance-inducing' tag is needed. Second gap: IGF-1-mediated proliferative/tumour-promotion concern with chronic use has no tag. Also unflagged for want of a tag: arthralgia, carpal tunnel, oedema, and tachyphylaxis. STORE exclude, and this is the non-obvious call in the batch. Regulatory position checked: CJC-1295 was on FDA's Category 2 (significant safety risk) 503A bulks list from Oct 2023 and was removed in Sept 2024 only because the nominator withdrew the nomination — removal reflects an abandoned nomination, not a safety clearance, so it remains an unapproved drug with no lawful compounded supply route and no approved indication anywhere (tesamorelin is the only approved GHRH analogue and is a different molecule with an HIV-lipodystrophy indication). Unlike BPC-157/TB-500/KPV in this batch, there is no quasi-therapeutic framing to preserve: the documented purpose is GH/IGF-1 elevation for body composition and anti-aging, and the entry carries an explicit stack row ('CJC DAC 1mg + Ipamorelin 200mcg'), which is precisely the protocol-table-with-stack-suggestions posture Play's unapproved-substance rule targets, plus it is a WADA S2 prohibited substance. If store policy is more permissive than my read and GH-axis peptides are retained as a class, the minimum acceptable alternative is a full reframe: all dose and stack rows deleted, described purely as an investigational GHRH analogue benchmarked against tesamorelin. Not scheduled; no anabolic ratio applies.

dasatinib.notes: FDA-approved BCR-ABL/Src tyrosine kinase inhibitor (Sprycel) for Ph+ CML and Ph+ ALL. Every tag here is label-verified. cyp3a4-substrate: dasatinib is primarily cleared by CYP3A4, so strong inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin, grapefruit, ritonavir) markedly raise exposure and strong inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, St John's wort) markedly lower it — this is the single most consequential interaction tag on the record, and it also means the compound interacts with the two flavonoid senolytics it is co-dosed with in the D+Q protocol, since both fisetin and quercetin are CYP3A4 inhibitors. That interaction is intrinsic to the protocol the entry documents and should be surfaced in the entry text. cyp3a4-inhibitor: dasatinib is itself a time-dependent (mechanism-based) inhibitor of CYP3A4 and can raise exposure of narrow-index 3A4 substrates such as simvastatin — bidirectional, and easy to miss. absorption-sensitive: absorption is strongly pH-dependent; the label directs that H2 antagonists and PPIs NOT be co-administered, with antacids separated in time as the alternative. qt-prolonging and cardiotoxic are both label Warnings and Precautions — QT prolongation, plus cardiac dysfunction/heart failure and post-marketing pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH is why I applied cardiotoxic rather than bp-raising; the pressure effect is pulmonary, not systemic). immunosuppressive for myelosuppression — severe neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and anaemia are the dose-limiting toxicities and drive the CBC monitoring the entry requires. hepatotoxic for transaminase and bilirubin elevations, consistent with the entry's own liver-enzyme monitoring. teratogenic: the label states dasatinib can cause fetal harm, with embryo-fetal toxicity and skeletal malformations in animals, and requires effective contraception — non-negotiable given the longevity use case reaches women of childbearing age who are not oncology patients. warfarin-potentiating: applied for bleeding risk rather than a pharmacokinetic mechanism (dasatinib does not inhibit CYP2C9) — it causes platelet dysfunction independent of thrombocytopenia and the label warns about severe haemorrhage with concomitant anticoagulants or antiplatelets. Considered and not applied: electrolyte-disturbing (hypophosphataemia and hypocalcaemia occur but are secondary and modest), nephrotoxic (not a characteristic toxicity), and fluid retention/pleural effusion, which is a very common and clinically important dasatinib toxicity with no v1 tag — flagging that gap, since pleural effusion is the adverse event most likely to surface in intermittent low-dose use. Caveat on dose-dependence: the 100mg x 2-3 days pulse is far below cumulative oncology exposure and most of these toxicities are exposure-dependent, so several tags are conservative at the documented dose — but the interaction tags (3A4 both directions, PPI, anticoagulant) apply fully even to a single pulse, and teratogenicity does not become safe at low dose. STORE reframe, not ok: this is an approved drug but the entry documents an off-label anti-aging indication that FDA has not approved, for a cytotoxic kinase inhibitor, aimed at healthy users. Not prohibited outright by Play or Apple (it is neither an unapproved substance nor an illegal drug), so exclude is wrong, but 'D+Q Longevity protocol: 100mg/day for 2-3 days' presented as a self-administration dose row is the problem. Rewrite to lead with the approved oncology indication, present senolytic use strictly as investigational and trial-context (Mayo IPF and diabetic-kidney-disease pilots were small, open-label, surrogate-endpoint studies — the entry overstates 'improved physical function and frailty measures'), and make prescription-only status and physician supervision structural rather than a cons bullet. Not a controlled substance — prescription-only is a different thing from scheduled, so dea is null. Anabolic ratio not applicable.

dhea.notes: Deliberately NOT tagged 'aas', and this is the tagging decision in this batch most worth a second opinion. DHEA is an endogenous adrenal androgen PRECURSOR, not an anabolic-androgenic steroid: it is statutorily and explicitly excluded from the Anabolic Steroid Control Act's definition of anabolic steroid, is a lawful DSHEA dietary supplement in the US, and is not Schedule III (hence dea=null, which is a real exemption rather than an oversight). Tagging 'aas' would misfire the Schedule III default and the store-exclusion filter on a legal OTC supplement. Its androgenic character is captured instead by 'virilizing' and 'aromatizing'. Note for completeness that WADA does prohibit DHEA as an anabolic agent, and that it is prescription-only in several countries (UK, Canada, Australia) — so 'ok' is a US-market call. 'aromatizing' — DHEA converts through androstenedione to oestrone and oestradiol, and this is quantitatively significant in older men and in postmenopausal women where peripheral aromatisation is the dominant fate; the app's own monitoring row tracks E2 for this reason. 'virilizing' — acne, oily skin, hirsutism and scalp hair thinning are the commonest reported effects in women, and the documented women's row goes to 25mg/day, well above the 10-25mg typically studied. 'lipid-suppressing' — DHEA lowers HDL-C, an effect most consistently demonstrated in women; the monitoring row already includes a lipid panel. 'neuropsychiatric' — mood elevation is the intended effect, but irritability, agitation and case-report mania/hypomania are the flip side. NOT tagged 'hpta-suppressive': at 25-50mg/day in men, controlled data show little or no change in LH, FSH or total testosterone; the feedback suppression the entry's cons refer to is of endogenous adrenal DHEA-S output, which is not the gonadal axis. Recording that at doses well above those documented here, oestrogenic feedback could suppress LH — if the app ever adds a higher dose row, revisit this. NOT 'hepatotoxic' (not 17α-alkylated). Prostate/PSA concern in men has no v1 tag but is in the monitoring row. STORE 'ok': legal OTC supplement in the US described at supplement doses for a supplement indication.

dianabol.notes: 17alpha-methyl-delta1-testosterone: testosterone-derived, NOT DHT-derived, so no dht-derived tag. 17aa-oral applied — this is the hepatotoxicity driver (cholestatic jaundice, peliosis hepatis on prolonged use) and at the documented 20-50mg/day it is clinically meaningful. Aromatizing applied: it converts via aromatase to 17alpha-methylestradiol, a more potent and non-degradable estrogen than estradiol itself, which is why the water retention/gyno is disproportionate to the aromatization rate. cardiotoxic applied for the AAS class LVH/ischaemic signal at supraphysiologic dosing, separate from the explicit BP effect the entry already documents. warfarin-potentiating is a labelled class interaction for AAS and is strongest with 17aa orals — INR can rise sharply. teratogenic applied on androgen-induced virilization of a female fetus (established, pregnancy-contraindicated); the entry has no female framing but women do use this. Considered electrolyte-disturbing for the sodium/water retention and left it off — the intent of that tag reads as K/Mg disturbance; recording here that androgen-driven sodium and water retention is the mechanism behind the BP rise. store=exclude: Schedule III AAS, never an approved product for this indication, entry is entirely performance-framed with cycle-kickstart language. No reframe path.

dihexa.notes: peptide: dihexa is a synthetic angiotensin-IV-derived oligopeptide (N-hexanoic-Tyr-Ile-(6)-aminohexanoic amide). neuropsychiatric applied under the uncertainty rule - this compound's entire purpose is CNS activity (synaptogenesis via HGF/c-Met), human data is essentially absent, and 'other CNS effects' at unknown doses is exactly the case the tag exists for. Third instance of the carcinogenicity gap: HGF/c-Met agonism is a well-recognised oncogenic signalling axis and the entry itself flags 'synaptogenesis could promote certain tumor growth'; v1 cannot express this. DATA GAPS in the record: medium is null and halfLifeHours is null, yet a dose row ('Research dose: 1-10mg') exists - a dose with no route and no interval is not actionable and should not ship in any build. CONTENT FLAG: '10 million times more potent than BDNF' is an in-vitro potency comparison from the original preclinical work and reads as an efficacy claim in the pros list; it should not ship as written. store=exclude, and I want to be explicit about why this is exclude rather than reframe, since dihexa has no performance framing and does have a legitimate academic origin (Harding, WSU). The reframe path requires an approved or clinically-supervised indication to state instead. Dihexa has none - it has never entered human trials, has no established human safety data, and is sold only as a grey-market research chemical. Stripping the dose row would leave nothing but an unapproved-compound description attached to a dosing UI, and shipping a dosing row for a c-Met agonist with zero human data is promotion of an unapproved substance under Google Play's rule. Exclude.

dsip.notes: Nonapeptide, no approval in any jurisdiction, not federally scheduled — an unapproved drug, which is not the same as a controlled substance. neuropsychiatric is the core pharmacology, not a side effect: slow-wave sleep architecture change, reduced sleep latency, sedation, and the vivid dreams the entry lists; it should fire against other sedative-hypnotics and against the GHRP timing issue the summary mentions. CHECKED AND REJECTED gh-axis: rat work shows DSIP raising GH and inhibiting somatostatin via a dopaminergic mechanism, and raising LH via a hypothalamic site, but the human study in normal women found no effect on basal GH, on the GH circadian rhythm, on arginine-stimulated GH, or on prolactin — so the endocrine claims do not survive translation and I did not tag gh-axis, prolactin-raising or hpta-suppressive. The cortisol/ACTH modulation the entry claims has no v1 tag (HPA-axis effects are unrepresented; v2 candidate). Store reframe rather than exclude: DSIP has a genuine 1974-onward clinical research literature with human sleep trials, its documented use here is sleep and stress rather than performance enhancement, and it is not scheduled — so it fits the vocabulary's 'research peptide with legitimate clinical literature and no performance framing' path. It must lose the peptide-clinic/TRT-protocol framing and be stated plainly as investigational with no approved use and no large-scale human safety data.

dutast.notes: Two drugs in one record (finasteride Type II ~70% DHT reduction; dutasteride Type I+II ~90%, terminal half-life ~5 weeks — the 840h in the record is the ~35-day figure). Tags cover both. 'teratogenic' is unambiguous and is the strongest single warning here: 5-ARIs cause hypospadias/external genital abnormalities in a male fetus, which is why the label prohibits women who are or may become pregnant from handling crushed/broken tablets, and why dutasteride donors are deferred from blood donation for 6 months. 'neuropsychiatric' for Post-Finasteride Syndrome and the label-level depression/suicidal-ideation signal — persistent sexual dysfunction, anhedonia, cognitive complaints; causation is contested but the regulatory warnings exist and this is the risk users most want flagged. 'assay-interfering' applied with a caveat about the mechanism: 5-ARIs roughly HALVE serum PSA within 6-12 months, so a PSA result must be doubled to compare against an untreated reference range. Strictly this is analyte suppression (a true biological effect), not immunoassay cross-reactivity like biotin — but the consuming rule is identical ('this lab value must be reinterpreted in the presence of this compound') and the app documents PSA in its monitoring row, so leaving it untagged would be the more damaging error. If v2 splits 'assay-interfering' into assay-artefact vs analyte-shift, this belongs in the second bucket. 'cyp3a4-substrate' — both are cleared by CYP3A4 (dutasteride label warns on chronic co-administration with strong 3A4 inhibitors such as ritonavir/ketoconazole; finasteride likewise). NOT 'hpta-suppressive' — 5-ARIs slightly RAISE serum testosterone by blocking its conversion; they suppress DHT, not the axis. NOT 'hepatotoxic'. NOT 'lipid-suppressing' (no meaningful lipid effect). STORE 'ok': both are FDA-approved (finasteride 1mg for androgenetic alopecia and 5mg for BPH; dutasteride 0.5mg for BPH) and both documented dose rows are exactly the approved doses. Dutasteride for hair loss is off-label in the US but at the approved BPH dose, and the entry contains no cycle, stack or performance language — it is a hair-loss/prostate reference that happens to sit in a TRT context. No reframe needed, though the reviewer may want the fetal-handling warning promoted out of the cons list into a prominent position.

enclo.notes: Enclomiphene is the trans/E-isomer of clomiphene, so it inherits the SERM class tags. cyp3a4-substrate: the primary route for the E-isomer is CYP2D6 with CYP3A4 secondary — weaker here than for racemic clomiphene, but applied under the asymmetry rule so a 3A4 interaction rule still fires (v2 should add `cyp2d6-substrate`, which for this compound is the more important pathway). neuropsychiatric applied deliberately even though the entire selling point of enclomiphene is the ABSENCE of zuclomiphene-driven mood effects — headache, nausea and hot flushes were reported in the Androxal trials and the residual CNS risk should not read as zero; note in the entry that the mood burden is materially lower than clomiphene's. teratogenic applied as a property of the molecule (isomer of a pregnancy-contraindicated drug); practically relevant only if used in women, which is not the documented use. Deliberately NOT applied: hematocrit-raising — the trials specifically showed enclomiphene raises testosterone WITHOUT the erythrocytosis seen on exogenous TRT, which is one of its main clinical advantages; tagging it would misrepresent the compound. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: SERM-class venous thromboembolism risk; also the record's own con that long-term testicular and bone effects are unstudied. store=reframe, not exclude: enclomiphene has no FDA approval (the Androxal NDA did not go through) and reaches patients via compounding, but it has a substantial phase III clinical literature and a real therapeutic target (secondary hypogonadism with fertility preservation) — this is the 'unapproved but legitimate research base' case the default reasoning describes. It cannot ship as written because the dose table contains a 'PCT: 25mg/day' row and the pros list 'Testosterone restoration after cycle'. Ship it as an investigational/compounded therapy for secondary hypogonadism under supervision, with the post-cycle rows removed and its unapproved status stated up front.

epi.notes: Epithalon (AEDG tetrapeptide). `neuropsychiatric` applied on the documented melatonin/circadian action — the record claims melatonin regulation and sleep improvement, and the tag's definition explicitly covers 'insomnia or other CNS effects'. This is a property tag, not a harm claim, and it should gate co-use with melatonin, sedatives and other sleep agents. No other risk tag clears the bar: no hepatic, renal, cardiac or haematologic signal at 5-10mg/day, and the toxicity profile in the available literature is benign. VOCABULARY GAP (same as follistatin): telomerase activation carries a theoretical tumour-promotion concern that no current tag expresses — the entry actually claims the opposite (anti-cancer effects in animal models), and both directions rest on the same single research group. A v2 `tumor-risk` tag should carry this. Evidence caveat worth keeping in the entry: essentially all of it is Khavinson-group work, largely unreplicated independently. dea null; aa null. STORE reframe: no approval in any jurisdiction (Epithalamin, the pineal extract predecessor, was used in Russia), no performance framing, but three dose rows including injectable and intranasal protocols. Remove the dose rows and present it as an unvalidated longevity research peptide; the telomerase-lifespan claim in particular needs hedging before it ships.

estriol.notes: E3, the weakest of the three main estrogens; v1 has no estrogen structural tag (serm and aromatase-inhibitor are both wrong — estriol is a direct ER agonist). Not aromatizing: it is a terminal estrogen metabolite, it does not convert to estradiol. assay-interfering is the highest-value tag here — estriol cross-reacts in estradiol immunoassays, and this entry's own monitoring block asks the user to track E2 and E3 side by side, so an unexplained 'high E2' on immunoassay is a predictable false alarm; LC-MS/MS should be specified. hpta-suppressive: applied, weakly. Exogenous estrogen exerts negative feedback on FSH/LH and the entry monitors both; at 0.5-2mg/day topical/vaginal the systemic effect is small, so this is a low-magnitude true positive rather than a strong one. teratogenic: applied on the class contraindication — estrogen products are contraindicated in pregnancy — while noting the genuine tension that estriol is itself the dominant physiological estrogen of pregnancy, so exogenous estriol is a weaker teratogenic candidate than estradiol or the synthetics. Applied under the asymmetry rule; low confidence. Not expressible in v1 and flagged for v2: VTE/thromboembolic risk (the real safety issue with systemic estrogen, and 'cardiotoxic' does not mean this) and unopposed-estrogen endometrial hyperplasia risk — the entry correctly notes progesterone is required with an intact uterus, but no tag encodes it. Store = ok: the entry is already written in a clinical HRT frame with no performance or cycle language, indications are the supervised menopausal ones, and estriol is an approved medicine in the EU/UK. It is not FDA-approved in the US and is supplied by compounding — worth a line of copy, but the entry's own con list already discloses this, so it needs no rewrite.

exemest.notes: Steroidal irreversible (Type I/suicide) aromatase inactivator. Deliberately NOT tagged 'aas': it is a 6-methylene androstadienedione, and its major metabolite 17β-hydroexemestane is a genuine AR agonist, but exemestane is not used as, marketed as, or legally classified as an anabolic steroid (not Schedule III, dea=null). Tagging 'aas' would wrongly fire the AAS store filter and the Schedule III default. The androgenic metabolite is instead captured by 'virilizing'. 'virilizing' applied on the uncertainty asymmetry rather than on strong evidence — at 25mg the androgenic signal is mild (label lists hypertrichosis, alopecia, acne), and frank virilization is a high-dose (600mg) phenomenon; a woman-facing caution is still warranted. 'lipid-suppressing' applied despite the entry's pro claiming a favourable cholesterol profile: exemestane lowers HDL-C and ApoA1 in trial data (the claim in the entry is relative to anastrozole/letrozole, not absolute), and at the documented 25mg EOD 'cycle support' dose it is stacked on top of AAS that also suppress HDL. 'neuropsychiatric' for AI-driven oestrogen deprivation — mood disturbance, depression, insomnia, hot flushes. 'teratogenic' — embryo-fetal toxicity, contraindicated in pregnancy. 'cyp3a4-substrate' confirmed against the Aromasin label: rifampicin 600mg x14d cut exemestane Cmax 41% and AUC 54%, and the label directs 50mg daily with a strong 3A4 inducer. NOT tagged 'hepatotoxic' (transaminase elevation is uncommon and mild at 25mg, not a meaningful hepatic burden) and NOT 'hpta-suppressive' (AIs raise LH/FSH — the opposite). Bone mineral density loss on long-term over-suppression has no tag in v1; it is in the entry's cons and monitoring and should be preserved in text. STORE: FDA-approved drug (adjuvant/advanced breast cancer, 25mg daily), so it belongs in a store build, but both documented dose rows are off-label — 'TRT E2 Management' and explicitly 'Cycle support: 25mg EOD'. The cycle-support row and the AAS-stack framing must be removed and the indication restated as the approved oncology one (with supervised off-label E2 management at most described neutrally).

fisetin.notes: Dietary flavonol (strawberries, apples, onions), used here as a senolytic. No structural tag in section A fits — it is not a peptide, hormone, sympathomimetic or any listed class — so the record is carried entirely by interaction tags, which is correct for a supplement whose main real-world risk is drug interaction rather than direct toxicity. Verified: fisetin is a competitive inhibitor of multiple CYP isoforms, most potently CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and CYP1A2, with moderate CYP2D6 and weak-to-moderate CYP3A4 inhibition. cyp3a4-inhibitor applied — inhibition of 3A4 is at the weaker end of its profile, but the app documents 1000-1500mg/day pulse dosing, which is 10-50x typical dietary intake, so a weak in-vitro inhibitor becomes plausibly relevant in vivo; this is a deliberate cautious application. VOCABULARY GAP: the stronger and better-documented inhibition is of CYP2C9/2C19/1A2, which v1 cannot express — a generic 'cyp-inhibitor' or per-isoform tags would be more accurate here. warfarin-potentiating follows directly from the CYP2C9 inhibition (warfarin's principal clearance route) plus the general antiplatelet activity of flavonols; senolytic clinical trials formally exclude or withhold interacting CYP substrates for two days around fisetin dosing, which is the strongest available signal that this is treated as real, not theoretical. absorption-sensitive: fisetin has poor and highly variable oral bioavailability with rapid glucuronidation/sulfation; absorption is materially improved by fat co-ingestion and by liposomal/phytosome formulations, so the same milligram dose is not the same exposure across products — relevant given the entry notes 'quality varies significantly'. Not applied: hepatotoxic (no signal even at gram doses), nephrotoxic, neuropsychiatric (the 'temporary fatigue during pulse' is mild and self-limiting). STORE ok: a naturally occurring dietary constituent sold as a supplement, described with an honest evidence caveat ('human optimal dose not firmly established'). Not scheduled; anabolic ratio not applicable.

follistatin.notes: CORRECTION TO THE RECORD: the pro 'No androgenic side effects or HPTA suppression' is pharmacologically wrong in its second half. Follistatin's defining action is activin binding, and activin at the pituitary gonadotrope is the principal drive on FSH — verified against primate data showing 48-65% FSH suppression after systemic follistatin (90-180 mcg/kg IV), and follistatin specifically inhibits pituitary FSH release in vitro. At the 100mcg/day SC the app documents, systemic exposure is likely far below that, and injected recombinant follistatin has poor bioavailability and a very short half-life, so real-world axis suppression is uncertain — but the mechanism is direct, the claim in the entry is affirmatively reassuring, and a false negative here is exactly the kind of gap the asymmetry rule exists for. Tag applied; the entry's claim should be deleted regardless of the tag decision. It is a 315-aa glycoprotein rather than a short peptide, but `peptide` is the correct vocabulary bucket. NOT AN AAS — no androgen receptor activity, so aa is null (no assay ratio exists or would be meaningful). dea null: not an anabolic steroid under the CSA definition and not otherwise scheduled. VOCABULARY GAP: myostatin/activin blockade carries a real theoretical tumor-promotion concern (activin/TGF-beta signalling is tumour-suppressive in several epithelial tissues), which the record's own cons raise and which no current tag can express — recommend a `tumor-risk` or `oncogenic-concern` tag in v2; it would also serve Epithalon and any future IGF-1/GH entries. STORE exclude: there is no approved follistatin product anywhere (the legitimate literature is AAV gene therapy in muscular dystrophy, not injectable peptide), the only documented human use is muscle-growth biohacking, and the entry frames it as an anabolic adjunct — 'Potential for synergistic effect alongside testosterone' is stack language for an unapproved anabolic. Reframe is not sufficient because once the performance framing and the dose row are removed there is no supervised clinical use left to describe.

ghkcu.notes: Copper-binding tripeptide (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine) complexed with Cu2+, so peptide is structural. NO risk tags at the documented doses, which I want to justify because it is easy to over-tag a metal-containing compound: at 1-2mg/day of GHK-Cu the copper payload is roughly 160-320mcg (copper is ~16% by mass), i.e. at or below the 900mcg/day dietary RDA and well below the 10mg/day tolerable upper intake. I therefore did not tag hepatotoxic or nephrotoxic — the liver and kidney are where copper toxicity lands, but you do not get there from these doses. Genuine caveats that v1 cannot express and that belong in the entry text rather than in tags: (1) anyone with Wilson's disease or another copper-handling disorder must not use this at all, and that is an absolute contraindication rather than a caution; (2) chronic supraphysiologic copper antagonises zinc, and this app's audience commonly runs high-dose zinc, so the interaction runs in both directions; (3) parenteral copper bypasses the intestinal regulatory step that normally protects against copper loading, so the SubQ route deserves the copper monitoring the entry already lists, whereas the topical route does not. UNCERTAINTY: systemic long-term safety of injected GHK-Cu is genuinely unestablished — nearly all of the Pickart literature is in vitro, animal or topical. store=reframe on the same logic as argireline: the topical cosmetic use is unproblematic and would ship as ok, but the entry also publishes SubQ and intranasal self-dosing schedules for a material with no approval anywhere and no human systemic safety data, alongside 'gene expression reset toward youthful patterns' language that reads as an anti-ageing drug claim. Keep the topical framing and the cosmetic evidence, mark the injectable and intranasal routes as investigational with no established dose rather than tabulating them, and soften the genomic-rejuvenation claim to what the in vitro data supports.

ghrp2.notes: Ghrelin/GHS-R1a agonist, so gh-axis and peptide are structural. prolactin-raising is applied on the compound's own cons text ('Moderate cortisol and prolactin elevation') and its monitoring row lists prolactin — this is the tag the app's prolactin rule needs, even though the elevation is smaller than Hexarelin's. Deliberately NOT tagged: hematocrit, lipid, hepatic — no signal at 100-200mcg.
