Vocabulary gaps I could not express: (1) ACTH/cortisol elevation of roughly 25-35%, which is a real and documented effect and arguably deserves a v2 'cortisol-raising' tag; (2) GH secretagogues worsen insulin sensitivity and can raise fasting glucose — the monitoring row asks for fasting glucose — but the vocabulary only has 'hypoglycemic', which is the wrong direction, so a v2 'hyperglycemic'/'insulin-resistance' tag is needed. I did not apply insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue for that reason. Also unexpressible: GH-mediated fluid retention and carpal tunnel. I considered bp-raising for the fluid retention and rejected it — no meaningful BP signal at these doses. Store: pralmorelin is genuinely approved in Japan (PMDA, Oct 2004, GHRP Kaken 100) as a GH-stimulation diagnostic, so there is a real supervised medical use, but the entry as written is performance-framed — body-composition claims and a 'With CJC-1295' stacking row — which is promotion of an unapproved-in-US injectable under Play policy. Reframe: drop the stack row, state the indication as GHD diagnostic testing.

ghrp6.notes: Same structural profile as GHRP-2. prolactin-raising is if anything better supported here — the cons say 'Most cortisol and prolactin elevation of common GHRPs'. Same vocabulary gaps as GHRP-2 apply and matter more: cortisol elevation is the largest of the common GHRPs and has no tag, and the GH-driven insulin-resistance/glucose rise has no tag in the correct direction. Water retention is listed in the compound's own cons and has no tag either. I considered neuropsychiatric for the intense CNS-mediated hunger and rejected it — the tag's stated scope is mood/aggression/anxiety/insomnia, and appetite stimulation is an on-target effect rather than a mood effect; recorded here in case v2 wants an 'appetite-stimulating' tag, which would be genuinely useful since it is this compound's main differentiator. Store: this is the closest call in the batch and I want the reasoning on record. GHRP-6 has no regulatory approval anywhere, and the dose rows are 'Bulking and Mass' plus a CJC-1295 stack row — that is squarely the performance framing the exclude rule points at. I chose reframe rather than exclude because there is a substantive legitimate clinical literature (cachexia, GH deficiency, Cuban cardioprotection work) and the entry's own summary already cites cachexia recovery, so a compliant clinical/reference version of this entry is writable. If the reviewer wants a stricter line, this is the entry in the batch to move to exclude.

glycine-supp.notes: Amino acid, food substance, not scheduled, no realistic toxicity ceiling at the documented 3-10 g/day. neuropsychiatric applied because glycine is a bona fide inhibitory neurotransmitter at spinal/brainstem strychnine-sensitive glycine receptors and a co-agonist at the NMDA receptor glycine site — the sleep-latency and sedation effects the entry documents at 3-5 g are the tag's substance, and the cons list explicitly warns of excessive sedation at very high doses. This should fire additively with other CNS depressants and with the taurine and GlyNAC entries in this same batch. Nothing else in v1 applies; GI upset above 30 g has no slot and is not clinically meaningful at documented doses. Store ok — plain dietary supplement, no performance or cycle framing.

gonadorelin.notes: Synthetic GnRH/LHRH decapeptide. hpta-suppressive is applied deliberately and is the single most important tag on this record: pulsatile delivery stimulates, but continuous or too-frequent exposure downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors and produces gonadotropin suppression — the same mechanism that makes leuprolide a chemical-castration agent. The app's own cons row calls this out ('continuous use suppresses the axis (pharmaceutical castration)'), and the 0.3h half-life plus real-world SubQ dosing outside a pump makes mis-timing the likely failure mode, so the rule needs to fire. Same v2 gap as kisspeptin-54: no 'hpta-stimulating' tag exists to express the intended (pulsatile) direction. No hepatic, lipid, haematocrit, pressor or QT signal at 100mcg or at 5-20mcg/90min. Verified regulatory status: gonadorelin was FDA-approved (Factrel, Lutrepulse) for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and diagnostic testing and was withdrawn for commercial, not safety, reasons; it is not on FDA's Category 2 'significant safety risk' bulks list and is compoundable under 503A, so it is meaningfully better-positioned than the research peptides in this batch. STORE: reframe rather than ok only because of framing, not substance — the entry sells it as an HCG substitute for testicular maintenance on TRT and carries a protocol dose row ('TRT Testicular Maintenance: 100mcg'). Play's hCG rule bars hCG promoted alongside anabolic steroids, and an entry positioning gonadorelin as the drop-in replacement for that exact use sits in the same posture even though gonadorelin is not hCG. Rewrite to lead with the approved indications (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, GnRH stimulation testing) and describe adjunct use as physician-directed. A store call of 'ok' would be defensible if the rewrite is done; 'reframe' records that the rewrite is required first. Not scheduled.

hcg2.notes: peptide applied with a caveat: hCG is a ~237-residue glycoprotein heterodimer, not a small peptide, so this is the broad reading of the tag — flagging in case the store filter treats `peptide` as 'small synthetic peptide'. aromatizing is INDIRECT but clinically real and is the record's own first con: hCG drives intratesticular testosterone, and testicular aromatase converts it, producing disproportionate E2 elevation relative to serum T. Tagging it is what makes the E2-monitoring rule fire, which is the correct behaviour even though hCG itself is not a substrate for aromatase. hpta-suppressive is counterintuitive but correct at the documented doses — exogenous hCG suppresses endogenous LH/FSH by negative feedback (the record's own monitoring line says 'LH/FSH will be suppressed — this is expected'), and the 1000-1500IU 3x/week 'blast restart' row risks Leydig cell desensitisation. hematocrit-raising applied under the asymmetry rule: hCG raises endogenous testosterone, and at the highest documented dose row that is enough to move haematocrit. assay-interfering is a genuine and frequently missed one: administered hCG produces positive serum and urine pregnancy tests and confounds hCG-based tumour marker interpretation (germ cell/trophoblastic disease) for days after the last dose. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and multiple gestation in female use; also gynaecomastia via the E2 route (partly captured by aromatizing). dea=null — hCG is a prescription biologic, not a federally controlled substance (it IS WADA-prohibited, S2). store=exclude, and this is the clearest call in the batch: Google Play prohibits hCG promoted in conjunction with anabolic steroids or with weight loss by name, and this entry does exactly that — it is framed as on-cycle testicular preservation and a pre-PCT primer, with a 'Blast restart' dose row. No reframe salvages it inside this app, because the AAS conjunction is the entry's whole purpose; a genuinely reframed hCG entry (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, male fertility, cryptorchidism) would be a different record.

hexarelin.notes: Hexarelin is a hexapeptide GHS-R1a agonist — peptide plus gh-axis. prolactin-raising is applied on strong grounds and is the tag that most distinguishes this record from ipamorelin in the same batch: hexarelin produces the strongest prolactin and cortisol elevation of the GHRPs, the entry states this in its cons, and the entry's own monitoring line already calls for prolactin testing. This should drive any rule about combining it with other prolactin-raising agents (19-nor AAS in particular) or about investigating prolactin-related symptoms. Cortisol/ACTH elevation is equally well documented and equally clinically relevant, but the vocabulary has no HPA-axis or cortisol-raising tag — that is a real gap, since the cortisol rise is a principal reason the entry says it is unsuitable for daily chronic use. Flagging for v2. Considered and rejected: cardiotoxic — hexarelin's distinctive non-GH property is direct CD36 binding in cardiac tissue producing CARDIOPROTECTIVE effects (improved LV function, protection against ischaemia-reperfusion injury), so the direction is inverted and tagging it would be a factual error; the vocabulary has no cardioprotective tag and none is needed. bp-raising withheld on the same reasoning as CJC-1295 and ipamorelin, though water retention is noted as more pronounced here. Rapid tachyphylaxis is the other key untaggable property — receptor desensitization is faster than any other GHRP, which is why the dose rows are labelled 'Pulsatile and Cycling'. dea=null, not federally scheduled. aa=null. store=reframe: unapproved substance with genuine research standing (the cardiac GHS-R/CD36 literature is legitimate), but the cycling dose rows and 'strong synergy with GHRH analogues' are protocol and stack language that must be rewritten to neutral pharmacology, and the prolactin/cortisol burden belongs in body text rather than a cons bullet.

hghfrag.notes: DUPLICATE — this is the same molecule as the 'aod9604' record in this batch (AOD-9604 is hGH 176-191 with an added N-terminal tyrosine; the aod9604 entry's own aka field lists 'HGH Fragment 176-191'). Tagged identically to aod9604 so the two cannot diverge, but the parent should merge them; leaving both live risks double-counting in any stacking or interaction logic. gh-axis applied with the same caveat as aod9604 — it is a GH-derived fragment and should be caught by GH-family rules, but the compound is specifically characterised as not raising IGF-1, so no rule should infer IGF-1 elevation from this tag here. The entry's monitoring line is actually well-designed and worth keeping: IGF-1 should remain unchanged, and a rise suggests the product is mislabelled or adulterated with real GH, which is a genuine gray-market risk. The '12.5x more potent than HGH for fat burning' claim is a rodent-adipocyte in vitro figure being presented as a human potency ratio and must not survive a rewrite — human trials of this fragment did not demonstrate meaningful fat loss. dea=null, not federally scheduled. aa=null. store=reframe, but this entry needs more aggressive rewriting than aod9604 for one specific reason: 'Popular in cutting protocols alongside testosterone' is explicit stacking-with-an-AAS language, which is the clearest promotion-of-unapproved-use text in the batch and is exactly what the Play rule targets. Remove that sentence, remove the 'Local and Spot' site-injection guidance (directive technique instruction), and the neutral pharmacology description that remains is shippable.

humanin.notes: 21-amino-acid mitochondrial-derived peptide. hypoglycemic is applied under the uncertainty-asymmetry rule and I want the weakness of the evidence recorded: humanin and the HNG analogue improve insulin sensitivity and lower glucose in rodent and primate work, the entry's own pros claim 'Improves insulin sensitivity', and the monitoring row asks for fasting glucose and HbA1c — but there is essentially no human dosing data, so the magnitude at the documented 2-4mg is unknown. The tag is here to make the additive-hypoglycaemia rule fire for anyone co-administering insulin, a sulfonylurea or a GLP-1, which is the correct caution even if humanin's own effect turns out to be small. No other risk tags: no endocrine axis effect, no hepatic or renal burden reported. Store: unapproved research peptide with a real aging-biology literature and no performance framing — the single dose row is labelled 'Research protocol' — which is the textbook reframe case. State it as a research compound, not a protocol.

igf1lr3.notes: peptide and gh-axis are definitional (the gh-axis tag explicitly covers IGF-1). hypoglycemic is the headline risk and is high-confidence - the entry itself says it must be used with carbohydrates nearby and puts fasting glucose first in monitoring; at 40-80mcg/day of a 20-30h analogue this is a genuine acute-harm pathway. insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue applied under the uncertainty rule: IGF-1 does not secrete insulin, but at supraphysiologic concentrations it cross-activates the insulin receptor and IR/IGF-1R hybrids and directly drives insulin-like glucose disposal, which is what the tag's downstream rule (do not stack with insulin/secretagogues, do not use fasted) needs to fire on. If v2 splits the tag, this belongs on the 'drives insulin action' side, not the secretagogue side. cardiotoxic applied for the 'organ growth concern with chronic supraphysiological use' the entry documents - IGF-1 is a direct driver of cardiac hypertrophy. Same carcinogenicity gap as Cardarine: IGF-1 is a mitogen and the entry lists 'cancer promotion risk' and 'tumor markers awareness' in monitoring, but v1 has no tag for it - second data point for adding `carcinogenic` or `mitogenic` in v2. store=exclude. Note this is NOT the same compound as mecasermin (rhIGF-1, FDA-approved for severe primary IGF-1 deficiency) - LR3 is a deliberately half-life-extended research analogue with no approval anywhere and no supervised indication, so there is nothing to reframe toward. The documented use is entirely performance: 'Performance: 40-80mcg/day' and 'Site injection: 20-40mcg' for site enhancement, plus 'Synergistic with HGH and testosterone' stack language.

insulin.notes: peptide is applied because insulin is a 51-residue two-chain polypeptide and the modern products are literal peptide analogues (lispro, aspart, glargine); if a rule set uses 'peptide' as a route/handling class this must be in it. insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue is definitional. hypoglycemic is the entire safety story and needs no defence. electrolyte-disturbing = insulin drives potassium intracellularly; hypokalaemia is the quiet second failure mode the entry correctly names, and it is the mechanism by which insulin is used to treat hyperkalaemia. neuropsychiatric applied because neuroglycopenia IS a CNS event — confusion, aggression, seizure, coma and, in the documented bodybuilder cases, permanent hypoglycaemic brain injury. qt-prolonging and cardiotoxic share one mechanism and I have tagged both deliberately: acute hypoglycaemia measurably prolongs QT via sympathoadrenal surge plus insulin-driven hypokalaemia, and this is the accepted explanation for nocturnal 'dead in bed' arrhythmic death in insulin users. Neither is direct ion-channel block, so rule text should say 'secondary to hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia' — but the combination with any other QT-prolonging agent in this reference (thyroid hormone, clenbuterol-type sympathomimetics) is exactly the stack that kills people. absorption-sensitive is a slight stretch of the tag wording, applied deliberately: the variable that moves injected insulin absorption is not a co-administered drug but heat, a hot shower, cardio, injection depth and site — plus meal timing, which is the single most safety-critical co-administration in this entire encyclopedia. A false positive here is harmless; the false negative is not. NOT tagged teratogenic — insulin is the PREFERRED glycaemic therapy in pregnancy and a teratogenicity flag would be actively wrong. NOT tagged bp-raising — the hyperinsulinaemia/sodium-retention association is epidemiological, not a dose-level effect. dea=null. store=ok, and this entry is already the model for what reframe is supposed to produce: it leads with the FDA-approved life-sustaining indication, explicitly refuses to publish a performance dose ('No dose is published here'), and states the bodybuilding use only to document that it has killed people. No edits needed to ship.

ipa.notes: Ipamorelin is a pentapeptide ghrelin-receptor (GHS-R1a) agonist — peptide plus gh-axis. Deliberately NOT prolactin-raising: selectivity for GH release without meaningful cortisol or prolactin elevation is the defining pharmacological property that distinguishes ipamorelin from GHRP-2 and hexarelin, and it is the reason the two are dosed differently. Tagging it would erase a real clinical distinction from the hexarelin record in the same batch, so this is one place I am overriding the apply-when-uncertain default — the evidence for selectivity is good, not uncertain. Same withheld tags and same reasoning as CJC-1295: no bp-raising at 100-300mcg, and the insulin-resistance/fasting-glucose direction has no vocabulary tag (v2 gap). Mild appetite stimulation via the ghrelin receptor is documented in the entry but is not a risk the vocabulary covers and is not neuropsychiatric in the intended sense. dea=null, not federally scheduled. aa=null. store=reframe: unapproved substance, and the entry's framing ('gold standard pairing with CJC-1295', paired dose rows) is combination-protocol language that must be removed. The underlying class has clinical legitimacy — ghrelin agonists such as anamorelin and macimorelin have regulatory approvals in some jurisdictions — so neutral reference framing is achievable.

isotretinoin.notes: teratogenic is the defining property — extremely high risk of major craniofacial, cardiac, thymic and CNS malformations, the reason for the iPLEDGE REMS, mandatory dual contraception and monthly pregnancy testing. If any single tag in this batch must not be missed it is this one. lipid-suppressing applied on the standard reading of the tag: isotretinoin raises triglycerides substantially (the most common lab abnormality, occasionally to pancreatitis-triggering levels), raises LDL and lowers HDL. Note this compounds directly with the AAS entries in this same batch — a user on a 17aa oral plus isotretinoin stacks two independent lipid and two independent hepatic insults, which is exactly the interaction rule this tag set should generate. hepatotoxic applied for dose-dependent transaminase elevation (the entry monitors LFTs). neuropsychiatric applied for the labelled depression/mood-change/suicidality signal — causality remains debated in the literature but the labelling and monitoring requirement are real. photosensitizing applied: increased UV sensitivity and marked skin fragility/xerosis are near-universal, and this compound is used by a population that tans and does contest prep. cyp3a4-substrate applied — metabolised by CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP3A4 and CYP2B6; 3A4 is a meaningful contributor. absorption-sensitive applied: standard (non-Lidose/Absorica) isotretinoin bioavailability roughly doubles with a high-fat meal, so fasted dosing materially underdoses. NOT TAGGED, recorded as vocabulary gaps: concurrent tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline — commonly used for the same acne) risk intracranial hypertension and are contraindicated; concurrent vitamin A or high-dose retinoid supplements risk additive hypervitaminosis A; skeletal/DISH changes and night blindness on prolonged use. store=reframe: FDA-approved and this is broadly its approved indication (severe recalcitrant nodular acne), so it belongs in a store build — but the entry as written is framed around steroid-induced acne with a dose row literally labelled 'common for AAS acne'. That row and the AAS framing must go; the entry should state the approved indication, the REMS/pregnancy-prevention requirement explicitly, and that it is prescription-only with mandatory monitoring.

keto-dhea.notes: Deliberately empty tag array — recording the reasoning explicitly so this does not read as an omission. 3-acetyl-7-oxo-DHEA is a terminal DHEA metabolite that cannot be converted back to androstenedione, testosterone or oestradiol, which is the entire point of the molecule; controlled trials at 100-200mg/day show no change in testosterone, oestradiol, DHEA-S or SHBG, and the app's own monitoring row correctly states no sex-hormone monitoring is required. That removes 'aromatizing', 'virilizing' and 'hpta-suppressive'. It is not 17α-alkylated, so not 'hepatotoxic'. Trials at these doses reported no significant change in heart rate or blood pressure, so not 'bp-raising' or 'cardiotoxic'. It is not a thyroid hormone and does not contain one, so 'thyroid-hormone' does not apply — but the one property v1 cannot express is that small trials report 7-keto raising free/total T3 (with TSH and T4 unchanged) as part of its thermogenic effect, which is presumably why the entry's monitoring row asks for thyroid function despite listing no thyroid tag-able mechanism. That is worth carrying in the entry text and is a candidate for a v2 'thyroid-modulating' tag distinct from 'thyroid-hormone'. Also not expressible: 7-keto-DHEA is WADA-prohibited under S1 as an anabolic agent despite being non-androgenic, which matters for any tested athlete using this app. Efficacy caveat rather than a safety one: the 'greater fat loss than placebo' and '1-2% RMR increase' claims rest on two small manufacturer-linked trials, so the pros are overstated. STORE 'ok': legal OTC dietary supplement in the US, not scheduled, no performance-dose framing.

kissp.notes: hpta-suppressive is the non-obvious call and I verified it before applying. Kisspeptin-10 is an HPG-axis STIMULANT when given pulsatile — that is its intended use here — but KISS1R desensitises rapidly, and continuous or frequent administration causes paradoxical suppression of LH and FSH, mechanistically analogous to continuous GnRH agonism; twice-daily kisspeptin-54 for 14 days cut the LH response by roughly 90% and the FSH response by roughly 95%. The compound's own cons say this in capitals ('Continuous dosing SUPPRESSES the axis'). Since the app documents a dosing pattern whose most likely user error produces axis suppression, the tag should fire. Any rule consuming it must read this note: the correct warning is 'do not dose continuously', not the AAS-style 'expect suppression, plan a restart'. This is a case where the tag alone is misleading and the note carries the meaning — worth a v2 'stimulatory-if-pulsatile' qualifier or a paired tag. neuropsychiatric applied for documented central effects: it is a hypothalamic neuropeptide with human fMRI evidence of limbic and sexual-processing modulation, and the entry itself claims pro-sexual and libido effects. Not tagged aromatizing or hematocrit-raising: those follow from the endogenous testosterone it restores, not from the peptide, and tags are properties of the compound — but note the monitoring row correctly asks for E2, so downstream oestrogen rise is a real consideration for the interaction layer. Store: reframe. Unapproved for testosterone restoration, genuine clinical use in fertility and reproductive endocrinology research, no performance framing; rewrite to the research/fertility indication and keep the continuous-dosing warning prominent.

kisspeptin54.notes: 54-aa full-length kisspeptin (metastin), Kiss1R agonist on GnRH neurons. hpta-suppressive is counterintuitive here and needs explanation: acutely KP-54 STIMULATES the HPG axis (LH surge 45-60 min post-dose, which the app uses as its response check), but continuous/non-pulsatile exposure desensitises Kiss1R and GnRH neurons and the net effect flips to gonadotropin suppression — the app's own cons row says exactly this ('Continuous dosing causes desensitization — pulsatile protocol essential'). The tag is therefore correct as a property (this compound can suppress the axis) and I would rather the rule engine fire a suppression caution on a mis-dosed continuous protocol than stay silent. Notes for v2: the vocabulary has no 'hpta-stimulating' tag, so bidirectional HPG agents (kisspeptin, gonadorelin, hCG, SERMs) cannot currently be distinguished from true suppressants — that is a genuine gap worth closing. No pressor, hepatic, lipid or haematological signal at the 1-3 nmol/kg doses documented. STORE: no marketing approval in any jurisdiction, but a substantial and legitimate clinical-research literature (Imperial College reproductive-endocrinology trials in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, IVF trigger use, HSDD) and no performance or physique framing — this is the 'research peptide with real clinical literature' case, so reframe rather than exclude. The rewrite needs the 'Fertility protocol: per clinical protocol' row removed or restated as investigational-under-supervision, and the not-approved status stated up front. Not federally scheduled; no anabolic:androgenic ratio concept applies.

kpv.notes: Lys-Pro-Val, the C-terminal tripeptide of alpha-MSH(11-13). immunosuppressive is applied with recorded uncertainty and is the only non-structural call here: KPV's entire documented mechanism is inhibition of NF-kB nuclear translocation and downstream pro-inflammatory cytokine transcription (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8), it penetrates to the nucleus, and the entry itself claims 'systemic NF-kB suppression' and 'immune modulation' at 250mcg-2mg. NF-kB is the master transcriptional switch of innate and adaptive immunity, so a compound whose selling point is suppressing it systemically should carry the flag — chiefly to drive cautions around live vaccines, active infection, and stacking with other immunomodulators or biologics. Uncertainty stated plainly: there are no human trials quantifying systemic immunosuppression with KPV, the entry claims 'no significant side effects in research', and it is entirely possible the effect is local/gut-restricted at oral doses and clinically negligible systemically. This is a deliberate false positive under the asymmetry rule. Explicitly NOT applied: photosensitizing. Although KPV is an alpha-MSH fragment, it lacks the core His-Phe-Arg-Trp melanocortin pharmacophore and does not drive MC1R melanogenesis — it does not tan skin or darken nevi, and tagging it alongside Melanotan II would be a genuine error rather than a cautious one. Also note the record has no halfLifeHours value (KPV is very short-lived, minutes), which the cons acknowledge. STORE reframe: no marketing approval anywhere; the entry's claim of 'FDA Orphan Drug designation for IBD in progress' should be verified or removed before shipping, since an unsubstantiated regulatory-status claim is its own store risk. Framing is therapeutic (IBD, eczema, psoriasis) with no performance angle and there is a legitimate preclinical literature, so reframe not exclude: delete the four dose rows, state unapproved status, and drop the implied treatment claims for Crohn's and ulcerative colitis, which are the most exposure-generating text on the record. Not scheduled.

larazotide.notes: absorption-sensitive is applied with a caveat about the tag's literal wording, which does not quite fit and should be revisited in v2. Larazotide acetate is deliberately NOT systemically absorbed — it acts locally in the gut lumen on the zonulin pathway — so 'its own systemic absorption is altered' is not the issue. What is true and clinically load-bearing is that its efficacy is food-timing dependent (dosed before meals in the celiac trials), so the tag is applied to make the food/timing rule fire, which is the practically correct behaviour. There is also a plausible reverse interaction the vocabulary cannot express: by tightening intestinal tight junctions, larazotide could in principle reduce the paracellular absorption of co-administered drugs. That is a property affecting OTHER compounds, and v2 would benefit from an 'alters-absorption-of-others' tag distinct from the current inward-facing one — the same gap applies to semaglutide's gastric-emptying effect. No systemic risk tags: negligible systemic exposure means no hepatic, renal, cardiac or endocrine burden at 0.5-1mg. Store: reframe — unapproved (the celiac programme did not convert to approval), substantial legitimate clinical trial literature, zero performance framing. Textbook reframe case.

ldn.notes: neuropsychiatric = the vivid/disturbing dreams and sleep architecture changes the entry itself lists, plus reported mood and anxiety changes and the acute dysphoria of precipitated withdrawal. DELIBERATELY NOT TAGGED hepatotoxic, and this is the one non-obvious call in this record. Naltrexone's hepatotoxicity boxed warning was REMOVED by FDA in July 2013 on evidence it was an artefact of the very high (up to 300mg/day) doses used in early trials; there are no established cases of naltrexone-induced hepatic failure, and a hepatotoxicity warning survives only in the Warnings and Precautions section. At the 1.5-4.5mg documented here — one-tenth of even the approved 50mg dose — this is the vocabulary's own aspirin case, not its Superdrol case. The entry's 'liver enzymes' monitoring line is a vestige of the 50mg-era label and should be relabelled as baseline/reassurance testing rather than implying hepatic burden. If the store owner wants maximum conservatism the tag is cheap to add, but it would be a genuinely false positive. Also NOT tagged immunosuppressive: LDN's documented direction is immune UP-regulation and TLR4 modulation, so an immunosuppression rule firing here would be backwards. The single most important interaction in this record has no v1 tag: naltrexone is a competitive opioid antagonist — it precipitates acute withdrawal in anyone opioid-dependent, blocks opioid analgesia (a surgical and emergency-care problem), and after chronic blockade leaves upregulated receptors and elevated overdose risk on discontinuation. That deserves a v2 'opioid-antagonist' tag; recording it here in the meantime. dea=null: naltrexone is an antagonist with no abuse liability and is not federally scheduled. store=ok: FDA-approved non-controlled drug, compounded off-label at a sub-approved dose, no performance framing anywhere in the entry.

lgd.notes: dea=null - not federally scheduled; unapproved drug and WADA-prohibited, which is a separate matter. hepatotoxic is the strongest-evidenced of the three SARMs here: 8 of the 15 published SARM DILI case reports are LGD-4033, including a case requiring transplant evaluation after combined SARM use. The entry's 'hepatotoxicity in rare case reports' should be upgraded to a first-class warning. hpta-suppressive is high-confidence and the app's own cons confirm suppression at 1mg/day - LGD is the most suppressive of the common SARMs, and the documented 15-20mg/day row is 15-20x the dose that already suppresses. lipid-suppressing confirmed (HDL reduction more pronounced than ostarine, dose-dependent in Phase I). hematocrit-raising applied per the asymmetry rule; Phase I showed only modest haemoglobin change, so this is a precautionary tag. virilizing and teratogenic applied on AR-agonism grounds - no women's dose row is documented here, but the 26h half-life plus 'slow washout' means exposure persists, which matters for the teratogenic rule. aa=null on the same reasoning as ostarine: I checked and the commonly quoted figures for LGD are inconsistent (10:1 in some sources, >500-fold muscle:prostate selectivity in the preclinical rat work) and neither is a Hershberger testosterone=100 figure, so no valid value exists for this field. DATA QUALITY: this record has duplicated/conflicting dose rows - two separate 'Standard' entries at 10mg/day and 5mg/day, plus overlapping conservative/advanced rows, and the pros array repeats several claims verbatim. It looks like two source entries merged badly and should be deduplicated regardless of the store decision. store=exclude.

lithium-or.notes: Lithium salt sold OTC as a supplement in the US; not scheduled. Dose here is 5-20 mg elemental, roughly 1/20th of the 170-340 mg elemental delivered by psychiatric lithium carbonate, and serum levels at these doses do not approach the therapeutic range — so all three risk tags are class-derived and precautionary rather than demonstrated at the documented dose, and I am flagging that explicitly so a reviewer can calibrate the warning text down. neuropsychiatric is the intended effect (GSK-3beta inhibition, BDNF, mood stabilisation) and is uncontroversial. nephrotoxic: I checked, and renal toxicity has not been observed across 40+ years of supplement-dose commercial use — but lithium is the textbook cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic interstitial nephritis, the entry itself prescribes creatinine/eGFR monitoring and warns that dehydration concentrates lithium, and the top dose row (20 mg for 'mood support') is the edge of the range, so I applied it per the false-positive-preferred rule. teratogenic: Ebstein anomaly is an established first-trimester lithium risk at therapeutic levels; negligible at micro-dose, but pregnancy avoidance is the right default for any lithium product. NOT TAGGED and recorded here instead: (1) thyroid suppression/hypothyroidism — real class effect, the entry's own 6-monthly TSH monitoring is correct, but v1 has no thyroid-suppressing tag and thyroid-hormone means 'contains a thyroid hormone', so this is a v2 gap; (2) the most important interaction on this compound is unexpressible in v1 — NSAIDs, thiazides, ACE inhibitors/ARBs and sodium depletion all raise lithium levels, and taurine (also in this batch) may do the same, so lithium is a 'levels raised by other drugs' compound rather than an electrolyte-disturber, and I did not apply electrolyte-disturbing on that reasoning; (3) QT prolongation and T-wave change occur in lithium toxicity but not at micro-dose, so qt-prolonging was not applied. Store ok: marketed as a dietary supplement at supplement doses with no performance framing. Worth noting the entry's central marketing claim — that orotate delivers more lithium to brain per mg than carbonate — is poorly supported, and a 2007 case report showed toxicity symptoms after a large orotate overdose at a serum level of only 0.3-0.4 mEq/L.

ll37.notes: LL-37 is the sole human cathelicidin, a 37-residue cationic antimicrobial peptide; peptide is the correct and only structural tag. Deliberately NOT immunosuppressive — the direction is inverted. LL-37 is immunostimulatory and pro-inflammatory (it is a chemoattractant and drives type I interferon responses), so applying immunosuppressive would be an active factual error that could drive exactly the wrong interaction rule, e.g. wrongly cautioning against combining with vaccines or wrongly clearing it in autoimmune disease. The vocabulary has no 'immunostimulatory' tag, which is a real gap for this compound and I am flagging it for v2. The clinically important consequence that I therefore cannot tag: LL-37 is an established autoantigen in psoriasis, rosacea and lupus — LL-37/self-DNA complexes activate plasmacytoid dendritic cells and drive interferon production — so the entry's con 'may exacerbate autoimmune conditions' is mechanistically real and is the main reason someone should not take this casually. Considered and rejected: photosensitizing — LL-37 does drive psoriasiform skin change, but that tag is plainly aimed at genuine photosensitivity and pigmentary agents (tetracyclines, melanotan), and stretching it here would misroute a sun-exposure caution instead of an autoimmune one. Also untaggable: cationic antimicrobial peptides are cytotoxic and haemolytic at high local concentration, which is the basis of the entry's injection-site inflammation. dea=null, not federally scheduled. aa=null. store=reframe: an endogenous human peptide with a large and genuinely legitimate research literature (antimicrobial peptides are a mainstream field) and no performance framing at all, which is squarely the reframe branch. Needs the autoimmune contraindication stated prominently in body text and the 'apply to wound' instruction removed, since that is directive self-treatment guidance.

mast.notes: Injectable 2a-methyl-DHT ester. NOT 17aa and not a 19-nor, so no 17aa-oral/19-nor and no hepatotoxic despite the entry listing liver enzymes in monitoring - hepatic burden of an oil-based non-alkylated ester at these doses is not clinically meaningful. Not aromatizing (2a-methyl blocks aromatisation) - this is the compound's selling point and the pros row is correct. aromatase-inhibitor IS applied: DHT derivatives are competitive aromatase substrates/inhibitors in vitro and the entry explicitly claims users 'may reduce AI use', which is exactly the kind of claim an interaction rule needs to catch (co-administered AI + Masteron = risk of over-suppressing E2). Evidence for meaningful in-vivo aromatase inhibition is weak; applied under the uncertainty-favours-tagging rule and because the app's own copy asserts the effect. lipid-suppressing is strong here, not mild - non-aromatising DHT derivatives at 300-500mg/wk crush HDL harder than testosterone at equivalent doses; the entry understates this by calling the profile 'relatively mild'. bp-raising and cardiotoxic applied on the supraphysiologic-AAS class basis (LV hypertrophy, adverse remodelling) rather than compound-specific data. virilizing is high-confidence: strong DHT, non-reducible, and the entry itself flags significant hair loss. teratogenic applied class-wide for AAS (androgenic virilization of a female fetus; androgens are pregnancy-contraindicated). aa [62,25] is the conventionally cited rodent Hershberger-derived figure, not a measured human ratio, and should not be presented to users as predictive. NOT tagged nephrotoxic: AAS-associated FSGS is a real class concern but is documented mainly with high-dose long-term polypharmacy, not drostanolone specifically - flagging here rather than tagging. store=exclude: Schedule III controlled substance, entry is entirely performance-framed with cutting/recomp dose rows and no approved indication retained (the historical breast-cancer indication is withdrawn), so there is no reframe target.

mastenan.notes: 2alpha-methyl-DHT with an enanthate ester — dht-derived, non-aromatizable, not 17aa (injectable), so no hepatotoxic and no 17aa-oral tag. aromatase-inhibitor APPLIED, and this is the non-obvious one: drostanolone is not merely estrogen-neutral, it competes with aromatizable substrates at the aromatase enzyme and has weak direct anti-aromatase activity (the reason drostanolone propionate was historically a breast-cancer agent). Verified by search. The effect is weak and is NOT a substitute for a real AI, but the tag matters for interaction logic — stacking 400-600mg/week with anastrozole or exemestane can drive estradiol below the floor, and low-E2 symptoms on masteron-containing stacks are commonly misattributed. virilizing applied strongly despite the low nominal androgenic ratio: as a non-reducible DHT derivative masteron is a well-known driver of androgenic alopecia and, in women, virilization at these doses. lipid-suppressing is significant — non-aromatizing DHT derivatives are among the worst for HDL. hematocrit-raising and bp-raising at 300-600mg/week; the entry monitors both. warfarin-potentiating as an AAS class labelled interaction. store=exclude: Schedule III; the enanthate ester was never an approved product (only the propionate, as Drolban/Masteril, long discontinued), and the entry is contest-prep framed throughout.

melatonin-ther.notes: Indoleamine hormone, no structural tag in v1 fits it. neuropsychiatric: at the documented 10-60mg (60-200x physiological) sedation, morning grogginess, vivid dreams/nightmares and occasional dysphoria are the dominant adverse effects — the entry's own con list leads with grogginess. warfarin-potentiating: the entry itself states 'Interacts with anticoagulants'; case reports of raised INR on melatonin + warfarin exist, so the tag is applied rather than left to prose. hpta-suppressive: applied with uncertainty. High-dose melatonin has been trialled as a male contraceptive and suppresses LH/GnRH pulsatility in some human work; the entry flags 'theoretical concern about reproductive hormones' and its own monitoring block asks for reproductive hormones at high dose. Weak evidence but the asymmetry rule favours applying it. Deliberately NOT applied: teratogenic (pregnancy is discouraged by convention, but there is no established fetal-risk signal — melatonin is physiologically the dominant maternal indoleamine); serotonergic (melatonin is synthesised FROM serotonin but has negligible 5-HT receptor activity); immunosuppressive (it is immune-stimulating, which is the opposite problem and is not expressible in v1 — relevant for transplant/autoimmune users, flag for v2); cyp3a4-substrate (melatonin is a CYP1A2 substrate, not 3A4 — fluvoxamine/ciprofloxacin raise levels several-fold; v1 has no CYP1A2 tag, flag for v2). Store = reframe, not ok: melatonin itself is a lawful OTC dietary supplement in the US so the substance is fine, but the entry carries an explicit disease-treatment dose row ('Anticancer adjunct: 20-40mg') plus breast/prostate cancer claims. That is an unapproved-indication claim for a supplement and a health-misinformation exposure at review; strip the anticancer dose row and soften the oncology claims to 'under investigation' and it ships.

metformin.notes: 'hypoglycemic' applied on the 'can cause OR POTENTIATE' clause: metformin as monotherapy essentially does not cause hypoglycaemia (no insulinotropic action), but it meaningfully potentiates it when combined with insulin, sulfonylureas or a GLP-1 agonist — all of which this app documents elsewhere — and in the fasted, carbohydrate-restricted, hard-training user this entry is aimed at. Without the tag the insulin and GLP-1 stacking rules would not fire. 'gastric-emptying-delaying' applied on the uncertainty asymmetry and flagged as my softest call in this record: metformin raises GLP-1 and there is human evidence it slows gastric emptying, which plausibly underlies part of its GI side-effect profile, but it is nothing like a GLP-1 agonist in magnitude. It matters because the app documents metformin alongside GLP-1 agonists, where the additive effect on emptying is the clinically relevant concern (and is an anaesthesia/aspiration consideration). Downgrade this one if the reviewer prefers a higher evidence bar. NOT tagged 'nephrotoxic' — the direction is reversed and getting this wrong would be actively misleading: metformin does not injure the kidney, it is renally cleared, so impaired renal function causes metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis. eGFR gates the dose (contraindicated below 30, do not initiate below 45) and it should be held for iodinated contrast and around surgery. That relationship needs to live in the entry text since no v1 tag captures 'renally cleared / renal impairment is a contraindication'. NOT 'insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue' — metformin suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves peripheral sensitivity; it neither is insulin nor drives its secretion, and the hypoglycaemia rule is already carried by the tag above. Two further untaggable items to preserve in text: B12 malabsorption on long-term use (the entry's annual B12 monitoring is correct and should be kept), and lactic acidosis as the boxed warning. STORE 'ok': FDA-approved, prescription, and both documented rows (500-1000mg/day; ER 500-2000mg/day) sit within the approved dose range. The longevity indication is off-label but is transparently labelled 'Longevity / Off-label' in the dose row, is a mainstream research topic with a registered FDA trial (TAME), and carries no performance, cycle or weight-loss framing.

mk677.notes: CLASSIFICATION CORRECTION: MK-677 is very commonly mislabelled a SARM. It is not — it is a non-peptide, orally active ghrelin/GHS-R1a agonist. So `sarm` is wrong AND `peptide` is wrong (it is a spiropiperidine small molecule, not a peptide analogue), and `aa` is null because an anabolic:androgenic ratio is meaningless for a non-androgen. gh-axis is the correct structural tag. cardiotoxic is evidence-based, not speculative: the Adunsky phase IIb hip-fracture trial was TERMINATED EARLY for a congestive heart failure signal (6.5% ibutamoren vs 1.7% placebo), and Merck discontinued development; the events clustered in subjects over 80 with pre-existing HF, and the mechanism is GH-driven sodium/water retention unmasking diastolic dysfunction — which is also why bp-raising is applied (the record's own con lists water retention and bloating). prolactin-raising is stated in the record's cons and reflected in its monitoring line. lipid-suppressing is my weakest tag: modest LDL rise reported in the Nass trial, and the record's monitoring text does list a lipid panel — flagged as low confidence. neuropsychiatric is also soft, covering the strong hypothalamic appetite drive, altered sleep architecture/vivid dreams and commonly reported lethargy. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: the elevated fasting glucose and HbA1c seen in trials (the most consistent metabolic harm) has no tag — see sermorelin note. Also untagged: cortisol elevation, and the transient paraesthesia/carpal-tunnel-like symptoms in the record's cons. dea=null — not federally scheduled; it is an unapproved investigational drug, which is a different legal status from being controlled (it is separately WADA-prohibited, S2). store=exclude: no approval in any jurisdiction, development abandoned after a cardiac safety signal, sold only as a grey-market 'research chemical', and the entry's entire documented use case is physique/anti-ageing enhancement. Same posture as the SARM default.

mots.notes: peptide: 16-aa mitochondrial-derived peptide encoded in mtDNA. hypoglycemic applied under the uncertainty rule and I want the reasoning recorded because it is the only non-obvious tag here - MOTS-c is not itself a glucose-lowering drug, but its documented mechanism is AMPK activation and increased skeletal-muscle glucose uptake independent of insulin, i.e. it acts on the same endpoint as insulin from a different direction. A user on insulin, a sulfonylurea or a GLP-1 could plausibly see additive glucose lowering, and the entry's own monitoring row leads with fasting glucose. A false positive here is a harmless 'watch your glucose' note; a false negative is a missed additive-hypoglycaemia interaction. I did NOT apply insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue - MOTS-c neither is insulin nor directly drives insulin secretion or receptor signalling, it improves sensitivity upstream via AMPK, so that tag would overstate the mechanism and the hypoglycemic tag already carries the rule that matters. DATA GAP: this record is missing halfLifeHours entirely (the field is absent, not null, unlike other records in the batch) and the only dose row is 'Research protocol: 5-10mg' with no frequency - both should be fixed regardless of store outcome. store=exclude, consistent with dihexa: no approval in any jurisdiction, no approved or clinically-supervised indication to reframe toward, human interventional data is minimal (the literature is largely observational, animal and mechanistic), and it is sourced only as a research peptide. The entry is not performance-framed in the bodybuilding sense - the framing is longevity/exercise-mimetic - but that does not create a reframe target, and shipping an injectable dosing row for an unapproved compound with no human safety data is promotion of an unapproved substance. If the reviewer disagrees and prefers reframe, the minimum would be removing the dose row entirely and presenting it as a preclinical research topic with no self-administration guidance.

mt2.notes: Cyclic alpha-MSH analogue, non-selective melanocortin agonist (MC1/3/4/5R). photosensitizing is the anchor tag and is used in the vocabulary's second sense ('drives pigmentary/skin change needing monitoring'): MC1R-driven melanogenesis, darkening of existing nevi, new nevi, and case reports of melanoma/eruptive dysplastic naevi during MT-2 use — the app's own monitoring text (photograph moles q3mo, dermatology referral) confirms this is clinically meaningful at the 0.25-1mg doses documented. bp-raising per the app's own monitoring line (transient elevation), consistent with the labelled transient pressor effect of its clinical descendant bremelanotide. gastric-emptying-delaying is extrapolated, not directly measured for MT-2: bremelanotide (a fragment/analogue of MT-2 acting on the same MC4R) carries an FDA-labelled gastric-emptying delay that cuts oral naltrexone Cmax ~60%/AUC ~40%; MT-2 hits the same receptor with a broader spectrum and produces the same dose-limiting nausea, so I applied it under the false-positive-preferred rule. Flagging it also correctly warns that oral co-medication timing matters. nitrate-contraindicated likewise extrapolated from the PT-141 entry's own text; note the pharmacological logic is weak (melanocortins raise rather than lower BP, so nitrate co-use is a haemodynamic-instability caution rather than a PDE5-style hypotension synergy) — flag for v2 review. neuropsychiatric applied for the dose-dependent yawning/stretching syndrome, drowsiness and spontaneous erections, all centrally mediated CNS effects. STORE: unapproved anywhere; UK MHRA/EU regulators have issued explicit consumer warnings; sold for cosmetic tanning plus fat loss plus libido. Not a controlled substance and there is a real clinical literature (afamelanotide is an approved MC1R agonist, bremelanotide an approved MC4R agonist), so it is not exclude-level, but the current entry is a cosmetic-use dosing table for an unapproved injectable — that is promotion under Play's rule. Reframe: strip the tanning/fat-loss dose rows, state it is unapproved with a documented melanoma-surveillance concern, and point to afamelanotide/bremelanotide as the approved counterparts. No AAS/SARM ratio applies.

nad.notes: Empty tag array is correct and intentional, not an oversight - NMN and NR are orally dosed vitamin B3 metabolites with no clinically meaningful hepatic, cardiac, hormonal, haematologic or interaction signal at 300-1000mg/day, and trials to date show a benign safety profile. Nothing in v1 applies. Specifically NOT tagged: no flushing/vasodilation issue (that is nicotinic acid, a different B3 form - do not let a rule confuse them), no lipid tag, no hypoglycemic tag despite the insulin-sensitivity claim, which is modest and not a hypoglycaemia pathway. store=ok - oral dietary supplement dosing, no performance framing, no protocol/stack language. ONE COMPLIANCE FLAG for the reviewer, which does not change my call but should be checked: FDA has taken the position (2022) that NMN is excluded from the dietary supplement definition under 201(ff)(3)(B)(ii) because it was authorised for investigation as a new drug, and has issued warning letters on that basis; NR is unaffected and is a lawful NDI. So the NR half is cleanly ok, and the NMN half is a contested-supplement-status question rather than a controlled-substance one. If the store reviewer wants zero exposure, splitting this into two records (NR ok, NMN ok-with-status-note) is cleaner than the current merged entry. Minor content note: 'Some debate whether oral NMN survives digestion without IV' should not imply IV use is a recommended route.

nad-iv.notes: No tag in v1 fits this compound, which is a real gap rather than an oversight — NAD+ is a nucleotide coenzyme, not a peptide, hormone or xenobiotic, and the vocabulary has no structural slot for it. CHECKED AND REJECTED hepatotoxic despite the entry's own 'liver enzymes if frequent high-dose infusions' monitoring line: the 2026 retrospective tolerability data on NAD+ vs NR IV found no clinically significant liver enzyme or inflammatory change during infusion or at 30 days, with enzymes stable or improved. Also rejected cardiotoxic: the chest tightness/chest pain in the cons is a rate-dependent infusion reaction attributed to supraphysiologic extracellular NAD+ acting as a proinflammatory/purinergic signal, not myocardial injury — real and common (nausea, cramping, flushing, dizziness, headache) but not cardiac damage, and slowing the rate resolves it. v1 has no tag for 'infusion reaction', which is the single most useful thing to say about this entry — v2 candidate. Store reframe rather than ok: the substance is a dietary ingredient, but IV administration is an unapproved route for unapproved indications, and the entry carries overt commercial-promotional framing ('popular clinic revenue service — high patient satisfaction', per-session pricing) that reads as promotion of an unapproved use under Play policy. Ships if rewritten neutrally as a clinician-administered infusion with an explicitly thin evidence base, the revenue/marketing lines cut, and the infusion-reaction profile stated up front.

nalt.notes: Two distinct OTC compounds in one record, which is worth flagging to the data owner — the tags below apply to different halves of it and a rule engine cannot tell them apart. NAC is N-acetylcysteine, NALT is N-acetyl-L-tyrosine; neither is a peptide (both are single acetylated amino acids), so no structural tag applies. nitrate-contraindicated is applied to the NAC half with the wording caveat that it is potentiation rather than an absolute contraindication: NAC donates the sulfhydryl groups required for nitrate bioactivation, and NAC plus nitroglycerin is a well-documented combination producing severe headache and marked hypotension. Given this app's population overlaps heavily with PDE5-inhibitor and nitrate users, the caution is worth firing. warfarin-potentiating also applies to the NAC half, on antiplatelet activity and on the measurable PT/INR prolongation seen with NAC — best characterised at the high IV doses used in paracetamol overdose, so the effect size at 600-1800mg orally is uncertain; applied under the asymmetry rule. DELIBERATE OMISSIONS: (1) Not tagged sympathomimetic for NALT. Tyrosine is a catecholamine and thyroid hormone precursor rather than a receptor agonist, and 300-500mg is small against a normal dietary tyrosine intake of 1.5-3g/day — tagging it would put a food amino acid in the same bucket as clenbuterol. The real cautions, which v1 cannot express, are with MAO inhibitors (hypertensive response), with levodopa (competition for the LAT1 transporter, both directions), and theoretically with thyroid hormone. (2) Not tagged hepatotoxic — NAC is hepatoPROTECTIVE and is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning; a hepatic-burden flag here would be exactly backwards. (3) Not tagged assay-interfering: NAC is reported to lower measured serum creatinine without a corresponding change in cystatin C or true GFR, which will make eGFR look better than it is on a monitoring panel — that is a real reporting hazard for this app, but v1 defines the tag as immunoassay interference (biotin), so I recorded it here instead. v2 should widen that tag. Also worth keeping: NAC may blunt the efficacy of some chemotherapy and, in high-dose inhaled form, can cause bronchospasm. store=reframe, and this is the non-obvious call in the record — the COMPOUNDS are unremarkable OTC supplements that would ship as ok on their own. The problem is the entry text: the pros line 'NAC: liver protection (especially valuable on oral AAS)' and the monitoring line 'especially if on oral AAS — NAC is hepatoprotective' position the supplement as cycle support that makes oral anabolic steroid use safer, and the summary frames both as adjuncts within 'hormone optimization protocols'. That is stack language attached to a Schedule III context, and it is the kind of harm-reduction framing a store reviewer reads as facilitating controlled-substance use. Strip the AAS references — general hepatic antioxidant support and glutathione repletion carry the same information without the cycle frame — and the entry ships unchanged otherwise.

nandro.notes: Structural tags: aas + 19-nor (19-nortestosterone, decanoate ester; the record's aka field also lists NPP, the phenylpropionate ester — same parent, so the same structural tags apply, though the 180h half-life shown belongs to the decanoate only and NPP is far shorter). NOT dht-derived — nandrolone is 5alpha-reduced to DHN, which is LESS androgenic than the parent, the inverse of the testosterone/DHT relationship. Practical consequence worth stating in the entry: finasteride/dutasteride do not reduce nandrolone's androgenic effect and may slightly worsen it. prolactin-raising is mandatory here and is the reason the 19-nor tag matters — nandrolone has intrinsic progestogenic activity at the progesterone receptor, which drives both hyperprolactinaemia and progestogenic gynaecomastia (a different mechanism from oestrogenic gyno, as the record's cons correctly say); the record's own monitoring line singles prolactin out. aromatizing applied although nandrolone aromatises at roughly 20% the rate of testosterone — at the documented 300-400mg/week performance row that is still enough oestradiol to be clinically meaningful, and the tag drives the E2 monitoring rule. cardiotoxic and bp-raising apply at the performance row, not the 50-100mg therapeutic row (LV hypertrophy and impaired diastolic function are documented across supraphysiologic AAS use). lipid-suppressing: nandrolone is a heavy HDL suppressor. warfarin-potentiating: AAS-class labelled anticoagulant interaction — the Deca-Durabolin label warns that anticoagulant dose may need reduction. DELIBERATELY NOT APPLIED: hepatotoxic — nandrolone decanoate is not 17-alkylated and the record's own con says hepatotoxicity is low; since the vocabulary designates `17aa-oral` as the hepatotoxicity driver, tagging non-alkylated injectables as hepatotoxic would blunt exactly the signal the rule depends on. (The monitoring text still lists liver enzymes, which is fine — ALT/AST rises in AAS users are often skeletal-muscle in origin, and a CK or GGT check disambiguates.) Also not applied: nephrotoxic — AAS-associated FSGS is documented in high-dose long-term users, but it is not nandrolone's characteristic hazard at these doses; recording here rather than tagging. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: 'deca dick' — androgen-adequate but progestogen-driven erectile/libido failure, which is the compound's signature complaint and is not captured by hpta-suppressive; also the very long detection window (months), which matters for tested athletes. aa=[125,37] is the conventionally cited rodent assay figure reproduced in the record's own summary — it is a Hershberger-type ratio with poor human correlation and must not be presented as a measured human ratio. dea=3 (AAS are Schedule III under the Anabolic Steroid Control Act). store=exclude per the Schedule III AAS default: the entry documents a 300-400mg/week performance row and cycle language ('must run with Test base'), which is stack instruction for a controlled substance.

ndt.notes: Porcine desiccated thyroid, dosed in grains (1 grain = 60-65mg, ~38mcg T4 + ~9mcg T3). Tagged identically to T4 plus the T3 considerations, because it contains both: the T3 fraction gives it real peak-and-trough kinetics, so the cardiac and CNS tags carry more weight per unit dose than T4 alone — the T4:T3 ratio of roughly 4:1 is substantially more T3 than the human thyroid's own ~14:1 output, which is the actual pharmacological objection to NDT and is not stated in the entry. 'absorption-sensitive' and 'warfarin-potentiating' as for the other thyroid entries. The 60-120mg/day therapeutic row is a normal replacement range, so no supraphysiologic escalation is documented here. TWO THINGS THE VOCABULARY CANNOT EXPRESS, both worth recording: (1) Armour Thyroid and its peers are NOT FDA-approved — they are pre-1938 grandfathered, legally marketed prescription drugs, which is a different regulatory status from levothyroxine and is misrepresented by the entry's 'Standardized by USP for iodine content' pro; (2) the monitoring row's instruction that 'TSH typically suppresses — guide dose by Free T3 target' is off-guideline and, followed literally, produces iatrogenic subclinical thyrotoxicosis with AF and bone-loss consequences. STORE 'ok' on platform grounds — it is a legally marketed prescription product described neutrally for its traditional hypothyroidism indication with no performance, weight-loss or stack framing, and it carries no scheduling. Recording that the unapproved-drug status in (1) is the one thing that could push a conservative reviewer to 'reframe'; my call is that a neutral reference description of a legally prescribable product does not amount to promoting an unapproved substance, but the TSH-suppression advice in (2) should be corrected regardless of the store decision.

nolv.notes: warfarin-potentiating is a hard labelled interaction — Nolvadex is contraindicated with coumarin anticoagulants in the risk-reduction population because of marked INR elevation; this is one of the highest-value tags in the batch. cyp3a4-substrate: tamoxifen is a prodrug, N-demethylated by CYP3A4 and 4-hydroxylated by CYP2D6 to endoxifen — 3A4 inducers/inhibitors genuinely shift exposure (CYP2D6 has no tag in v1; note that strong 2D6 inhibitors such as paroxetine/fluoxetine/bupropion reduce endoxifen and are the more important interaction, and v2 should add `cyp2d6-substrate`). qt-prolonging: verified — tamoxifen is listed by CredibleMeds as possible risk of TdP, with case reports and phase I data; the measured effect is small alone (~12ms longer QTc when combined with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor) so the real rule is 'do not stack with other QT drugs'. teratogenic: labelled fetal harm, contraception required during and for 2 months after. neuropsychiatric: mood effects are in the record's own cons. hepatotoxic applied under the stated asymmetry and flagged as a judgement call — at 6 weeks of PCT dosing hepatic burden is low, but tamoxifen causes hepatic steatosis and steatohepatitis with prolonged use and the record documents an open-ended 10-20mg/day gyno-prevention regimen. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: venous thromboembolism (a boxed warning) has no tag and is arguably tamoxifen's single most important acute risk — v2 needs `thrombogenic`; also untagged are endometrial hyperplasia/uterine malignancy (boxed) and severe hypertriglyceridaemia with pancreatitis. Deliberately NOT applied: lipid-suppressing — tamoxifen lowers LDL and does not suppress HDL, so it fails both halves of the tag definition (its lipid harm is triglycerides, which the tag does not cover). store=reframe: approved drug, but this entry is written wholly as post-anabolic-cycle recovery ('Critical PCT component', week-by-week PCT taper). Ship it framed on gynaecomastia treatment/prevention and clinician-supervised hypogonadism use, with the PCT scheduling removed.

npp.notes: Nandrolone with the short phenylpropionate ester — aas + 19-nor mandatory; 19-nor is what should drive the prolactin rule, and prolactin-raising is also tagged directly because nandrolone's progestogenic AR/PR activity causes clinically real hyperprolactinaemia, gynaecomastia and sexual dysfunction. The entry monitors prolactin monthly and its cons mention cabergoline, which confirms this fires at the documented 300-400mg/week. aromatizing: applied. Nandrolone does aromatize, at roughly 20% the rate of testosterone — lower, not zero — and the entry monitors estradiol; the combination of modest estrogen plus strong progestogenic activity is exactly why 19-nor gynaecomastia is hard to manage with an AI alone. hpta-suppressive at maximum weight (profound and slow-recovering; 'deca dick' and prolonged post-cycle hypogonadism are characteristic). lipid-suppressing, hematocrit-raising, bp-raising, cardiotoxic per AAS class at 300-400mg/week. neuropsychiatric: mood and libido effects are prominent with 19-nors. virilizing/teratogenic per androgen class. assay-interfering: verified, not inferred — nandrolone causes clinically significant false-positive elevation on testosterone immunoassays (documented on the Roche assay, most pronounced in women), and this entry asks users to track testosterone, so LC-MS/MS should be specified or the monitoring plan produces wrong numbers. warfarin-potentiating: androgen class effect on anticoagulant sensitivity. hepatotoxic NOT applied — nandrolone is not 17-alkylated and hepatic burden by the intramuscular route is low, despite the entry listing liver function in monitoring. aa = [125, 37], the conventionally cited rodent figure only. dea = 3. Store = exclude: Schedule III, explicit stack language ('must run with testosterone base').

osta.notes: dea=null: SARMs are not federally scheduled in the US. They are unapproved new drugs - illegal to market for human consumption, and ostarine specifically has drawn FDA warning letters and is WADA-prohibited - but that is a different legal category from a DEA schedule, and the distinction matters if any UI copy is generated from this field. hepatotoxic is CONFIRMED, not speculative: the published SARM DILI series counts 3 ostarine cases among 15 total, cholestatic pattern; the entry's soft 'liver enzyme elevations reported at higher doses' understates it. lipid-suppressing is well established (dose-dependent HDL reduction was seen in the GTx Phase II work itself). hpta-suppressive confirmed even at therapeutic doses - the entry's 'minimal suppression' framing is contradicted by its own cons and monitoring rows. hematocrit-raising applied under the uncertainty rule: enobosarm trials showed only small haemoglobin increases and this is the weakest tag in the set, but AR agonism at the documented 20-25mg/day performance row makes a false negative the worse error. virilizing applied because the app documents a women's dose row (5-10mg/day) - androgenic effects are lower than AAS but voice change and hair effects are reported and are irreversible, so this needs to be tagged for a women's-dosing rule to exist at all. teratogenic is extrapolated from AR agonism rather than direct data; applied under the asymmetry rule. aa=null deliberately - the '10:1'-style figures quoted for SARMs are muscle-vs-prostate tissue-selectivity ratios, which are NOT the same scale as the Hershberger anabolic:androgenic figures where testosterone=100:100. Populating aa with a selectivity ratio would make ostarine look directly comparable to an AAS row and would be misleading. store=exclude: unapproved drug, no approved indication anywhere to reframe toward, and the entry documents an explicit performance dose row plus mini-PCT protocol guidance. Being the best-researched SARM does not change the store posture.

oxan.notes: Structural: aas + 17aa-oral (oxandrolone is 17alpha-methylated — the 2-oxa ring substitution reduces but does not remove hepatic burden) + dht-derived (it is 2-oxa-17alpha-methyl-DHT). hepatotoxic applied despite the record's 'mild hepatotoxicity' framing: the Oxandrin label carries the AAS class boxed warning for peliosis hepatis and hepatic neoplasms, and cholestatic jaundice occurs; at the documented 40-80mg/day performance row this is meaningful, not theoretical. The entry's own countermeasure line (TUDCA + milk thistle) should not be read as making the risk optional. lipid-suppressing is arguably oxandrolone's WORST property and directly contradicts its 'mild' reputation — 17-alkylated orals are the most aggressive HDL suppressors of any AAS class, with HDL reductions of 50%+ reported; this tag matters more here than the hepatotoxicity. warfarin-potentiating is a specific, quantified labelled interaction, not a class inference: co-administration with oxandrolone has required warfarin dose reductions of roughly 85% to maintain target INR. This is the single most actionable interaction in the batch. virilizing applied and I want to flag a factual problem with the entry text: the pro 'Women can use at low doses without virilization risk' is not accurate — virilisation (clitoromegaly, voice deepening, hirsutism) occurs in women on oxandrolone and voice change in particular is irreversible; at the documented 5-10mg/day female row the risk is reduced, not absent. That claim should be corrected regardless of the store decision. bp-raising is my softest tag here (oxandrolone causes little water retention, so the usual oedema route is weak) — applied under the asymmetry rule on the strength of the AAS-class hypertension signal and severe dyslipidaemia. cardiotoxic follows from the same dyslipidaemia plus supraphysiologic dosing. DELIBERATELY NOT APPLIED: aromatizing — oxandrolone is a DHT derivative and is not an aromatase substrate, so oestradiol does not rise and an AI is not indicated; a false positive here would produce actively wrong advice. Also not applied: nephrotoxic. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: androgenic alopecia in susceptible individuals (the record's own con), and the grey-market counterfeiting/underdosing problem it flags. aa=[322,24]: the conventionally cited figure is a RANGE, 322-630 anabolic to 24 androgenic (the record's own summary gives it as 322-630:24); I have entered the conservative lower bound since the schema takes a single pair — the range should be preserved in display text. As with all such figures this is rodent assay-derived with poor human correlation. dea=3. store=exclude per the Schedule III AAS default. Worth noting for the record that oxandrolone is one of the few AAS with live FDA approval (adjunctive weight gain after weight loss/trauma, chronic infection; burn and Turner syndrome literature), so a purely clinical entry is conceivable — but this entry documents 40-80mg/day performance dosing, a women's physique row and hepatic-support stacking, which is well past what a reframe could repair.

oxytocin.notes: Nonapeptide, FDA-approved as Pitocin for obstetric use only; not scheduled. neuropsychiatric is unambiguous and the entry says so itself ('emotionally sensitizing — can intensify negative as well as positive emotions'), plus documented anxiety/mood effects with repeated intranasal dosing. qt-prolonging and cardiotoxic: QTc prolongation, tachyarrhythmia and myocardial ischaemia are listed postmarketing effects; verified by search — the signal is strongest with IV bolus in the obstetric setting, well above the 8-24 IU intranasal / 5-10 IU SubQ this entry documents, so both tags are precautionary at these doses but retained per the stated false-positive-preferred asymmetry (they matter for anyone stacking other QT-prolonging agents). electrolyte-disturbing: oxytocin has intrinsic vasopressin/V2 cross-activity, and dilutional hyponatraemia with seizures, coma and death is a well-documented, fatal-capable effect — again an infusion-context risk, but the app documents parenteral SubQ self-administration, which is the case where a user could push dose and free water together. teratogenic applied under the vocabulary's 'established fetal risk' wording rather than in the strict malformation sense: oxytocin is a uterotonic and is contraindicated in pregnancy outside supervised induction (uterine hyperstimulation, fetal distress, rupture) — this is the pregnancy-block rule and it must fire. CHECKED AND REJECTED: prolactin-raising — evidence is genuinely mixed, bolus and infusion oxytocin did not change basal or TRH-stimulated prolactin in human studies (it only potentiates the VIP-driven response), so this is not applied. Also checked and rejected hpta-suppressive: prolonged intranasal oxytocin left reproductive hormones stable. Store reframe, not ok: oxytocin is approved, but this entry documents an entirely off-label self-administered use (libido, bonding, 'performance and recovery' dosing, TRT-clinic adjunct) for an injectable prescription drug. To ship it must be restated as the approved obstetric indication plus a clearly-labelled investigational intranasal research literature, with the 'Performance and recovery' dose row removed.

p21pep.notes: CNTF-derived small peptide mimetic (the literature compound is P021, Iqbal/NYS IBR lab). 'peptide' is the only clean structural tag; it is not a GH-axis agent so 'gh-axis' does not apply. 'neuropsychiatric' applied on the rule-of-application asymmetry: the entire documented effect is CNS (neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, mood), the app's own monitoring row is cognitive and mood tracking, and a compound whose target organ is the brain should trip CNS interaction rules even though no specific adverse psychiatric signal is characterised in humans. The 'theoretical cancer risk from uncontrolled neurogenesis' con has no tag in v1 — a proliferative/oncogenic-risk tag would be a reasonable v2 candidate, and it is the single most important warning on this entry. STORE: 'reframe' rather than 'exclude'. It is not a controlled substance, not scheduled anywhere, has no performance-enhancement framing, and does have a genuine (if entirely preclinical, rodent-only) research literature — that fits the vocabulary's 'research peptide with legitimate clinical-research literature and no performance framing' case. But it has zero human trials and no approval in any jurisdiction, so the row 'Research dose: 100-200mcg' functions as a human dosing protocol for an unapproved drug and must be removed before a store build; the entry needs rewriting as a description of preclinical research with no dose guidance. Flagging that this is the closest call in the batch — if the reviewer wants a conservative posture on unapproved research peptides generally, this is the one entry here that could defensibly go to 'exclude'.

pct1.notes: NOT A COMPOUND — this is a protocol record with medium=null, halfLifeHours=null and no single substance. I have tagged it with the union of its constituents' properties so that interaction rules still fire when a user has this protocol active: the SERM tags come from tamoxifen (serm, cyp3a4-substrate, warfarin-potentiating, qt-prolonging, teratogenic, neuropsychiatric) and clomiphene (serm, cyp3a4-substrate, teratogenic, neuropsychiatric). I did NOT propagate tamoxifen's `hepatotoxic`, since the protocol's tamoxifen exposure is the 6-week course where hepatic burden is low. The third dose row ('TRT discontinuation: HCG 500IU 3x/wk x 3 wks then Nolva + Clomid standard') additionally carries hCG's properties — peptide, aromatizing, hpta-suppressive, hematocrit-raising, assay-interfering (see record hcg2) — which I have deliberately left off the tag array to avoid attributing hCG properties to the two SERM-only variants; if the rules engine resolves protocols by expanding constituents rather than by reading protocol-level tags, that is the better mechanism and these tags should be treated as a fallback. dea=null and aa=null because it is not a substance. store=exclude, unambiguous: the record exists solely to instruct recovery from a suppressive anabolic steroid cycle. It presupposes and therefore facilitates Schedule III AAS use (Apple 1.4.3 — encouraging consumption of controlled substances), it is protocol/stack content rather than neutral reference (the distinction Google Play draws), and its third row pairs hCG with cycle discontinuation, hitting the explicit Play prohibition on hCG promoted in conjunction with anabolic steroids. There is no reframe that preserves the record, because removing the cycle premise removes the record's reason to exist.

pda.notes: Pentadeca arginate is a BPC-157 analogue with arginate salt substitution intended to improve stability; peptide is the only defensible structural tag. No risk tag can be justified because there is essentially no data in either direction — and that absence is itself the point. This is the weakest-evidence entry in the batch by a wide margin: the entry's own cons concede 'even more limited human data than BPC-157', 'long-term safety completely unknown', and 'mechanism not fully characterized'. Its commercial existence is largely a downstream consequence of BPC-157 being restricted from compounding, which is a marketing pathway rather than a scientific one. Any claim of superiority over BPC-157 in the current text is unsupported and must not survive a rewrite. dea=null, not federally scheduled. aa=null. store=reframe, but this is the least confident store call I am making and I want that flagged for a human reviewer. The rule in section D offers two branches — thin-evidence-but-legitimate-research-literature to reframe, whole-documented-use-is-performance to exclude — and PDA fits neither cleanly: its framing is therapeutic (healing, vascular repair) rather than performance, which argues against exclude, but it lacks the 'large legitimate clinical-research literature' that the reframe branch presumes. I land on reframe because neutral risk-describing reference about a non-controlled substance is permitted, but a stricter reviewer could reasonably call this exclude, and if the policy posture tightens this is the first entry in the batch that should move.

pinealon.notes: Khavinson tripeptide Glu-Asp-Arg. neuropsychiatric is applied for CNS activity, not for a documented adverse psychiatric signal — I want that distinction on record so it is not misread. The entire documented action of this compound is central (sleep architecture, circadian regulation, cognition, neuronal gene expression), and the tag exists to drive additive-CNS-effect rules, so a compound whose whole purpose is CNS modulation should trigger them — particularly stacking with melatonin or other sedatives, which is a plausible real-world combination given the sleep claims. Applied under the asymmetry rule. No other risk tags apply. Store: no approval outside the Russian bioregulator market, no Western clinical data, but also no performance framing — the dose row is cognition and sleep. Reframe as an unapproved investigational peptide with the evidence base stated honestly, including that the research is near-entirely from a single group and lacks independent replication, which the current entry does concede in its cons.

pregnenolone.notes: The most upstream steroid (cholesterol -> pregnenolone) and a neurosteroid in its own right. 'neuropsychiatric' is the core tag and is bidirectional, which is unusual and worth preserving in the entry text: pregnenolone and its metabolite allopregnanolone are positive allosteric modulators at GABA-A while pregnenolone sulfate is a GABA-A negative modulator and an NMDA positive modulator — hence the entry's contradictory cons ('anxiolytic' and 'may worsen anxiety in some individuals' are both true, in different people and at different doses). It has additive sedative potential with alcohol, benzodiazepines and other GABAergics, and stimulation/insomnia at the 100-200mg rows. 'aromatizing' applied on the uncertainty asymmetry and on the app's own framing rather than on strong human data — I want this recorded as a soft call. Oral pregnenolone reliably raises pregnenolone sulfate, allopregnanolone and DHEA-S; downstream conversion to oestradiol and testosterone is enzyme-limited, tissue-dependent and inconsistently demonstrated in humans. But the entry itself says 'can convert to any steroid — unpredictable conversion pathway' and 'conversion to unwanted hormones possible', and its monitoring row tracks oestradiol, progesterone and cortisol, so an oestrogen-conversion rule should fire. NOT tagged 'virilizing' by the same evidence standard — conversion to androgens is even less well demonstrated than conversion to oestrogens — though I acknowledge the inconsistency of applying one conversion tag and not the other; a v2 'hormone-precursor / unpredictable-downstream-conversion' tag would express this correctly and would be the right fix for both this record and DHEA. NOT 'aas'. The 'can increase cortisol' con has no v1 tag. Note the record's pros and cons arrays are visibly duplicated (two overlapping sets merged) and should be de-duplicated in the entry regardless of tagging. Also note the dose rows conflict: 'Neurological Support: 10-30mg/day' sits beside 'Cognitive / Mood: 50-100mg/day' for what is effectively the same indication. STORE 'ok': legal OTC dietary supplement in the US at supplement doses, not scheduled, no performance framing.
