primo.notes: CONTENT ERROR TO FIX: methenolone acetate is a 1-methyl (1-methyl-5a-androst-1-ene) oral, NOT 17a-alkylated - verified. So 17aa-oral must NOT be applied here even though the app documents an oral row at 100-150mg/day, and the cons line 'Oral form has hepatotoxicity' overstates the mechanism. I still applied hepatotoxic, deliberately and conservatively: the oral row is 100-150mg/day of a compound with only 3-15% oral bioavailability (the price of not being alkylated), methenolone acetate is reported to burden hepatic cholesterol handling more than testosterone or nandrolone, and the entry's own monitoring says 'liver enzymes (especially oral)'. Treat this as a soft hepatotoxic, an order of magnitude below any true 17aa oral - if the rules engine grades severity, this should be the lowest band. SECOND CONTENT ERROR: 'FDA-approved for immune deficiency conditions' is not supportable - methenolone was a Schering product, is not currently FDA-approved for any indication, and the immune-deficiency claim should be struck. Non-aromatising, so no aromatizing tag. Not a 19-nor. bp-raising/cardiotoxic/hematocrit-raising applied on the supraphysiologic-AAS class basis - 400-600mg/wk is well above any replacement equivalent, and the 'one of the safest AAS' framing in the summary is a dosing-independent claim that does not survive the dose rows actually documented. virilizing applied despite low androgenicity: methenolone is commonly used by women precisely because it is mild, but at the documented 400-600mg/wk it is virilizing. aa [88,44] is the conventionally cited rodent figure (sources give 88:44-57); not a human measurement. store=exclude: Schedule III, no current approved indication to reframe toward, and the entry is performance-framed throughout including the counterfeit-sourcing discussion, which reads as purchasing guidance.

primooral.notes: IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL CORRECTION: methenolone acetate is NOT 17alpha-alkylated. Oral bioavailability comes from 1-methylation of the DHT backbone plus the 17-beta acetate ester, not from 17aa. So no 17aa-oral tag — this is one of the few orals where that tag genuinely does not apply and the entry's claim of being gentler on the liver is structurally true. I still applied hepatotoxic, as a deliberate false-positive under the stated asymmetry rule: the documented 75-100mg/day taken daily is a large first-pass burden, mild transaminase elevation is reported, and the entry itself lists LFTs in monitoring. Downstream rules should treat this as a much lower hepatic tier than the 17aa orals in this batch. Non-aromatizing (DHT-derived, 1-methyl), so no aromatizing tag. virilizing applied despite the entry's 'mild enough some women use it' line — that line is the exact framing that produces missed virilization, and 88:44 is a rodent assay figure with poor human correlation. lipid-suppressing applied: mild per mg but the dose rows are high because potency is low, so total HDL burden is not mild. store=exclude: Schedule III; methenolone acetate (Primobolan tablets) has been discontinued in essentially all markets and the entry is performance-framed.

progesterone.notes: No structural tag fits — progesterone is a progestogen, not an AAS, SARM, peptide, SERM, AI or thyroid hormone. The vocabulary has no 'progestogen' or 'neurosteroid' tag; flagging both for v2, since a progestogen tag would be the correct driver for the prolactin/sedation/thrombosis rules rather than borrowing adjacent tags. neuropsychiatric is squarely supported and is the app's own listed con — sedation via the allopregnanolone metabolite acting as a positive allosteric modulator at GABA-A; this is why the 100-200mg dose is bedtime-only, and it matters for interaction rules with other CNS depressants. hpta-suppressive applied with moderate confidence: progesterone exerts genuine negative feedback on GnRH pulse frequency (the mechanism behind progestin contraception), though at 100-200mg oral micronized nightly the effect is luteal-physiologic rather than the full suppression an AAS produces — applied per the stated asymmetry, noted as modest. 5ar-inhibitor is the weakest call here and I want the uncertainty on record: progesterone is a competitive 5a-reductase substrate/inhibitor in vitro, and the entry itself claims 'reduces DHT conversion in men (modest)', but human data are unimpressive (Serafini/Lobo found a rise in serum progesterone had only minimal effect on circulating 5a-reduced androgen metabolites). Applied per the asymmetry rule since the app markets the men's 10-20mg dose specifically for this, but it should NOT be treated as finasteride-equivalent by any downstream rule — recommend v2 add a strength qualifier. cyp3a4-substrate is solid: oral micronized progesterone undergoes heavy first-pass CYP3A4 metabolism, so 3A4 inhibitors/inducers meaningfully shift exposure. absorption-sensitive covers two documented effects — food substantially increases oral bioavailability (labeled), and the entry's own con notes transdermal cream absorption is highly variable. Deliberately NOT teratogenic: unlike testosterone, micronized progesterone is given deliberately IN pregnancy for luteal support and IVF; tagging it would generate a caution that contradicts standard obstetric practice. Some synthetic progestins do carry first-trimester concerns, but this entry is bioidentical. dea=null, not federally scheduled. aa=null, not an AAS. store=ok: FDA-approved (Prometrium/Utrogestan), legal, non-scheduled, and all three dose rows sit within or below approved ranges. The sleep-optimization and men's-adjunct rows are off-label rather than performance or unapproved-substance use, which is not what the Play or Apple rules target.

proviron.notes: Mesterolone = 1a-methyl-DHT, so aas + dht-derived. Critically NOT 17aa-oral: the alkyl group is at C1, not C17, which is exactly why this oral is not hepatotoxic and why the entry's claim of 'low hepatotoxicity vs other orals' is correct. No hepatotoxic tag — the structural rule about 17-alkylation is doing real work here and a reflexive '17aa because it is an oral' call would have been wrong. aromatase-inhibitor: applied, verified. Mesterolone binds and weakly inhibits aromatase (notable but well short of anastrozole/exemestane) in addition to displacing estradiol from SHBG. This is the highest-value interaction tag on this entry — a user running Proviron 50-75mg/day ON TOP of an AI is a realistic estradiol-crash scenario, and the entry's own monitoring asks for E2. Not aromatizing (it cannot convert to estrogen). hpta-suppressive: the entry concedes LH suppression; at 50-75mg/day it is more than 'mild'. lipid-suppressing: the entry's own con list states HDL reduction; non-aromatizing DHT-class orals are disproportionately bad for HDL. hematocrit-raising and virilizing/teratogenic are androgen class effects ('not suitable for females' per the entry; female-fetus virilization is the established teratogenic mechanism for all androgens). assay-interfering: DHT-class androgens cross-react in testosterone immunoassays, and this entry asks users to track free testosterone and DHT — LC-MS/MS should be specified. warfarin-potentiating: androgens as a class increase sensitivity to oral anticoagulants (labelled interaction across testosterone products); applied as class inference. aa = [125, 35] as a midpoint of the conventionally cited 100-150 : 30-40. Emphasise in copy: these are rodent assay-derived figures with poor human correlation, and mesterolone is the textbook case where the number lies — the nominal anabolic rating exceeds testosterone but real anabolic activity is minimal because mesterolone is reduced to inactive diol metabolites in muscle, which is why the entry itself says 'minimal anabolic effect alone'. dea = 3 (AAS). Store = exclude: Schedule III, never FDA-approved in the US, and the entry carries an explicit 'Cycle Support' dose row.

pt141.notes: Bremelanotide, FDA-approved as Vyleesi for acquired generalised HSDD in premenopausal women. Verified against the label: (1) transient increase in blood pressure with reflex heart-rate reduction after each dose, peaking ~2-4h — bp-raising confirmed, and it is why the label contraindicates uncontrolled hypertension and known cardiovascular disease; (2) it slows gastric emptying and can reduce the rate and extent of absorption of co-administered oral drugs — oral naltrexone Cmax fell ~60% and AUC ~40%, and the label advises against co-use with oral naltrexone products — so gastric-emptying-delaying is label-supported, not inferred, and is the most under-appreciated interaction on this record; (3) focal hyperpigmentation (face, gingiva, breast) occurs and is more frequent with more-than-daily dosing and in darker skin types, and it may not fully resolve — photosensitizing in the vocabulary's pigmentary-change sense, matching the app's own 'skin hyperpigmentation assessment' monitoring line. nitrate-contraindicated applied because the app's own cons state 'cannot use with nitrates'; I could not confirm a nitrate contraindication in the Vyleesi PI (the actual contraindications are uncontrolled hypertension and known CVD), so this is most likely a carried-over PDE5-inhibitor caution. Left applied under the false-positive-preferred rule but flagged here as probably inherited error — worth correcting in the entry text, since it is also pharmacologically backwards (bremelanotide raises BP). Did not apply neuropsychiatric: nausea, flushing and headache are centrally mediated but are not mood/CNS-behavioural effects of the kind that tag exists to warn about. STORE ok: this is an FDA-approved prescription drug and the entry states the approved indication and mechanism accurately. Caveat recorded rather than escalated to reframe — the male dose rows ('Male Sexual Dysfunction: 1-2mg', and the internally inconsistent 'Standard: 1.75mg' / 'High Response: 1mg' rows, which look mis-entered and should be fixed regardless) are off-label; off-label discussion of an approved drug is standard in clinical reference material and is not what Play/Apple prohibit, but the male rows should be explicitly labelled off-label. Not scheduled; no anabolic ratio applies.

quercetin.notes: Dietary flavonol, the 'Q' of the D+Q senolytic protocol. Same shape as fisetin and the same absent structural tag. cyp3a4-inhibitor is well established for quercetin (in vitro and in vivo; documented interactions with cyclosporine, midazolam and other 3A4 substrates), and it also inhibits P-glycoprotein and OATP transporters and sulfotransferases — transporter inhibition has no v1 tag and is worth noting for v2, since P-gp inhibition is a real mechanism for raising exposure of co-administered drugs independent of CYP. warfarin-potentiating applied: quercetin inhibits CYP2C9, competes with warfarin for albumin binding, and has antiplatelet activity; the entry's own cons row flags interaction with blood thinners. absorption-sensitive: quercetin aglycone has notoriously poor and variable oral bioavailability, materially altered by formulation (phytosome, bromelain co-administration, fat) and by the glycoside form used — the entry flags this itself, and it means the 1000mg/day senolytic-pulse figure is formulation-dependent rather than absolute. Recorded but untagged: the quinolone-antibiotic interaction the entry mentions is not an absorption effect on quercetin — it is competition at bacterial DNA gyrase potentially reducing antibiotic efficacy, plus quercetin's own weak gyrase activity — and no v1 tag expresses 'may reduce efficacy of a co-administered drug'. Also untagged: high-dose intravenous quercetin has caused renal toxicity in oncology trials, but that is IV-specific and does not translate to the oral doses documented here, so nephrotoxic was deliberately not applied; and high-dose quercetin has weak thyroid-peroxidase-inhibitory activity in vitro, which is not clinically meaningful at these doses but is the one thing I would keep an eye on if daily gram dosing became long-term. STORE ok: dietary supplement, food-derived, widely sold OTC. Note that the monitoring text and cons import dasatinib-specific warnings (CBC monitoring, 'full senolytic effects require dasatinib combination') into a supplement entry — that cross-reference is what pulls a prescription chemotherapy agent into a consumer-facing supplement record and should be softened even though the store call stays ok. Not scheduled.

rad140.notes: dea=null - not federally scheduled. hepatotoxic CONFIRMED: 6 published RAD-140 DILI cases including a biopsy-proven canalicular cholestasis case with peak bilirubin 38.5 mg/dL in a 24-year-old after only 5 weeks of use. This is severe, fast-onset injury and the entry's 'liver enzyme elevations reported' badly undersells it. neuropsychiatric applied on the app's own documented aggression and mood changes at higher doses - RAD is the one SARM in this batch where that is consistently reported. hpta-suppressive is high-confidence (among the most suppressive SARMs). lipid-suppressing confirmed. hematocrit-raising precautionary. virilizing supported by the entry's own hair-loss con. teratogenic extrapolated from AR agonism; note the 60h half-life is the longest in this group, so washout guidance matters. CONTENT ERROR: the summary states RAD-140 has 'an anabolic:androgenic ratio of 90:1 compared to testosterone at 100:100'. That is a category error - the 90:1 figure is a tissue-selectivity ratio from preclinical work and is not on the Hershberger scale where testosterone is 100:100, so the two numbers are not comparable and the sentence implies RAD is somehow near-testosterone-anabolic with negligible androgenicity. I set aa=null rather than encode 90:1, because storing it would propagate the same error into any comparison table. The claim should be rewritten or removed. Also flagging: 'neuroprotective' and 'Alzheimer's research' claims are preclinical only and read as efficacy claims. store=exclude - unapproved drug, no approved indication, explicit performance dose rows.

raloxifene.notes: FDA-approved (Evista) for postmenopausal osteoporosis and breast cancer risk reduction; the use documented here — reversing established gynecomastia in men on androgens — is entirely off-label. serm is the structural tag; it is a benzothiophene SERM, ER antagonist at breast and (unlike tamoxifen) at uterus, agonist at bone. absorption-sensitive APPLIED: raloxifene undergoes extensive enterohepatic recycling, and cholestyramine (and by extension other bile-acid sequestrants) reduces absorption by roughly 60% — a real, labelled, clinically significant interaction. cardiotoxic APPLIED as a judgement call, and the reason is a vocabulary gap: raloxifene's serious cardiovascular signal is THROMBOEMBOLIC (VTE/PE, ~3x, boxed warning) plus increased fatal stroke in postmenopausal women with established CHD or at high stroke risk (RUTH trial, boxed warning). Neither is 'direct cardiac toxicity' in the hypertrophy/arrhythmia sense the tag defines, and strictly read the tag does not fit — but the entry's own con list flags clot risk and there is no thrombogenic/prothrombotic tag available, so leaving it untagged would drop the single most important safety property of this compound. Recommend a `thrombogenic` tag for v2 and re-tagging this entry then. teratogenic applied: pregnancy-contraindicated, fetal harm in animal reproduction studies, and no benefit in a population that could become pregnant. NOT TAGGED, recorded: raloxifene DECREASES prothrombin time when given with warfarin (about 10%) — that is the opposite direction to warfarin-potentiating, so tagging it would produce a wrong-signed warning; it still warrants INR monitoring on initiation. Not hepatotoxic in any meaningful sense, though it is contraindicated in hepatic impairment (glucuronidation-dependent clearance). Not hpta-suppressive — SERMs raise LH/FSH in men, the opposite. store=reframe: approved drug, but the entry text is written around cycle management ('not a substitute for an AI on cycle', 'in the performance context'). Ships once reframed to the approved osteoporosis/breast-cancer-risk indications with gynecomastia noted as a physician-directed off-label use.

rapamycin.notes: immunosuppressive is the approved indication itself, not a side effect — the entry's weekly-pulse rationale for avoiding it is plausible mechanistically (mTORC1 vs mTORC2 selectivity) but is not established in humans, so the tag stands at the documented 5-10mg weekly doses. lipid-suppressing applied in its 'raises LDL' sense: sirolimus causes hypercholesterolaemia and marked hypertriglyceridaemia — this is one of its most consistent metabolic effects and the entry lists it twice in cons. cyp3a4-substrate is the highest-value interaction tag in this record: sirolimus is a CYP3A4 AND P-gp substrate with a narrow therapeutic index, so azoles, clarithromycin, ritonavir and grapefruit can raise levels severalfold, while rifampin, carbamazepine and St John's wort collapse them. Note for the rule engine: resveratrol, also in this batch, is a CYP3A4 inhibitor and longevity stacks routinely combine the two — that pairing should fire. absorption-sensitive for the same reason plus the label's requirement to dose consistently with respect to food (a high-fat meal materially changes AUC). nephrotoxic applied on the asymmetry rule: sirolimus is less nephrotoxic than calcineurin inhibitors but causes de novo and worsening proteinuria and can impair recovery from ischaemic renal injury — the mechanism is podocyte/glomerular, not tubular. teratogenic: the label requires effective contraception during treatment and for 12 weeks after discontinuation, with embryo-fetal toxicity in animals — that is enough. bp-raising applied with recorded uncertainty: hypertension is a common adverse reaction in the transplant trials, but those patients were on calcineurin inhibitors and steroids and had renal disease, so attribution at weekly longevity doses is genuinely unclear. Applied per the asymmetry rule; flag the uncertainty in rule text. NOT tagged hypoglycemic — mTOR inhibition does the OPPOSITE, causing insulin resistance and new-onset hyperglycaemia/diabetes after transplant. v1 has no hyperglycaemia tag; that is a real gap for this compound and metformin/acarbose co-use is a rational response to it. Three further effects v1 cannot express and which belong in notes: impaired wound healing (stop before elective surgery), aphthous mouth ulcers (the dose-limiting nuisance), and myelosuppression — anaemia, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia, which also means rapamycin will LOWER haematocrit, the opposite direction from most of this app's catalogue. store=reframe, a light one: rapamycin is an approved, non-controlled prescription drug, so no platform rule prohibits it, and the entry already says physician supervision is required. But shipping a table of self-selected weekly doses ('Longevity Protocol: 2-6mg') for an off-label indication of a potent immunosuppressant is the promotional posture Play objects to. Lead with the approved transplant indication, label the longevity dosing as investigational and prescriber-set, and cite the PEARL/Dog Aging Project work as ongoing rather than as validation.

resveratrol.notes: This looks like an inert supplement and is mostly treated as one, but it carries one genuinely underappreciated interaction risk, which is why it gets three tags. cyp3a4-inhibitor is verified in humans, not just in vitro: in a 42-volunteer study (Chow et al., Cancer Prev Res 2010) 1g/day resveratrol inhibited CYP3A4, CYP2D6 and CYP2C9 phenotypic indices — a 33% geometric-mean rise in buspirone AUC in high-baseline-activity subjects — while inducing CYP1A2. Resveratrol is also a mechanism-based (irreversible) CYP3A4 inactivator in vitro. The documented 250-500mg/day is below the 1g study dose, so the effect size is uncertain at label dose, but the asymmetry rule applies. This matters concretely inside this batch: resveratrol plus rapamycin is a standard longevity stack and resveratrol will tend to raise sirolimus levels. warfarin-potentiating for the combination of CYP2C9 inhibition (the losartan probe in the same study) and resveratrol's documented antiplatelet/anti-aggregatory activity — bleeding risk with warfarin, DOACs, aspirin and fish oil, and it should be stopped before surgery. absorption-sensitive: resveratrol's oral bioavailability is famously poor (~20% vs ~80% for pterostilbene), it undergoes extensive first-pass glucuronidation and sulfation, and the entry itself says to take it with fat. UNCERTAINTY AND DELIBERATE OMISSIONS: (1) Not tagged serm or aromatase-inhibitor despite the cons list flagging 'estrogenic activity at high doses'. Resveratrol is a phytoestrogen with mixed ER agonist/antagonist behaviour and is a weak in vitro aromatase inhibitor, but neither is clinically meaningful at 250-500mg/day, and tagging it serm would wrongly bucket it with tamoxifen/raloxifene. This is worth a v2 'phytoestrogenic' tag — the estrogen question is not trivial for this app's audience. (2) Not tagged hepatotoxic or nephrotoxic: the entry's 'liver enzymes at high doses' line and the renal events seen in the SRT501 micronised-resveratrol multiple-myeloma trial both occurred at multi-gram doses in a sick population, not at the doses documented here. store=ok: dietary supplement sold OTC, honest about the weak mammalian evidence, no medical claim requiring reframing.

retatrutide.notes: Triple GIP/GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist; `glp1` applies directly under the vocabulary's dual/triple incretin clause. `insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue` for the GLP-1/GIP-driven glucose-dependent insulin secretion, and `hypoglycemic` because that becomes clinically real when stacked on insulin or a sulfonylurea — monotherapy hypoglycaemia risk is low, co-therapy risk is not, and the app's population stacks. `gastric-emptying-delaying` is a defining class action; note it also alters the absorption of co-administered oral drugs — I did not apply `absorption-sensitive` because that tag is scoped to the compound's OWN absorption, which for a weekly injectable is not meaningfully altered; the outbound effect is already carried by the gastric-emptying tag, but confirm the rule engine reads it that way. `nephrotoxic` applied not for direct tubular toxicity but for the labelled class risk of AKI secondary to volume depletion from nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea — at the 12mg/week the record documents, GI burden is the highest in the class, and the entry itself says GI effects are potentially more pronounced than tirzepatide. `cardiotoxic` is the judgement call in this entry: retatrutide produces dose-dependent heart-rate increases that peak around 24 weeks before declining, and the phase 3 commentary flags closer monitoring for pre-existing tachyarrhythmia. That is not classical cardiotoxicity, and the same trials showed improved systolic BP, non-HDL-C, triglycerides and hsCRP — so `bp-raising` and `lipid-suppressing` are affirmatively wrong here. I applied `cardiotoxic` anyway for the chronotropic signal, because this app's users co-administer clenbuterol, T3 and stimulants, and an additive tachycardia rule is worth a false positive; read the tag as 'heart-rate/arrhythmia caution', and consider a dedicated `hr-raising` tag in v2 so it stops overloading `cardiotoxic`. `neuropsychiatric` applied for the mood/suicidality monitoring advice carried on weight-management labels; EMA and FDA reviews found no causal association, so this is precautionary — recorded here so it is not mistaken for an established effect. Class risks with no tag available: pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, rodent thyroid C-cell tumours, and lean-mass loss. dea null — investigational, not scheduled. aa null. STORE reframe: verified still unapproved as of this tagging (TRIUMPH-1 phase 3 read out, regulatory submission anticipated 2026, no FDA decision), so the approved-drug-for-approved-indication exemption does not apply. Two things must be removed: the 1-12mg/week dose rows, which are trial doses being presented as a usable protocol for a drug obtainable only through grey-market research channels, and the 'Muscle loss without testosterone and resistance training' con, which is anabolic stack language. Rewritten as an investigational-pipeline reference with trial outcomes and no dosing, it ships.

rhgh.notes: peptide applied: somatropin is a 191-aa recombinant polypeptide - it sits at the protein end of the peptide tag but is aqueous injectable and behaves like the rest of the peptide cohort for handling/storage rules, so tagging it is more useful than not. gh-axis is definitional. DIRECTIONAL VOCABULARY GAP: the metabolic risk here is hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance, and I did NOT apply hypoglycemic because that tag points the wrong way - GH raises glucose. There is no hyperglycemic / insulin-resistance tag in v1, so the entry's own repeated warning ('can raise blood glucose / insulin resistance', HbA1c monitoring) is currently untaggable. Requesting `hyperglycemic` or `glucose-raising` for v2; this matters because a diabetic-user rule built from these tags would silently miss GH. electrolyte-disturbing applied for GH-driven renal sodium retention and the resulting fluid retention/oedema/carpal tunnel picture the entry documents; it is a slightly loose fit for a tag framed around K/Na/Mg but the sodium retention is real and dose-dependent. bp-raising follows from that fluid retention. cardiotoxic applied for the documented 'acromegaly features at chronic supraphysiological doses' at the 4-6+ IU/day performance row - acromegalic cardiomyopathy is the concern, not anything at replacement dosing. dea=null: somatropin is NOT a federally controlled substance. Flagging two things the legal reviewer needs: (1) distribution/possession of hGH for non-approved uses is separately criminalised under 21 USC 333(e), which is a real constraint even without a DEA schedule; (2) several US states (e.g. some schedule it alongside AAS) control hGH at state level, so 'null' is federal only. store=reframe, not ok: somatropin is genuinely FDA-approved with real supervised indications (adult GHD, HIV wasting, short bowel, Turner), which is exactly the reframe case. But it cannot ship as written - the 'Anti-aging / Wellness: 1-2 IU/day', 'Body Composition: 2-4 IU/day' and 'Performance: 4-6+ IU/day' rows are all non-approved uses, the anti-aging efficacy claims are unsupported, and 'Synergistic with peptide GH secretagogues' is stack language. Reframe = keep the compound, strip every non-medical dose row, state the approved indications, and keep 'Medical (GHD): Physician titrated' as the only dosing content.

selank.notes: Synthetic tuftsin analogue (heptapeptide). `neuropsychiatric` applied as a property, not a harm claim: GABA-A modulation, BDNF upregulation and documented anxiolytic/cognitive CNS action are exactly what the tag covers, and it should drive a co-sedative/benzodiazepine caution. `serotonergic` applied on the entry's own stated mechanism (affects serotonin and dopamine metabolism) plus rodent 5-HT turnover data; there are no clinical serotonin-syndrome reports, so this is a precautionary tag to gate SSRI/SNRI/MAOI co-use — applied under the false-positive-preferred rule. Deliberately NOT tagged immunosuppressive: tuftsin analogues are immunostimulant, and the vocabulary has no tag for that direction (v2 candidate). No hepatic, renal, cardiac or endocrine signal at 250-1500mcg intranasal/SubQ. dea null — not scheduled in the US at any level. STORE: approved in Russia for anxiety/asthenic conditions but an unapproved drug in the US/EU, and the record ships a four-row dose protocol including a 750-1500mcg/day nootropic regimen. That is a protocol table for an unapproved substance, which is what Play policy treats as promotion irrespective of legality. Reframe as neutral reference — mechanism, evidence base, Russian approval status — with the dose rows removed.

sema.notes: Structural: acylated 31-amino-acid GLP-1 analogue, so peptide and glp1 both apply. insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue applies on the vocabulary's own wording ('drives insulin action/secretion directly') — semaglutide directly stimulates beta-cell insulin secretion, glucose-dependently. hypoglycemic is paired with it deliberately: monotherapy hypoglycaemia risk is low precisely because secretion is glucose-dependent, but the labelled and clinically important risk is potentiation when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea, and that combination rule is exactly what these two tags should fire. gastric-emptying-delaying is explicit in the summary and is also the mechanism behind the anaesthesia/aspiration precaution now in practice guidance. teratogenic is verified against the current label: embryofetal mortality, structural abnormalities and growth alterations in rats at exposures below the maximum recommended human dose; discontinue when pregnancy is recognised and stop at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy because of the long half-life. Deliberate negatives worth recording. NOT cardiotoxic — the SELECT trial showed cardiovascular risk reduction, so the tag would invert the evidence; the only cardiac finding is a small heart-rate increase of a few bpm. NOT nephrotoxic — the label does warn of acute kidney injury from volume depletion during titration vomiting and diarrhoea, and I considered the tag for that, but FLOW establishes semaglutide as net renoprotective and tagging an approved renoprotective drug as nephrotoxic would mislead rather than caution; the dehydration-AKI warning belongs in the entry text instead. NOT absorption-sensitive as recorded, because this record is the weekly subcutaneous form (medium 'aq', mg/week dosing) — but flag for the entry author that ORAL semaglutide (Rybelsus) is extremely absorption-sensitive, requiring fasting administration with no more than 120mL water and a 30-minute wait, so if an oral variant is ever added it must carry that tag. Two things the vocabulary cannot express and that the entry text should carry: the boxed warning for rodent thyroid C-cell tumours with contraindication in personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2, and the pancreatitis and gallbladder-disease warnings. Store: ok — FDA-approved drug, entry describes the approved indication and dosing (0.25 titration to 2.4mg/week Wegovy) with no performance framing, which the platform rules explicitly permit. The 'muscle mass loss without resistance training' con is accurate and fine to keep.

semax.notes: ACTH(4-7)-PGP analogue. `neuropsychiatric` is well supported by the record's own cons: stimulant-like effect, anxiety at high doses, vivid dreams, sleep changes — plus the monitoring line already tracks mood and sleep. `serotonergic` applied at lower confidence than for Selank: the best-documented actions are BDNF/NGF upregulation and dopaminergic/enkephalinergic modulation, with serotonergic effects reported mainly in rodent neurochemistry. Applied anyway per the apply-when-uncertain rule so the SSRI/stimulant interaction rule fires; flagging the weaker evidence here explicitly. Important negative: although it is an ACTH fragment analogue, Semax is devoid of corticotropic activity and does not raise cortisol, so no adrenal/immunosuppressive tagging is warranted — worth stating in the entry text because readers assume otherwise from the ACTH lineage. dea null. STORE: same posture as Selank — Russian-approved, US-unapproved, and the record carries five dose rows up to 1800mcg. Reframe to reference with the dose protocol removed; also drop or heavily qualify 'No significant side effects reported in clinical literature', which conflicts with the stimulant/anxiety cons in the same record.

serm2.notes: Only two tags, and I believe that is correct rather than a miss: sermorelin is GHRH(1-29) acting inside intact pituitary negative feedback, at 200-300mcg it does not push IGF-1 out of range, and the classic GH-axis harms (oedema, carpal tunnel, insulin resistance, CHF) are not clinically meaningful at documented doses. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: GH-axis agents impair insulin sensitivity and RAISE fasting glucose — the vocabulary only has `hypoglycemic`, which is the wrong direction, so this property is untaggable for the whole GH-secretagogue class (sermorelin, tesamorelin, MK-677). It is why the record's monitoring line says fasting glucose, and it should get a `hyperglycemic` / `insulin-resistance-inducing` tag in v2. Also untagged: theoretical concern about stimulating occult malignancy via IGF-1, and the contraindication in active malignancy. store=reframe: sermorelin WAS FDA-approved (Geref/Geref Diagnostic, 1997) and was withdrawn in 2008 for commercial not safety reasons; it sits in an ambiguous 503A compounding position today (not on FDA's significant-safety-risk bulks category, but also not a component of any currently approved product). That legitimate clinical pedigree plus real research literature argues against exclude, but the entry is written for anti-ageing/body-composition use and carries an explicit stack row ('With GHRP: Sermorelin 200mcg + Ipamorelin 200mcg') pairing it with an unapproved GHRP — that row must go and the indication restated as supervised evaluation/treatment of GH deficiency before it ships.

sigumir.notes: Khavinson cartilage/bone bioregulator. No risk tags warranted — no human toxicology, no organ burden at 10mg/day, and the claimed action (proteoglycan/collagen synthesis in chondrocytes) has no systemic risk correlate. DATA ERROR, and a notable one: the record gives Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly (AEDG), which is Epithalon's sequence, not Sigumir's — published Sigumir is the tripeptide Ala-Glu-Asp (AED). Two entries in this batch therefore claim the same molecule; correct before any store build. dea null; aa null. STORE reframe: longevity/joint framing rather than performance, so not exclude, but the entry ties itself to 'TRT patients experiencing joint issues (common with high-dose testosterone)' — that phrase both assumes supraphysiologic androgen use and positions this as an adjunct to it, and must go. Remove the dose row and the BPC-157/TB-500 stack comparison, which chains one unapproved peptide to two others.

slupp332.notes: No structural tag in the vocabulary fits. It is a pan-agonist of the estrogen-RELATED receptors (ERRalpha/beta/gamma), which are orphan nuclear receptors that do NOT bind estradiol and are not the estrogen receptor — so serm is wrong, aromatase-inhibitor is wrong, and it is a small molecule, not a peptide or a SARM. Vocabulary gap: there is no 'metabolic/exercise-mimetic' or 'nuclear-receptor-agonist' tag; recording for v2. hepatotoxic and cardiotoxic APPLIED as deliberate precautionary tags under the stated asymmetry rule, not as established effects. Justification (checked by search): the published reviews of this class flag off-target hepatotoxicity and cardiac hypertrophy as the priority safety questions, and the cardiac work (Circulation 2023, pressure-overload HF models) found the pan-ERR agonists improved ejection fraction and fibrosis but did NOT prevent cardiomyocyte hypertrophy — i.e. the hypertrophy question is open, not answered reassuringly. ERRalpha/gamma are most highly expressed in heart and liver, which is why those are the two organs of concern. Any downstream rule should present these as 'unknown, flagged in preclinical literature', not as measured human toxicity — there is zero human data of any kind. dea null: not scheduled, and not an analogue of anything scheduled. store=exclude: no approval anywhere, no clinical trial, no compounding pathway, no established human dose (the entry's own dose row says so), and the entire documented use case in this entry is pharmacological fat loss and endurance enhancement. This fails Google Play's prohibition on promoting unapproved substances and has no legitimate-use frame to reframe toward.

spermidine.notes: Naturally occurring polyamine (wheat germ, soy, mushrooms, aged cheese), taken at 1-5mg/day, occasionally to 10mg — a range that is at or only modestly above ordinary dietary intake, which is the key fact for tagging. Empty tag array is deliberate, not an oversight: I worked through the full vocabulary and no section A structural class fits (not a peptide in the pharmacological sense the tag denotes — it is a small aliphatic polyamine, not an amino-acid chain), no section B risk tag is supported at these doses (no hepatic, renal, cardiac, pressor, glycaemic, haematological, endocrine or CNS signal; it is well tolerated, food-derived, and the entry's cons are all about cost, sourcing and evidence quality rather than harm), and no section C interaction mechanism is established — spermidine is handled by polyamine catabolism (spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferase, polyamine oxidase), not CYP, and does not meaningfully alter its own or other drugs' absorption. Applying a tag here purely to avoid an empty array would be a false positive with no rule behind it, which the asymmetry rule does not ask for. Two things recorded that v1 cannot express: (1) intracellular polyamines are required for cell proliferation and elevated polyamine levels are associated with tumour growth — the counterpart to the missing proliferative/oncogenic tag I flagged on TB-500 and BPC-157; the human epidemiology on dietary spermidine is favourable (inverse association with cardiovascular and all-cause mortality) and supplementation trials have been benign, so I judged this theoretical rather than clinically meaningful at 1-10mg/day, but the same v2 tag would let this nuance be stored rather than lost; (2) the entry's claim of synergy with fasting and rapamycin is a mechanistic autophagy claim with no human data, and there is no tag for mTOR/autophagy modulation. STORE ok: dietary constituent sold as a supplement, honest evidence framing, doses in the dietary range. Note the record carries duplicated pros/cons and four overlapping dose rows that look like a merge artefact and should be de-duplicated. Not scheduled; anabolic ratio not applicable.

ss31.notes: Mitochondria-targeted tetrapeptide binding cardiolipin; no endocrine, hepatic, haematologic or cardiovascular risk tags are warranted — trial adverse events are dominated by injection-site reactions. It is cardioprotective in intent, so cardiotoxic is affirmatively wrong. REGULATORY STATUS IS OUT OF DATE IN THIS ENTRY: the record says 'Clinical trials ongoing — not FDA approved', but elamipretide received FDA accelerated approval in September 2025 as FORZINITY (elamipretide HCl) for muscle weakness in Barth syndrome, patients 30kg and above — the first approved mitochondria-targeted drug. The entry text should be corrected regardless of the store decision. Store is reframe rather than ok precisely because approval does not rescue this entry: the approved indication is an ultra-rare genetic disease, while the documented doses here are 'Longevity and Mitochondrial: 5-10mg' and 'Performance: 3-5mg pre-training'. Performance dosing of a newly approved orphan drug is off-label promotion; rewrite to the Barth syndrome indication and drop the performance and longevity rows. Note also that the 'Clinical trial dose: 4mg/kg IV' row is an order of magnitude above the other rows and looks like a data error worth checking — TAZPOWER used 40mg/day subcutaneous, not 4mg/kg.

stanozolol.notes: DHT-derived pyrazole-fused 17a-alkylated steroid — aas + 17aa-oral + dht-derived all mandatory. hepatotoxic is the headline: stanozolol is among the most hepatotoxic orals in use, with cholestasis and peliosis hepatis on record, and the entry documents 25-50mg/day with fortnightly LFTs. lipid-suppressing is applied at maximum clinical weight, not as a formality — stanozolol produces some of the most severe HDL suppression of any AAS (falls of 30-50%+ are typical), which is the mechanism behind cardiotoxic here: accelerated atherogenic risk plus the AAS-typical LV hypertrophy, on top of bp-raising (the entry monitors BP). hpta-suppressive per the entry ('strongly suppresses testosterone'). hematocrit-raising as an androgen class effect. virilizing/teratogenic: stanozolol is strongly virilizing in women even at low dose, and androgen exposure in pregnancy causes established female-fetus virilization. neuropsychiatric: mood lability, irritability and aggression are consistently reported with high-dose 17aa androgens; applied under the asymmetry rule even though this entry's con list emphasises joint pain instead. warfarin-potentiating: this is not class inference for stanozolol, it is the textbook interaction — 17a-alkylated androgens markedly potentiate warfarin (stanozolol and oxandrolone are the classic offenders, often requiring large dose reductions), and its legitimate medical history in hereditary angioedema is precisely the population where this was characterised. High-value rule. NOT applied but flagged: nephrotoxic — AAS-associated FSGS is documented in the abuse literature, but it is not stanozolol-specific and this entry does not monitor renal function; recorded as a residual uncertainty. Also not expressible in v1: the severe tendon/joint desiccation and tendon-rupture risk, which is stanozolol's most distinctive practical harm — v2 candidate. aa = [320, 30], the conventionally cited rodent figure, not a measured human ratio. dea = 3. Store = exclude.

sustanon.notes: Blend of testosterone propionate/phenylpropionate/isocaproate/decanoate; pharmacologically it is testosterone, so aa [100,100] and the same risk set as any testosterone ester. Not 17aa, not 19-nor, not DHT-derived. Tag set is driven by the PERFORMANCE row (250-500mg/week), not the TRT row: at 125-250mg/week most of these are mild-to-absent, at 500mg/week hematocrit-raising, lipid-suppressing, bp-raising and cardiotoxic are all clinically meaningful. The entry documents both, so the tags follow the higher dose per the stated rule. warfarin-potentiating is a labelled testosterone interaction (anticoagulant dose adjustment warning). teratogenic on fetal virilization plus the risk of secondary virilization by skin/needle-free transfer is not relevant here (injectable). NOT TAGGED but recorded: Sustanon's vehicle is arachis (peanut) oil with benzyl alcohol — a genuine contraindication in peanut/soya allergy that the vocabulary has no tag for. store=reframe, and this is the one AAS in the batch that gets it: testosterone replacement for diagnosed male hypogonadism is a legitimate, supervised, approved indication and Sustanon 250 is an approved product in the UK/EU/AU. To ship, the entry must lose the 'Performance: 250-500mg/week' row, lose the cycle/PCT framing, and state the indication as physician-supervised replacement for confirmed hypogonadism. CAVEAT: Sustanon specifically is NOT FDA-approved in the US — if the store build is US-targeted and reviewers check approval status, this should drop to exclude, or the entry should be rebuilt around testosterone cypionate/enanthate instead, which are US-approved.

t3.notes: 'cardiotoxic' at the documented doses: 50-75mcg/day of liothyronine in someone who is not hypothyroid is frank exogenous thyrotoxicosis — atrial fibrillation, tachyarrhythmia, increased myocardial oxygen demand and angina in anyone with coronary disease. The entry's own con list concedes cardiac risk at supraphysiological doses; the app documents those doses, so the tag qualifies. 'bp-raising' for the tachycardia/widened pulse pressure/systolic rise of thyroid excess (the monitoring row already tracks resting heart rate and BP). 'neuropsychiatric' — anxiety, irritability, insomnia, tremor; also a mania/agitation risk in susceptible people. 'warfarin-potentiating' — thyroid hormone accelerates vitamin-K-dependent clotting factor catabolism, so starting or raising T3 in a warfarinised patient raises INR and bleeding risk; this is a label-level interaction and one of the most clinically actionable items in this record. 'absorption-sensitive' — separated dosing is required from calcium, iron, bile-acid sequestrants, sucralfate and PPIs; the entry only mentions this under T4 but it applies to T3 too. NOT 'qt-prolonging': thyroid hormone excess SHORTENS the QT interval — the arrhythmia risk is atrial and rate-driven, and tagging QT here would fire the wrong rule (hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism, prolongs QT). NOT 'sympathomimetic': T3 sensitises tissue to catecholamines and the clinical picture is adrenergic, but the tag is defined as beta-agonist or CNS stimulant and T3 is neither — the additive-adrenergic risk with clenbuterol/stimulants is real and should be captured in the interaction text instead. NOT 'electrolyte-disturbing' (thyrotoxic hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is real but rare and demographically narrow). Long-term bone density loss and TSH suppression have no v1 tag; both are in the entry and must survive any rewrite. STORE: FDA-approved as Cytomel and legitimately prescribed for hypothyroidism and T4/T3 combination therapy, so it ships — but the row 'Optimization: 50-75mcg/day', 'Enhances fat loss by increasing basal metabolic rate' and 'TSH will suppress — this is expected' describe deliberate supraphysiologic dosing of a prescription hormone in euthyroid people for body composition. That is weight-loss/performance framing of an Rx drug and must be removed; restate as physician-supervised treatment of diagnosed hypothyroidism titrated to a normal range.

t4.notes: 'absorption-sensitive' is the primary practical tag and is unusually strong for this compound: levothyroxine absorption is reduced by food, coffee, calcium, iron, magnesium, bile-acid sequestrants, sucralfate, PPIs and soy, and brand/generic switches shift bioavailability — the entry lists this itself. 'warfarin-potentiating' as for T3 (accelerated clotting factor turnover; INR rises on dose increases). 'cardiotoxic' and 'neuropsychiatric' applied on the over-replacement scenario rather than on replacement itself — the label's boxed warning is specifically that thyroid hormone must not be used for obesity/weight loss because large doses produce serious or life-threatening toxicity, and chronic over-replacement carries AF and bone-loss risk in older patients. Applied on the vocabulary's apply-when-uncertain rule. NOT 'bp-raising': unlike the T3 record, every documented dose row here (25-50 starting, 75-150 therapeutic mcg/day) is ordinary replacement, at which BP is not meaningfully raised — this is the deliberate difference in tagging between the T3 and T4 records and the reason they are not identical. STORE 'ok': FDA-approved, most-prescribed drug in the US, doses documented are the standard replacement range, indication stated is hypothyroidism. The 'poor converter / TSH-based dosing leaves patients symptomatic' framing is an active and legitimate clinical debate rather than promotional content, so no reframe is needed.

taurine.notes: Conditionally essential amino acid, OTC supplement, not scheduled. neuropsychiatric applied for the GABA-A/glycine-receptor modulation the entry itself markets (anxiolysis, sedation, sleep) at the documented 3-6 g/day — meaningful enough to stack additively with other sedatives; it is a benefit-side CNS effect rather than a harm, but the tag is defined by CNS activity, not valence. Deliberately NOT tagged bp-raising: taurine LOWERS blood pressure, and the vocabulary has no bp-lowering tag — the real interaction rule (additive hypotension with antihypertensives, per the entry's own monitoring text) cannot be expressed in v1 and should be a v2 candidate ('bp-lowering'). Also unexpressible: the lithium interaction in the cons list — taurine appears to reduce lithium clearance and raise lithium levels, so this compound and lithium-or in this same batch should carry a cross-reference. absorption-sensitive deliberately not applied: the lithium issue is taurine altering another drug, not taurine's own absorption. Mild insulin-sensitising effect noted in the entry was judged below the threshold for hypoglycemic.

tb5.notes: TB-500 is a synthetic fragment (the actin-binding LKKTETQ region) of thymosin beta-4; peptide is the only structural tag that applies. No risk tag clears the bar at 2-2.5mg once or twice weekly — no meaningful human toxicity signal exists. The important gap is the entry's own con, 'some cancer concern in animal studies': TB4 upregulates angiogenesis and cell migration, which is exactly the mechanism that raises a theoretical tumour-promotion question, and the vocabulary has no oncogenic-risk tag to carry it. That is the single most safety-relevant fact about this compound and it currently cannot be tagged — strong candidate for v2. Also untaggable: WADA-prohibited (S2, growth factors). dea=null, not federally scheduled. aa=null, not an AAS or SARM. store=reframe: unlike a pure performance peptide, thymosin beta-4 has a genuine clinical-research literature — RGN-259 reached late-phase trials for neurotrophic keratopathy and dry eye — so neutral reference framing is defensible. Requires rewriting: the 'Loading / Maintenance' schedule reads as a use protocol, and 'strong synergy with BPC-157' is stack language that must go. The animal cancer signal should be stated in the body text, not buried in a cons list.

tbnouveau.notes: TB-500 is the synthetic actin-binding fragment (Ac-LKKTETQ region) of thymosin beta-4, not full-length TB4 — the record's 'Thymosin Beta-4 systemic' aka blurs the two, which is worth fixing in the entry. Only one tag applies, and that is a vocabulary limitation rather than a clean safety profile: the dominant documented concern is the one the entry itself raises — angiogenesis, actin polymerisation and cell-migration promotion driving a theoretical tumour-growth/metastasis risk in animal models — and there is NO tag in v1 for proliferative or oncogenic risk. This is the clearest gap the batch exposes; a 'proliferative-risk'/'oncogenic-concern' tag is needed, because for TB-500 the app's own monitoring text ('given theoretical cancer concern, periodic comprehensive health screening') is currently unbacked by any structured field. Explicitly considered and rejected: immunosuppressive (TB4 is immunomodulatory/anti-inflammatory and wound-healing directed, not immunosuppressive in the sense the tag warns about — that is thymosin ALPHA-1 territory and even there the direction is stimulatory), and cardiotoxic (the cardiac effect described is anti-fibrotic protection, not injury). No hepatic, renal, pressor, lipid, glycaemic or endocrine signal at 2.5mg/week. STORE reframe: no approval anywhere, on FDA's Category 2 bulks list, and WADA-prohibited (S2) with a long doping history in both human and equine sport. Kept at reframe for consistency with BPC-157 — the framing is tissue repair rather than physique enhancement, and neutral reference text describing an unapproved peptide and its unresolved cancer signal can ship. The rewrite must remove all three dose rows (particularly the year-round 'systemic maintenance' framing, which is the highest-risk recommendation on the record given the proliferative concern), state the Category 2 status, and keep the oncogenic caveat prominent rather than in a cons bullet. Not scheduled; no anabolic ratio applies.

tc.notes: Structural: aas only — testosterone is the parent androgen, not 17a-alkylated (no 17aa-oral), not a 19-nor, and not a DHT derivative (it is the SUBSTRATE for 5a-reductase, not a product), so dht-derived is deliberately withheld. Deliberately NOT hepatotoxic: injectable esters bypass first-pass and carry no meaningful hepatic burden; the hepatotoxicity rule should fire on 17aa-oral, not on aas generally, and tagging this would dilute that signal. Risk tags are driven by the documented 300-500mg/week performance row, not the 100-150mg TRT row: at supraphysiologic dose HDL suppression is marked, hematocrit rise is the most common dose-limiting AE, and the Baggish LV-hypertrophy/reduced-EF literature in long-term supraphysiologic users justifies cardiotoxic beyond BP alone. bp-raising reflects both the fluid/hematocrit mechanism and the FDA-mandated hypertension warning now carried on testosterone labels. neuropsychiatric covers mood lability/aggression/insomnia at supraphysiologic dose. teratogenic = virilization of a female fetus; contraindicated in pregnancy. cyp3a4-substrate is solid — 6b-hydroxylation of testosterone is the canonical CYP3A4 probe reaction, so strong 3A4 inhibitors/inducers are a real interaction. warfarin-potentiating is a labeled androgen interaction (INR rise). Considered and rejected: qt-prolonging (androgens SHORTEN QTc), nephrotoxic, electrolyte-disturbing (sodium/water retention is real but not a clinically meaningful electrolyte derangement at these doses). aa = [100,100] by definition, the reference point of the conventional rodent assay scale, not a measured human ratio. store=reframe rather than exclude: this is an FDA-approved prescription drug with a mainstream approved indication (male hypogonadism), so it is not an 'unapproved substance' under the Play rule. But the entry as written is not shippable — the 'Performance: 300-500mg/week' row and the optimization framing must be removed and the indication restated as clinician-supervised TRT for diagnosed hypogonadism. Schedule III status means the store text must not read as encouragement to obtain or use it outside prescription.

te.notes: Pharmacologically identical to testosterone cypionate — same parent hormone, only the ester chain length differs (enanthate 7-carbon vs cypionate 8-carbon), giving ~7 vs ~8 day half-life. The ester is cleaved by serum esterases before the hormone reaches the receptor, so every tag rationale from the cypionate entry transfers unchanged and the two records must stay tag-identical or interaction rules will fire inconsistently depending on which ester a user logged. Not hepatotoxic (injectable, not 17aa). Not dht-derived (parent androgen). Documented 300-500mg/week performance row is what drives the risk tags. dea=3 as an AAS. aa=[100,100] by definition. store=reframe for the same reason as cypionate: approved prescription drug, legitimate hypogonadism indication, but the performance dose row and optimization framing must be stripped before it ships.

telmisartan.notes: FDA-approved ARB; the entry's 20-80mg/day rows are inside the approved label range, so there is no supraphysiologic escalation to account for here. teratogenic = the boxed warning: RAAS blockade in the 2nd/3rd trimester causes fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia and death; discontinue as soon as pregnancy is detected. electrolyte-disturbing = hyperkalaemia, amplified by K-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, trimethoprim and NSAIDs (the entry's own monitoring line already tracks potassium). nephrotoxic applied conservatively and against the compound's net effect: telmisartan is renoprotective long-term, but it causes functional/haemodynamic AKI in volume depletion, bilateral renal artery stenosis, or combined with NSAIDs + diuretics (the 'triple whammy'). This is reversible haemodynamic injury, not intrinsic tubular toxicity — flag it that way in any rule text. hypoglycemic applied on the uncertainty asymmetry rather than strong evidence: PPAR-gamma partial agonism plus the recognised ACEI/ARB class association with hypoglycaemia means it can potentiate insulin and sulfonylureas; it does not cause hypoglycaemia as monotherapy. DELIBERATELY NOT TAGGED, and each is a deliberate call: (1) bp-raising — it lowers BP; v1 has no bp-lowering tag, so telmisartan's real first-dose/volume-depleted hypotension risk is currently inexpressible and should be a v2 candidate. (2) hematocrit-raising — ARBs LOWER haematocrit (they are used for post-transplant erythrocytosis), which is precisely why the entry pairs it with TRT; do not let any rule infer the opposite. (3) No CYP tag: telmisartan is NOT meaningfully CYP450-metabolised — it is cleared by UGT1A3 glucuronidation and biliary excretion. Grapefruit/azole/CYP3A4 interaction rules must NOT fire on it, unlike most of the cardiovascular class. Two genuine interactions v1 cannot express: telmisartan inhibits P-gp and raises digoxin concentrations roughly 20-50%, and it raises lithium levels. store=ok: approved drug, approved indication, label doses, no cycle or stack language. The TRT reference is contextual (managing hypertension in a man on prescribed testosterone) and does not promote an unapproved substance.

tesam.notes: teratogenic is firm, not inferred: EGRIFTA is CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy on the label, and rat organogenesis studies showed hydrocephaly at ~2-4x clinical exposure and delayed skull ossification at 0.1-1x. bp-raising is my lowest-confidence tag here — applied under the stated asymmetry because GH-mediated sodium and water retention is a documented class effect and peripheral oedema is a common labelled adverse reaction at 2mg/day; hypertension is not itself a prominent labelled AE, so treat this as a soft flag. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB: the record's own con 'Can induce insulin resistance' is the dominant metabolic hazard and there is no tag for hyperglycaemia/insulin resistance (see sermorelin note) — this is the single biggest gap in v1 for this class. Also untagged: labelled contraindications for active malignancy and for disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, plus injection-site reactions and anti-tesamorelin antibody formation. store=reframe rather than ok despite full FDA approval, because the entry promotes off-label use directly in its dose table ('Off-label body composition: 1-2mg/day', 'Body Composition: 2mg/day') and its pros list leads with cognitive/NASH research. Ship it stating the approved indication (excess visceral abdominal fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy) at the approved 2mg/day, with the body-composition rows removed.

testpellets.notes: Testosterone as a crystalline SubQ implant (Testopel), FDA-approved, Schedule III under the Anabolic Steroids Act of 1990. aa is [100,100] by definition — testosterone is the reference compound for the ratio, not an assay result. Structural: aas yes; NOT 17aa-oral (implant, no first-pass alkylation, hence no hepatotoxic tag), NOT 19-nor, and NOT dht-derived — testosterone is the parent androgen that 5-alpha-reduces TO DHT, it is not itself DHT-derived, and that distinction matters because it is precisely why aromatizing applies here and does not apply to the drostanolone/stanozolol family. aromatizing and hpta-suppressive are definitional. hematocrit-raising is the single most likely real-world harm with pellets and the entry's own monitoring row calls for it. lipid-suppressing: the Testopel label lists increased serum cholesterol, and the documented male dose is supraphysiologic (see below), which is where HDL suppression becomes marked. bp-raising: not in the Testopel label specifically, but the modern testosterone class carries a blood-pressure warning (boxed on the oral undecanoates) and the effect is real — applied per the asymmetry rule. cardiotoxic: label lists myocardial infarction and stroke; TRAVERSE was non-inferior for MACE at replacement doses but showed excess atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism and acute kidney injury, and supraphysiologic exposure adds LVH risk. virilizing is not optional here and is arguably the highest-yield tag on this record: the entry documents a women's BHRT row of 75-225 mg, and pellets in women are the classic route for producing sustained supraphysiologic levels with irreversible virilization (voice deepening, clitoromegaly, alopecia) that cannot be stopped because the implant cannot be removed — the entry's own con, 'no ability to stop therapy immediately if side effects emerge', is exactly this. teratogenic: pregnancy category X, virilization of a female fetus. neuropsychiatric: label lists anxiety, depression, libido change, headache, paraesthesia; supraphysiologic dosing adds aggression and sleep disruption. electrolyte-disturbing is label-derived and not a judgement call — Testopel explicitly lists retention of sodium, chloride, water, potassium, calcium and inorganic phosphates. warfarin-potentiating is label-derived: androgens alter anticoagulant activity and the label directs INR monitoring. hypoglycemic is the softest tag in this list and I flag it as such — it rests on the androgen class statement that testosterone may decrease blood glucose and insulin requirements in diabetics; it is a potentiation rather than a direct hypoglycaemic action, and a reviewer may reasonably drop it, but it is applied under the asymmetry rule because it fires against insulin and sulfonylureas. cyp3a4-substrate applied on mechanism: testosterone 6-beta-hydroxylation is the canonical CYP3A4 probe reaction, so clearance via 3A4 is definitional — though for a depot implant the clinical significance of 3A4 inhibitors/inducers is much smaller than for oral androgens, and the rule text should say so. Considered and rejected: hepatotoxic (not alkylated, parenteral), prolactin-raising (that is the 19-nor rule, not testosterone), nephrotoxic (the TRAVERSE AKI signal is secondary and I judged it below threshold), qt-prolonging (androgens shorten rather than lengthen QTc). STORE = reframe, and the reason is dose, not legality: Testopel's approved dose is 150-450 mg every 3-6 months for androgen-deficient males, and this entry documents 600-1200 mg (8-16 pellets) for men — up to roughly 2.7x the top of the label — which is supraphysiologic clinic practice, not the approved indication. Combined with the overt commercial framing ('growing clinic revenue stream — high margin procedure'), the entry as written promotes above-label use of a Schedule III controlled substance and would not survive Play/Apple review. It ships only if the male dose row is corrected to the labelled 150-450 mg range, the revenue/marketing line is removed, the women's row is stated as off-label with the irreversibility-of-virilization warning attached, and the indication is stated as physician-diagnosed hypogonadism. Not exclude — this is an approved product with a legitimate supervised indication, so the reframe path is the correct one.

testsusp.notes: Unesterified testosterone in aqueous base — the reference androgen, so aa is [100,100] by definition rather than as a cited assay figure. Not 17aa, not 19-nor, not DHT-derived (it is the parent). aromatizing is primary: no ester means near-100% testosterone by weight and the peak-and-trough profile of 50-100mg boluses produces sharp estradiol spikes, so estrogenic effects are more pronounced per mg than with esterified testosterone. hematocrit-raising, lipid-suppressing, bp-raising and cardiotoxic all apply at the documented 50-100mg/day (roughly 350-700mg/week testosterone equivalent — squarely supraphysiologic, not replacement). neuropsychiatric applied for the mood/aggression/insomnia signal at these doses, amplified by the peaky kinetics. warfarin-potentiating is a labelled testosterone interaction. teratogenic on fetal virilization. NOT TAGGED but recorded: the aqueous suspension route carries its own risks the vocabulary cannot express — crystalline suspension injection site pain, sterile abscess, and a higher infection/injection-site reaction rate than oil vehicles, plus the daily/twice-daily frequency. store=exclude rather than reframe: unlike Sustanon there is no current approved aqueous testosterone product in the major markets, and every dose row here is explicitly performance-timing ('pre-workout', 'contest day'). There is no supervised medical use of this formulation to reframe toward.

thymalin.notes: Calf-thymus-derived polypeptide complex, not a defined single sequence. Deliberately NOT tagged immunosuppressive — the direction is opposite: it is claimed to restore thymic function and T-cell output, so tagging it immunosuppressive would be actively wrong. There is no 'immunostimulant' tag in the vocabulary, which is a genuine gap here, and it matters clinically: an immune-stimulating agent is the one to flag against autoimmune disease and against transplant immunosuppression, and no current tag can carry that. Recommend a v2 'immunostimulant' tag. Second gap: this is an animal-tissue-derived biological rather than a synthetic peptide, which carries hypersensitivity and batch-standardisation risk that no tag expresses — the entry's own cons acknowledge 'Polypeptide complex — harder to standardize'. Store: reframe. No Western approval, no performance framing, and a legitimate clinical literature including the frequently cited long-term mortality follow-up; ships only as neutral reference with the evidence quality and the Russian-only provenance stated plainly.

thymalpha.notes: peptide is definitional (28-aa thymic peptide). VOCABULARY GAP: Ta1 is an immune STIMULANT / modulator, and v1 only has immunosuppressive. I did not apply immunosuppressive - it would be actively wrong and could invert a rule. But the absence means a real interaction class is currently unrepresentable: T-cell/NK-activating agents warrant caution in autoimmune disease, in transplant recipients on immunosuppressants, and alongside checkpoint inhibitors. Requesting `immunostimulant` (or making the existing tag directional) for v2 - this is a genuine missing safety rule, not a cosmetic gap. No other v1 tag applies; Ta1 is well tolerated with essentially injection-site-level toxicity, so a sparse tag set here is correct. store=reframe, not ok and not exclude. It is approved as Zadaxin/thymalfasin in 35+ countries for chronic hepatitis B and C and as a vaccine/chemotherapy immune adjuvant, so there IS a real supervised indication to state - that is the reframe target. It cannot ship as written because: (1) the framing is longevity/biohacking 'immune optimization' in healthy people, which is not an approved use anywhere; (2) the dose row 'Active illness / Cancer adjuvant: 1.6mg' is a self-administered cancer-treatment protocol, which is the most serious health-claim problem in this batch and must be removed outright, not softened; (3) 'Synergistic with BPC-157' is stack language pointing at another unapproved peptide; (4) the parenthetical '(TB-500 is its partner)' appears to be an editing error conflating thymosin alpha-1 with thymosin beta-4 - different peptide, different mechanism - and needs correcting. US REGULATORY STATUS IS UNSETTLED, verify before shipping: FDA moved Ta1 into Category 2 of the interim 503A bulks list in Sept 2023 on safety grounds, then removed it in Sept 2024 after the nomination was withdrawn, with subsequent PCAC review; the entry's flat claim that US compounding-pharmacy sourcing is available may not be current.

tirz.notes: 39-aa synthetic dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist, so peptide + glp1 both apply. gastric-emptying-delaying is a core mechanism and is dose-dependent up to 15mg/wk. hypoglycemic applied even though the insulinotropic effect is glucose-dependent: real hypoglycaemia risk appears in combination with insulin or sulfonylureas, which is exactly the interaction a rule should catch. insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue applied on the literal reading of the vocabulary ('drives insulin action/secretion directly') — GIP/GLP-1 receptor engagement on beta cells is direct secretagogue action; flagging as a deliberate call since it overlaps `glp1` and could be judged redundant. teratogenic applied on labelled pregnancy guidance (discontinue on pregnancy; animal reproductive toxicity; weight loss is itself harmful in pregnancy) rather than proven human teratogenicity. NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN v1 VOCAB, for the v2 list: (a) boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumours / contraindicated in MTC and MEN2 — `thyroid-hormone` is the wrong tag (that means 'contains thyroid hormone') so this hazard is currently untagged; (b) tirzepatide reduces the efficacy of ORAL drugs including combined oral contraceptives via delayed emptying — `absorption-sensitive` is defined as its OWN absorption being altered, which is false for a SC peptide, so the outbound absorption interaction has no tag; (c) pancreatitis and gallbladder disease; (d) sarcopenic weight loss (the record's own con). Did not apply neuropsychiatric — the FDA/EMA reviews of the suicidal-ideation signal found no causal association. store=ok: FDA-approved (Mounjaro/Zepbound), entry is neutral clinical text and the dose rows match the label (2.5mg start, 15mg max).

tprop.notes: Testosterone with the short propionate ester — the reference compound, aa = [100, 100] by definition. Not 17aa, not 19-nor, not DHT-derived (it is the parent). aromatizing and hpta-suppressive are definitional. The risk tags are calibrated to the dose rows actually documented, per the vocabulary's own worked example: the entry lists 'Performance: 100mg EOD' = ~350mg/week, roughly 3-5x replacement, at which lipid-suppressing (HDL suppression), hematocrit-raising (the most common real-world reason a TRT patient needs intervention — the entry monitors it), bp-raising and cardiotoxic (LV hypertrophy and adverse remodelling at supraphysiologic exposure) are all clinically meaningful rather than theoretical. neuropsychiatric: mood elevation/irritability/aggression at supraphysiologic dose, plus the withdrawal dysphoria pattern. virilizing/teratogenic: virilization in women is dose-limiting and androgen exposure in pregnancy causes established female-fetus virilization; note the transdermal-style secondary-transfer concern does not apply to an injectable. warfarin-potentiating: labelled androgen interaction, increased INR/anticoagulant sensitivity — a genuine prescription-level rule, not inference. Store = reframe rather than exclude, and this is the deliberate exception to the 'Schedule III AAS -> exclude' default. Testosterone is an FDA-approved drug with a legitimate, supervised, approved indication (male hypogonadism) and prescribed TRT is the app's core lawful use case; excluding testosterone entirely would gut the reference for the population it legitimately serves, and the platform rules exempt approved drugs used for their approved indication. To ship it must lose the 'Performance: 100mg EOD' row, keep only the replacement-range row, state hypogonadism diagnosis and prescription supervision as the indication, and drop the 'identical anabolic profile' / ester-selection-for-cycling framing. Note the specific wrinkle that testosterone propionate itself is no longer a marketed US product (cypionate and enanthate are), so the reframed copy should reference the class approval honestly rather than implying this ester is separately available. dea = 3.

trenace.notes: Trenbolone with the acetate ester — aas + 19-nor mandatory. Deliberately NO aromatizing tag: trenbolone cannot be aromatized, which is why an AI is useless against tren-driven gynaecomastia; the estrogenic-appearing side effects are progestogenic, so prolactin-raising is tagged directly as well as via 19-nor. The entry monitors prolactin and its cons name progesterone-related effects. neuropsychiatric is applied at maximum weight and is arguably this compound's leading harm at the documented 75-100mg EOD: insomnia, night sweats, anxiety, aggression and mood destabilisation are near-universal rather than idiosyncratic, and the entry's own monitoring block asks for mental health and sleep. cardiotoxic and bp-raising: trenbolone produces the most severe HDL suppression of the injectables plus marked BP elevation and adverse cardiac remodelling; the entry monitors BP 'frequent' and notes 'HDL crashes'. nephrotoxic: applied on the entry's own kidney-function monitoring and the documented renal stress/reduced-eGFR pattern in trenbolone users. hepatotoxic: applied despite trenbolone not being 17-alkylated — this is a deliberate exception to the usual 'injectable therefore not hepatotoxic' reasoning, as trenbolone-associated cholestatic hepatic injury is reported at the high doses documented here; moderate confidence, recorded as such. hpta-suppressive at maximum weight (near-total, slow recovery). hematocrit-raising: strong erythropoietic stimulus, and the entry monitors it. virilizing: extreme — trenbolone is effectively unusable in women. teratogenic per androgen class. assay-interfering: 19-nor steroid, cross-reactivity in testosterone immunoassays plausible by the same mechanism verified for nandrolone; specify LC-MS/MS. warfarin-potentiating: androgen class effect. aa = [500, 500], the conventionally cited rodent figure — poor human correlation as always, but unusually the anabolic and androgenic ratings are both ~5x testosterone, which is the honest summary of why this compound behaves as it does. dea = 3 (Schedule III; veterinary implant origin, never approved for human use). Store = exclude, unambiguously — the entry as written is a performance protocol for an unapproved Schedule III steroid.

trenenan.notes: Same molecule as trenace with a longer enanthate ester, so the pharmacological tag set is identical and intentionally so — all reasoning in the trenace note applies here unchanged: no aromatizing tag (progestogenic, not estrogenic, hence prolactin-raising direct as well as via 19-nor); neuropsychiatric and cardiotoxic weighted highest at the documented 300-400mg/week; hepatotoxic applied as the deliberate non-17aa exception at moderate confidence; nephrotoxic on the entry's own renal monitoring; assay-interfering by 19-nor cross-reactivity in testosterone immunoassays. The one clinically meaningful difference the tags cannot express is a risk MULTIPLIER rather than a new risk: the ~110h half-life documented here means that once the severe neuropsychiatric or cardiovascular effects appear, they cannot be withdrawn quickly — the entry concedes 'longer to clear if sides become severe'. Where a protocol tool weights the same tag by reversibility, the enanthate ester should score worse than the acetate on neuropsychiatric, cardiotoxic and bp-raising for that reason alone. Flag for v2: v1 has no way to encode 'slow to reverse'. aa = [500, 500], conventionally cited rodent figure, not a measured human ratio. dea = 3. Store = exclude.

turinabol.notes: 4-chloro-17alpha-methyl-delta1-testosterone — a chlorinated methandrostenolone analogue, so testosterone-derived, NOT DHT-derived and NOT a 19-nor. No aromatizing tag: the 4-chloro substitution blocks aromatase, which is correct as the entry states. 17aa-oral applied — hepatotoxicity is genuine even though milder than oxymetholone. lipid-suppressing is the standout risk here: turinabol is notably harsh on HDL relative to its mild anabolic showing, and the documented 40-60mg/day is well above any historical clinical dose. The cited a:a of 54:6 is the conventionally quoted rodent assay figure and badly understates real-world potency — the near-zero androgenic number should not be read as 'no virilization risk', so virilizing is tagged regardless of the ratio. warfarin-potentiating as a 17aa class effect. teratogenic on androgen fetal virilization. store=exclude: Schedule III, never approved anywhere as a current product (East German Jenapharm product long discontinued), documented use is entirely performance and doping.

urolithin.notes: Gut-microbiome-derived ellagitannin metabolite sold as a supplement (Mitopure has FDA GRAS notification and is the material used in the Nature Aging RCT); not scheduled. No v1 tag applies — this is a genuinely clean record, not an incomplete one. Human trial data at 500-1000 mg/day report tolerability comparable to placebo with no signal on liver enzymes, lipids, blood pressure, glucose or CNS. Nothing in the mechanism (PINK1/Parkin mitophagy induction) maps to a v1 risk tag, and mitophagy induction itself has no vocabulary slot. Duplicate/near-duplicate rows are present in the source record (both pros and cons repeat, and the four dose rows collapse to 500 mg standard / 1000 mg therapeutic) — worth a data-hygiene pass, but it does not change the tagging. Store ok: commercially available supplement, described at label doses, no performance-enhancement or cycle framing.

ventfort.notes: Khavinson vascular bioregulator (Lys-Glu-Asp per most sources; some list HAEE — sequence attribution across this series is unreliable). No risk tags: claims are endothelial-function and vascular-tone normalisation, and there is no human evidence that it meaningfully raises or lowers blood pressure, so `bp-raising` would be a fabrication rather than a precaution. No hepatic/renal/endocrine signal at 10mg/day. dea null; aa null. STORE reframe, and this one needs more rewriting than the rest of the group: the summary explicitly positions it as a complement to 'cardiovascular TRT management' and the pros list synergy with Cardiogen. That is adjunct-to-anabolic-therapy stacking language attached to an unapproved injectable — remove the TRT tie-in, remove the stack pairing, drop the dose row, and state the evidence base as single-group Russian research.

vilon.notes: Khavinson dipeptide Lys-Glu. No risk tags — no documented toxicity signal at 1-2mg, and the claimed mechanism (chromatin-level regulation of gene expression) is too poorly characterised to support any specific risk tag rather than a general one. Same gap as Thymalin: the claimed effect is T-lymphocyte differentiation and immune restoration, i.e. immunostimulant, which the vocabulary cannot express and which is the property an autoimmune-disease rule would need. I did not apply immunosuppressive — wrong direction. Store: reframe on the same basis as the other Khavinson peptides — unapproved, no performance framing, thin but non-performance research base. The entry's cons are unusually honest about the evidence ('Extremely limited Western data', 'Broad mechanism not fully characterized'), so the rewrite is mostly a framing change rather than a content change.

vip.notes: 28-amino-acid neuropeptide, so peptide is structural and unambiguous. immunosuppressive applied on the asymmetry rule and on mechanism: VIP is one of the most potent endogenous anti-inflammatory mediators known — it shifts Th1 to Th2, induces regulatory T cells, downregulates macrophage activation and suppresses a broad panel of pro-inflammatory cytokines (the entry's own '50+ inflammatory mediators' claim IS an immunosuppression claim). Anything that potent on innate and adaptive signalling should carry an infection-risk caution, particularly stacked with rapamycin, which is in this same batch. electrolyte-disturbing is the non-obvious one and I am confident in it: the defining clinical syndrome of VIP excess is VIPoma / pancreatic cholera / WDHA — Watery Diarrhoea, Hypokalaemia, Achlorhydria. Pharmacologic VIP drives intestinal secretion and potassium loss by exactly that mechanism, so a potassium caution is warranted at the SubQ doses documented, less so intranasally. UNCERTAINTY RECORDED: I did not tag gastric-emptying-delaying despite the asymmetry rule, because VIP's two GI actions point in opposite directions — it mediates fundic receptive relaxation (would delay emptying) but drives secretory diarrhoea and accelerated transit (would not). A tag either way risks being actively wrong, so this is a v2 question. Also not tagged: hypotension and flushing from vasodilation are real at higher doses and are inexpressible in v1 (no bp-lowering tag) — same gap as telmisartan. store=reframe, not exclude: VIP is not a performance compound in any sense, the synthetic analogue aviptadil is an approved drug in some EU markets for erectile dysfunction and has been through serious COVID-ARDS trials, and there is a real clinical-research literature. But the entry as written is a self-administration protocol for a compounded, non-FDA-approved product built around the Shoemaker CIRS framework, which is a contested diagnostic model. To ship: state the investigational status plainly, drop the standing 4x/day self-dosing table, and frame CIRS/MCAS use as physician-directed.

yk11.notes: Structure checked rather than assumed, and the common description is wrong. YK-11 is (17a,20E)-17,20-[(1-methoxyethylidene)bis(oxy)]-3-oxo-19-norpregna-4,20-diene-21-carboxylic acid methyl ester — a 19-NORPREGNANE with a D4-3-one A-ring, structurally in gestrinone/19-norprogesterone territory. Consequences: (1) dht-derived is NOT applied despite the near-universal community claim that YK-11 is 'derived from DHT' — the A-ring is unsaturated, not 5a-reduced; (2) 17aa-oral is NOT applied — position 17a carries an oxygen in the methoxyethylidene bridge, not a 17a-alkyl group, so this compound is not a 17-alkylated oral. That is a deliberate departure from the blanket structural rule and I want it visible: the hepatotoxicity here is empirical (reported hepatotoxicity, monthly LFTs in the entry's own monitoring) rather than 17-alkylation-driven, so hepatotoxic is tagged on its own merits. (3) 19-nor IS applied, with a caveat: v1 defines it as '19-nortestosterone derivative' and this is a 19-norpregnane, so it is off-definition, but the tag drives the prolactin/progestogenic rule and a gestrinone-scaffold steroid is exactly the case where that caution should fire. Recommend v2 either widen the 19-nor definition or add a separate progestogenic tag. Tagged both sarm and aas: it is marketed and behaves as a SARM (partial AR agonist plus myostatin/follistatin effect) but it is literally a steroid, and the aas tag is what drives the androgenic risk rules. hpta-suppressive, lipid-suppressing, hematocrit-raising all follow from AR agonism at 10-15mg/day and match the entry's own monitoring list (testosterone, LH/FSH, lipids, hematocrit); virilizing and teratogenic follow from AR agonism in women/female fetuses. warfarin-potentiating is class inference from androgens generally — no YK-11-specific data exists. dea = null: SARMs are not federally scheduled, and the SARMs Control Act has not passed. However, flag for legal review that YK-11 is an unambiguous steroid that promotes muscle growth, so it arguably falls inside the statutory Anabolic Steroid Control Act definition even though DEA has never listed it by name — 'null' here means 'not explicitly scheduled', not 'confirmed lawful'. Store = exclude: unapproved, zero human trials, entry explicitly frames cycles and PCT.
